Effect of doubling one mass: m₁→2m₁. F = G×2m₁×m₂/r² = 2F_original. Force doubles.
Earth and Moon: The gravitational force between Earth and Moon causes the Moon to orbit Earth and also causes ocean tides on Earth.
Weight on Moon: 60kg person weighs 60×9.8=588N on Earth. On Moon (g≈1.63 m/s²): 60×1.63≈98N — about 1/6.
Cavendish experiment: Two small balls placed near two large balls. Tiny gravitational attraction between them twisted a suspended rod — allowed G to be calculated.
grav-2.summary: Newton's Law of Gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Every mass attracts every other mass. G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ Nm²/kg² universally. Force is proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of distance. Doubling distance reduces force to 1/4. Gravity is always attractive. Mass is constant; weight (=mg) varies with location. This law explains planetary orbits, tides, satellite motion, and free fall.

ce-1.title: Electric Current, Ohm's Law and Electrical Resistance
ce-1.notes:
Electric current, Ohm's Law, and resistance are the three foundational concepts of current electricity. Together they form the basis for understanding every electrical circuit from a simple torch to a complex computer. This is part of Current Electricity (15 marks) in NEA Paper III.

ELECTRIC CURRENT. Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor. Mathematically: I = Q/t, where I is current in Amperes (A), Q is charge in Coulombs (C), and t is time in seconds (s).

1 Ampere = 1 Coulomb per second. This means if 1 Coulomb of charge passes through a cross-section of a wire every second, the current is 1 Ampere.

Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a battery through the external circuit. Electrons (which are negatively charged) actually flow in the opposite direction — from negative to positive. The conventional direction was established before electrons were discovered, and it is still used today.

DRIFT VELOCITY. Inside a conductor, electrons move randomly in all directions at high speeds (about 10⁶ m/s). When an electric field is applied (by connecting a battery), the electrons acquire a small net drift velocity in the direction opposite to the field (towards the positive terminal). This drift velocity is very small — typically around 0.1 mm/s to 1 mm/s. The current we measure is due to this slow drift, not the random thermal motion.

OHM'S LAW. At constant temperature, the current (I) flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference (V) across it. Mathematically: V ∝ I, or V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor.

This can be rearranged as: I = V/R (current = voltage / resistance), or R = V/I (resistance = voltage / current).

Ohm's Law applies only to ohmic conductors — those that maintain a constant resistance regardless of voltage. Examples: copper wire, nichrome wire, carbon resistors at constant temperature. Non-ohmic conductors (like diodes, bulb filaments at varying temperatures, thermistors) do not follow Ohm's Law — their V-I graph is not a straight line.

RESISTANCE. Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric current through it. SI unit: Ohm (Ω). 1 Ohm = 1 Volt per Ampere.

Resistance of a conductor depends on:
(a) Length (L): R ∝ L — longer wire, higher resistance.
(b) Cross-sectional Area (A): R ∝ 1/A — thicker wire, lower resistance.
(c) Material (ρ — resistivity): depends on the nature of the material.
(d) Temperature: resistance increases with temperature for metals.

Combining these: R = ρL/A, where ρ (rho) is the resistivity of the material.

RESISTIVITY (ρ). Resistivity is a material property that measures how strongly a material opposes electrical flow. Unit: Ohm-metre (Ω·m). Good conductors like copper have very low resistivity (~1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m). Insulators like rubber have very high resistivity (~10¹³ Ω·m). Semiconductors like silicon lie in between.

EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE ON RESISTANCE. For metals: as temperature increases, atoms vibrate more, causing more collisions with moving electrons, increasing resistance. For semiconductors and insulators: resistance typically decreases with temperature (more electrons become available to conduct).
points: Current I = Q/t (Amperes). 1A = 1C per second.
Conventional current: + to - externally. Electron flow: - to + (opposite direction).
Drift velocity of electrons: very slow (~mm/s), but thermal speed is very fast (~10⁶ m/s).
Ohm's Law: V = IR. Valid only for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.
V-I graph: straight line through origin = ohmic conductor. Curved = non-ohmic.
Resistance R = ρL/A. Increases with length. Decreases with cross-sectional area.
Resistivity ρ: material property. Low for conductors, high for insulators.
Resistance increases with temperature for metals (more lattice vibrations).
Unit of resistance: Ohm (Ω). 1Ω = 1V/A.
SI unit of current: Ampere (A). Of voltage: Volt (V). Of resistance: Ohm (Ω).
examples: A charge of 90C passes through a wire in 30s. Current = Q/t = 90/30 = 3A.
Ohm's Law: A 12V battery connected to a 6Ω resistor. Current = V/R = 12/6 = 2A.
Resistance: Two wires of same material and same length. Wire A has twice the cross-sectional area of Wire B. R_A = ρL/(2A) = R_B/2. Wire A has half the resistance.
Wire stretched: A wire of resistance R is stretched to twice its length. Volume stays same, so area halves. R_new = ρ×2L/(A/2) = 4ρL/A = 4R. Resistance quadruples.
Non-ohmic: A diode allows current in only one direction. Its V-I graph is exponential, not a straight line — it does not follow Ohm's Law.
ce-1.summary: Electric current I = Q/t measures charge flow rate. Ohm's Law V = IR applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature. Resistance R = ρL/A depends on material, length, and area. Resistance increases with temperature for metals. Conductors have low resistivity; insulators have high resistivity. A straight-line V-I graph through the origin confirms an ohmic conductor. These fundamentals apply to all circuit analysis problems in the exam.

ce-3.title: Carbon Resistors, Colour Code, Series and Parallel Combinations
ce-3.notes:
This topic covers how to read resistor values from their colour code and how to calculate the combined resistance when multiple resistors are connected together. It is part of Current Electricity (15 marks) in NEA Paper III.

CARBON RESISTORS. Carbon resistors are small, low-cost resistors made from a mixture of carbon and binding material. They are the most common type of resistor used in electronic circuits. Their resistance value cannot be easily read by looking at them — instead, a colour code system is used.

COLOUR CODE FOR RESISTORS. The colour code consists of coloured bands painted around the resistor body. For a 4-band resistor (the most common type):
Band 1: First digit of resistance value.
Band 2: Second digit of resistance value.
Band 3: Multiplier (multiply the two-digit number by 10 to the power of this colour's value).
Band 4: Tolerance (how accurate the resistance is).

COLOUR CODE VALUES. The standard mnemonic to remember is: BB ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife — or simply: Black Brown Red Orange Yellow Green Blue Violet Grey White.
Black = 0
Brown = 1
Red = 2
Orange = 3
Yellow = 4
Green = 5
Blue = 6
Violet = 7
Grey = 8
White = 9

For the multiplier band: the value is 10 raised to the power of the digit. So Red (2) as multiplier = ×100.

TOLERANCE BAND:
Gold = ±5%
Silver = ±10%
No band = ±20%

EXAMPLE: A resistor has bands Brown, Black, Red, Gold.
Brown = 1, Black = 0, Red = ×100, Gold = ±5%.
Resistance = 10 × 100 = 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ ± 5%.

RESISTORS IN SERIES. When resistors are connected end-to-end in a single path, they are in series. Key properties:
The same current flows through all resistors.
The total voltage is shared across the resistors.
Total resistance: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ... (resistances simply add).
Total resistance is always greater than the largest individual resistance.

For two resistors of R₁ and R₂ in series: R_total = R₁ + R₂.
Voltage across each: V₁ = IR₁, V₂ = IR₂. Total V = V₁ + V₂ = IR_total.

RESISTORS IN PARALLEL. When resistors are connected between the same two points (sharing both terminals), they are in parallel. Key properties:
The same voltage appears across all resistors.
The total current is divided among the resistors.
Total resistance formula: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ...
Total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

For two resistors of R₁ and R₂ in parallel: R_total = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) (product over sum formula).
Current through each: I₁ = V/R₁, I₂ = V/R₂. Total I = I₁ + I₂.

For n identical resistors of resistance R in parallel: R_total = R/n.

APPLICATIONS IN EVERYDAY LIFE. Series connection: old string lights (if one bulb fails, all go out). Parallel connection: home electrical wiring (each appliance gets full mains voltage; if one fails, others continue working). This is why all household appliances are wired in parallel.
points: Colour code: Black=0, Brown=1, Red=2, Orange=3, Yellow=4, Green=5, Blue=6, Violet=7, Grey=8, White=9.
Mnemonic: BB ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife.
4 bands: digit-digit-multiplier-tolerance. Gold tolerance=±5%, Silver=±10%.
Series: same current, voltages add, R_total = R₁+R₂+... (always bigger than largest R).
Parallel: same voltage, currents add, 1/R_total = 1/R₁+1/R₂+... (always smaller than smallest R).
Two parallel resistors: R_total = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂).
n identical resistors in parallel: R_total = R/n.
Series connection: if one component fails, whole circuit breaks.
Parallel connection: used in home wiring — each appliance gets full voltage independently.
Total resistance in parallel is always LESS than the smallest individual resistance.
examples: Colour code: Yellow-Violet-Orange-Gold = 4,7,×1000,±5% = 47,000Ω = 47kΩ ±5%.
Series: 4Ω + 6Ω + 10Ω = 20Ω total. Battery 20V. Current = V/R = 20/20 = 1A through all three.
Parallel: 6Ω and 12Ω in parallel. R = 6×12/(6+12) = 72/18 = 4Ω. Less than 6Ω (smallest).
4 identical 20Ω resistors in parallel: R_total = 20/4 = 5Ω.
Home wiring: Three appliances of 1000W, 500W, 200W all connected at 220V — they share current but each gets 220V independently.
ce-3.summary: Carbon resistors use a colour code (BB ROY...) to indicate resistance value and tolerance. 4-band code: digit-digit-multiplier-tolerance. In series connection, resistances add (same current, voltages divide). In parallel, reciprocals add — total resistance is less than the smallest (same voltage, currents divide). Home wiring uses parallel so each appliance gets full voltage. Memorise the colour code mnemonic and practice both series and parallel calculations.

tv-5.title: Correct Usage of Prepositions
tv-5.notes:
A preposition is a word placed before a noun or pronoun to show its relationship with another word in the sentence. Prepositions indicate time, place, direction, manner, or cause.

PREPOSITIONS OF TIME:
'At' is used for specific clock times and fixed time points: at 6 AM, at noon, at midnight, at sunrise, at Christmas, at the moment.
'On' is used for specific days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August, on New Year's Day, on my birthday.
'In' is used for months, years, seasons, centuries, and longer periods: in January, in 2024, in winter, in the morning, in the 21st century.

PREPOSITIONS OF PLACE:
'At' for a specific point or location: at the station, at the door, at home, at school.
'In' for enclosed spaces, cities, countries: in the room, in Delhi, in India, in the box.
'On' for surfaces: on the table, on the wall, on the floor, on the ceiling.

PREPOSITIONS OF DIRECTION/MOVEMENT:
'To' for movement towards a destination: go to school, travel to Mumbai.
'Into' for movement entering an enclosed space: walk into the room.
'Onto' for movement to a surface: jump onto the stage.
'From' for point of origin: come from Delhi.
'Through' for movement inside and out: walk through the tunnel.

FIXED PREPOSITIONAL PHRASES (collocations):
Good at (skill): She is good at mathematics. NOT good in.
Interested in: He is interested in science.
Responsible for: She is responsible for the report.
Depend on / depend upon: You can depend on me.
Congratulate on: I congratulate you on your success.
Suffer from (illness): He suffers from fever.
Die of (disease): She died of cancer.
Die in (accident): He died in a road accident.
Married to (passive): She is married to him. NOT married with.
Listened to: always requires 'to'.
Look at (direct gaze), Look for (search), Look after (care), Look into (investigate).
Afraid of, proud of, ashamed of, tired of, fond of.
Angry with (person), angry at/about (situation).
Different from: His style is different from mine. NOT different than/to.
Similar to: This is similar to that.

COMMON ERRORS:
'He is good in English' ✗ → 'He is good at English' ✓
'She married with him' ✗ → 'She married him' OR 'She is married to him' ✓
'I am waiting since morning' ✗ → 'I have been waiting since morning' ✓
'He is suffering with fever' ✗ → 'He is suffering from fever' ✓
'Different than' ✗ (informal) → 'Different from' ✓
points: AT = specific time/point (at 6 PM, at home, at the station).
ON = days, dates, surfaces (on Monday, on the table).
IN = enclosed spaces, periods, months, years (in the room, in 2024).
TO = movement toward destination; INTO = entering enclosed space.
Good at (not in); Interested in; Responsible for; Depend on.
Suffer from (illness); Die of (disease); Die in (accident).
Married to (passive form); Listen to (always with 'to').
Different from (not than); Similar to; Afraid of; Proud of.
Angry with a person; angry at/about a situation.
Look at (see), Look for (search), Look after (care), Look into (investigate).
examples: The meeting is at 9 AM on Monday in December. (at=time, on=day, in=month)
She is good at science but interested in history.
He died of malaria but his brother died in a road accident.
The principal is responsible for discipline in the school.
I have been waiting for the bus since 8 o'clock.
tv-5.summary: Prepositions show time (at/on/in), place (at/in/on), and direction (to/into/from). Fixed collocations must be memorised: good at, interested in, responsible for, depend on, suffer from, die of, married to, different from. Common errors include using 'good in', 'married with', 'different than', and 'suffering with'. These collocations are directly tested in NEA.

questions.question: Which preposition correctly fills the blank: 'She is good ___ mathematics'?
questions.explanation: 'Good at' is the correct collocation for ability or skill. 'Good in' is a common error.

questions.question: The train arrives ___ 6 AM ___ Monday.
questions.explanation: 'At' is used for specific times; 'on' is used for days of the week.

questions.question: He has been suffering ___ malaria for two weeks.
questions.explanation: 'Suffer from' is the correct collocation for illness/disease.

questions.question: The keys are ___ the table.
questions.explanation: 'On' is used for surfaces. The table is a surface, so 'on the table' is correct.

questions.question: She is married ___ a naval officer.
questions.explanation: In passive construction, 'married to' is correct. 'Married with' is a common error.

questions.question: His approach is different ___ mine.
questions.explanation: 'Different from' is the standard British English usage. 'Different than' is informal/American.

questions.question: I will meet you ___ the bus stop ___ noon.
questions.explanation: 'At the bus stop' (specific point) and 'at noon' (specific time) — both use 'at'.

questions.question: He died ___ a heart attack.
questions.explanation: 'Die of' is used for diseases and medical conditions. 'Die from' can also be used but 'die of' is standard for illness.

questions.question: Please look ___ the matter immediately.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means to investigate. 'Look at' = observe; 'Look for' = search; 'Look after' = take care.

questions.question: She is interested ___ joining the Indian Navy.
questions.explanation: 'Interested in' is the fixed collocation. 'Interested for' and 'interested about' are incorrect.

questions.question: He is angry ___ his colleague for the mistake.
questions.explanation: 'Angry with' a person is correct. 'Angry at' is used for situations or things, not people.

questions.question: The soldiers are responsible ___ guarding the border.
questions.explanation: 'Responsible for' is the correct collocation. 'Responsible of' is always wrong.

questions.question: We were born ___ the same year ___ March.
questions.explanation: 'In' is used for years and months. Born in 1999, born in March.

questions.question: She congratulated me ___ passing the examination.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulate on' is the correct collocation — congratulate someone on an achievement.

questions.question: The soldier walked ___ the gate and ___ the building.
questions.explanation: 'Through' for passing from one side to another; 'into' for entering an enclosed space.

tv-6.title: Use of Conjunctions, Words and Their Usage
tv-6.notes:
A conjunction is a word that connects words, phrases, or clauses. Choosing the right conjunction determines the logical relationship between two ideas — contrast, cause, condition, addition, or result.

TYPES OF CONJUNCTIONS:

1. COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS (FANBOYS): Connect two independent clauses of equal weight.
For (because/reason): He was tired, for he had worked all day.
And (addition): She studied hard and passed the exam.
Nor (negative addition): He neither ate nor slept.
But (contrast): She tried hard, but she failed.
Or (alternative): Study now, or you will regret it.
Yet (unexpected contrast): He is rich, yet he is unhappy.
So (result): It was raining, so we stayed inside.

2. SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS: Connect a dependent clause to the main clause.
Cause/Reason: because, since, as — 'She cried because she was hurt.'
Contrast: although, though, even though, whereas, while — 'Although it rained, the match continued.'
Condition: if, unless, provided that, as long as — 'Unless you study, you will fail.'
Time: when, while, before, after, since, until, as soon as — 'He left before I arrived.'
Purpose: so that, in order that — 'He trained hard so that he could qualify.'
Result: so...that — 'She was so tired that she slept immediately.'

3. CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTIONS: Work in pairs.
Both...and: Both Ram and Shyam are here.
Either...or: Either study or leave.
Neither...nor: Neither the captain nor the crew survived.
Not only...but also: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
Whether...or: Tell me whether you agree or not.

CONFUSED CONJUNCTIONS:
'Although/Though' vs 'But': Never use both in the same clause. 'Although he tried, he failed' ✓. 'Although he tried, but he failed' ✗.
'Because' vs 'So': 'He was tired because he worked' (reason). 'He worked, so he was tired' (result).
'Unless' = 'if...not': 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the train' = 'If you do not hurry, you will miss the train.'
'Until' vs 'Unless': Until = up to the time (time). Unless = if not (condition).

WORD USAGE:
'Much' for uncountable nouns: much water, much money.
'Many' for countable nouns: many students, many books.
'Few' (some, small number) vs 'A few' (some, positive): Few students passed (almost none). A few students passed (some did).
'Little' vs 'A little': similar distinction for uncountable nouns.
points: FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So — coordinating conjunctions.
Subordinating: because/since (reason), although/though (contrast), if/unless (condition).
Correlative pairs: both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also.
Never use 'although' and 'but' together in the same sentence.
Unless = if...not (condition); Until = up to the time (time). Never confuse them.
'Because' gives reason; 'So' gives result — they are opposites in direction.
'Much' with uncountable nouns; 'Many' with countable nouns.
'Few' = very little/almost none (negative sense); 'A few' = some (positive sense).
'Little' = very little/almost nothing; 'A little' = some small amount (positive).
Correlative conjunctions must be placed immediately before the parallel elements.
examples: Correct: Although she was tired, she kept working. (NOT: Although she was tired, but she kept working.)
Unless you practise daily, you will not improve. (= If you do not practise daily, you will not improve.)
Not only did he win the gold medal, but he also broke the record.
Few soldiers survived the battle. (almost none) vs A few soldiers survived. (some did)
He was so exhausted that he could not stand. (so...that = result)
tv-6.summary: Conjunctions connect words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating (FANBOYS) join equals. Subordinating join a dependent clause to main clause (because, although, if, unless, when). Correlative come in pairs (both...and, either...or, neither...nor). Key rule: never use 'although' and 'but' together. 'Unless' means 'if not'. 'Much' for uncountable, 'many' for countable. 'Few' is negative; 'a few' is positive.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Although he worked hard, but he failed.
Although he worked hard, he failed.
Though he worked hard but he failed.
Even he worked hard, he failed.
questions.explanation: 'Although/Though' and 'but' cannot be used together. Use one or the other.

questions.question: ___ you leave now, you will miss the flight.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' = 'if not'. 'Unless you leave now' = 'If you do not leave now'.

questions.question: She is ___ intelligent ___ hardworking.
questions.explanation: 'Not only...but also' is the correct correlative conjunction for adding positive qualities.

questions.question: He failed ___ he did not study.
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason/cause. 'So' introduces the result/effect.

questions.question: There is ___ water in the desert.
questions.explanation: Water is uncountable, so use 'little' (not 'few' which is for countable nouns).

questions.question: Wait here ___ I return.
questions.explanation: 'Until' refers to time — 'wait up to the time I return'. 'Unless' would be conditional.

questions.question: ___ students passed the test. (Almost none passed)
questions.explanation: 'Few' without the article means a very small number, almost none — a negative sense.

questions.question: It was raining, ___ we cancelled the match.
questions.explanation: 'So' introduces a result. 'It was raining' is the cause; 'cancelled the match' is the effect.

questions.question: He trained hard ___ he could qualify for the Navy.
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces purpose — he trained with the purpose of qualifying.

questions.question: ___ he nor his friends were present.
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' is used for negative parallel structures with two subjects.

questions.question: She had ___ money to pay the fee.
questions.explanation: 'Money' is uncountable → use 'little'. 'Few' is for countable nouns.

questions.question: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Study hard ___ you will succeed.'
questions.explanation: 'And' is used here to show the expected positive result: study hard AND succeed.

questions.question: He is poor ___ he is honest.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' = unexpected contrast. He is poor (bad) YET honest (good) — the contrast is unexpected.

questions.question: ___ Ram ___ Shyam attended the parade.
questions.explanation: 'Both...and' adds two items together positively.

questions.question: The assignment was ___ difficult ___ none of us could finish it.
questions.explanation: 'So...that' expresses degree and result: so difficult THAT no one finished.

tv-7.title: Punctuation and Correction of Sentences
tv-7.notes:
Punctuation marks are symbols used in writing to clarify meaning, indicate pauses, show emotion, and organise sentences. Correct punctuation is essential for clear communication and is tested in NEA.

MAJOR PUNCTUATION MARKS AND THEIR RULES:

FULL STOP (.) — ends a declarative or imperative sentence. Also used in abbreviations: Mr., Dr., etc.

COMMAS (,):
— Before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses: 'She studied, and she passed.'
— After introductory phrases/clauses: 'After the match, we celebrated.'
— To separate items in a list: 'He bought bread, butter, milk, and eggs.'
— Around non-restrictive (extra info) clauses: 'Rajesh, who is my friend, won the prize.'
— In direct address: 'Come here, Ravi.'
— After yes/no in short answers: 'Yes, I agree.'

SEMICOLON (;) — connects two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction: 'He studied hard; he still failed.'

COLON (:) — introduces a list, explanation, or quotation: 'He had three qualities: honesty, courage, and loyalty.'

QUESTION MARK (?) — ends a direct question: 'Where are you going?' NOT used with indirect questions: 'He asked where I was going.'

EXCLAMATION MARK (!) — shows strong emotion: 'What a brave soldier he is!' Use sparingly.

APOSTROPHE ('):
— Possession (singular): Captain's cabin, soldier's rifle.
— Possession (plural ending in s): soldiers' rifles.
— Contraction: don't = do not, can't = cannot, it's = it is (NOT possessive 'its').
— Its vs It's: 'Its wing was broken' (possessive, no apostrophe). 'It's a beautiful ship' (= it is).

INVERTED COMMAS / QUOTATION MARKS (' ' or " "):
— Direct speech: He said, 'I will serve the nation.'
— Titles of books/films (often italicised instead).

COMMON SENTENCE ERRORS:
— Run-on sentence: two sentences joined without proper punctuation or conjunction.
— Sentence fragment: an incomplete sentence missing subject or verb.
— Double negative: 'I don't know nothing' ✗ → 'I don't know anything' ✓
— Wrong subject-verb agreement: 'The boys was late' ✗ → 'The boys were late' ✓
— Dangling modifier: 'Walking down the road, a dog bit him' ✗ → 'Walking down the road, he was bitten by a dog' ✓
points: Full stop ends declarative/imperative sentences. Also used in abbreviations.
Comma: before coordinating conjunctions, after introductory phrases, in lists, around extra info.
Semicolon joins two related independent clauses without a conjunction.
Colon introduces a list, explanation, or quotation.
Question mark only for direct questions — not indirect questions.
Apostrophe: possession (captain's), plural possession (soldiers'), contraction (don't).
Its (possessive) vs It's (it is) — common error in exams.
Direct speech uses inverted commas; the first word inside quotes is capitalised.
Avoid double negatives: 'I don't know anything' NOT 'I don't know nothing'.
Dangling modifier error: the modifier must logically refer to the subject of the main clause.
examples: Correct: The general, who was known for his bravery, led the charge. (commas around non-restrictive clause)
Correct: He packed his gear; the mission was about to begin. (semicolon between related clauses)
Error: The ships cabin was locked. ✗ → The ship's cabin was locked. ✓ (possessive apostrophe)
Error: He asked, 'Where are you going?' ✓ vs He asked where are you going? ✗ (indirect question, no ?)
Double negative: I cannot do nothing about it. ✗ → I cannot do anything about it. ✓
tv-7.summary: Punctuation gives structure and meaning to sentences. Full stops end statements. Commas separate elements and follow introductory phrases. Semicolons join related independent clauses. Colons introduce lists. Question marks end direct questions only. Apostrophes show possession (captain's) or contraction (don't). Its vs It's is a common trap. Avoid double negatives, run-on sentences, fragments, and dangling modifiers.

questions.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation: 'Soldiers'' with apostrophe after the s shows plural possession — belonging to multiple soldiers.

questions.question: Choose the correct option: '___ a beautiful sunrise!'
questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences with nouns use 'What': 'What a beautiful sunrise!' Adjectives use 'How': 'How beautiful!'

questions.question: He asked me where ___ going.
questions.explanation: In indirect questions, statement word order is used: 'where I was going' or 'where you are going'. No question mark.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'I didn't do nothing wrong.'
options: Double negative — should be 'I didn't do anything wrong'
questions.explanation: Double negatives are incorrect in standard English. 'Didn't' + 'nothing' = double negative. Use 'anything'.

questions.question: '___ wing was broken' — which word correctly fills the blank?
questions.explanation: 'Its' without apostrophe is the possessive pronoun. 'It's' = it is. Possessive pronouns never take apostrophes.

questions.question: Which sentence has a correct use of semicolon?
questions.explanation: Semicolons join two complete, related independent clauses. Do not use a semicolon before 'but'.

questions.question: He had three goals___ discipline, fitness, and courage.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration. It signals 'namely' or 'that is'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
questions.explanation: In direct address (vocative), a comma is placed before the name: 'Come here, Ravi.'

questions.question: Which sentence is a run-on sentence?
options: He ran fast, and he won.
He ran fast he won the race.
questions.explanation: A run-on sentence joins two independent clauses without punctuation or conjunction.

questions.question: 'After the parade the soldiers rested.' — where should a comma go?
questions.explanation: A comma goes after an introductory phrase/clause: 'After the parade, the soldiers rested.'

questions.question: Which abbreviation is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation: Abbreviations of titles take a full stop: Dr. (Doctor), Mr. (Mister), etc.

questions.question: Identify the sentence fragment:
questions.explanation: 'Running along the shore' has no subject or main verb — it is an incomplete sentence (fragment).

questions.question: She said ___ I will not give up ___
questions.explanation: In direct speech: comma after the reporting verb, then inverted commas, then the spoken words with the first word capitalised.

questions.question: The boys___ who were late___ were punished. (Extra information about the boys)
questions.explanation: Non-restrictive (extra information) clauses are enclosed in commas: 'The boys, who were late, were punished.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses the question mark correctly?
options: He asked if I was ready?
Are you coming to the parade?
I want to know who won?
questions.explanation: Question marks are used only for direct questions. Indirect questions (asked if, wondered where) end with a full stop.

tv-8.title: Idioms, Phrases and Transformation of Sentences
tv-8.notes:
This topic combines two skills: understanding idioms and phrases, and transforming sentences from one grammatical form to another while keeping the meaning the same.

IDIOMS AND PHRASES:
An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be guessed from the individual words.
A phrase is a group of words that functions as a single unit (noun phrase, verb phrase, prepositional phrase).

COMMON IDIOMS:
A blessing in disguise — something bad that turns out to be good.
Beat around the bush — avoid saying the main point directly.
Bite the bullet — endure something painful or difficult bravely.
Burning the midnight oil — working very late at night.
Hit the nail on the head — describe something exactly right.
Kill two birds with one stone — solve two problems with one action.
Let the cat out of the bag — accidentally reveal a secret.
Once in a blue moon — very rarely.
Pull someone's leg — joke/tease someone.
Spill the beans — reveal a secret.
On the fence — undecided.
Through thick and thin — through all difficulties.
A dime a dozen — very common, not special.
Under the weather — feeling ill.
The ball is in your court — it is your decision now.
Cost an arm and a leg — very expensive.
Break a leg — good luck (informal).
Hit the books — study hard.
Cut corners — do something carelessly to save time.

TRANSFORMATION OF SENTENCES:
Sentences can be transformed without changing their meaning. The NEA exam tests several types:

1. AFFIRMATIVE ↔ NEGATIVE:
'He is brave' → 'He is not a coward.'
'Everyone likes her' → 'There is no one who does not like her.'

2. SIMPLE ↔ COMPOUND ↔ COMPLEX:
Simple: 'Despite being tired, he finished the work.'
Compound: 'He was tired, but he finished the work.'
Complex: 'Although he was tired, he finished the work.'

3. DEGREE OF COMPARISON:
Superlative: 'Iron is the strongest metal.'
Comparative: 'Iron is stronger than all other metals.'
Positive: 'No other metal is as strong as iron.'

4. EXCLAMATORY ↔ ASSERTIVE:
Exclamatory: 'What a brave soldier he is!'
Assertive: 'He is a very brave soldier.'

5. ACTIVE ↔ PASSIVE:
Active: 'The captain gave the order.'
Passive: 'The order was given by the captain.'

6. DIRECT ↔ INDIRECT SPEECH:
Direct: She said, 'I will help you.'
Indirect: She said that she would help me.
points: Idiom meaning ≠ literal word meanings; fixed expressions must be memorised.
Beat around the bush = avoid direct answer; Hit the nail on the head = say exactly right.
Kill two birds with one stone = solve two problems at once; Spill the beans = reveal secret.
Transformation: same meaning in different grammatical form.
Degree transformation: Superlative → Comparative → Positive (all mean same thing).
Simple → Complex → Compound transformation using different conjunctions.
Affirmative → Negative: 'Everyone likes him' → 'There is no one who dislikes him'.
Exclamatory → Assertive: 'What a hero!' → 'He is a great hero.'
Active → Passive: object becomes subject + be + V3.
Direct → Indirect: tense backshift, pronoun change, time word change.
examples: Idiom: 'He burned the midnight oil to prepare for NEA.' = He studied very late at night.
Degree: 'Gold is the most precious metal' → 'Gold is more precious than all other metals' → 'No other metal is as precious as gold'.
Affirmative to negative: 'He always tells the truth' → 'He never tells a lie'.
Exclamatory to assertive: 'How beautiful the sea is!' → 'The sea is very beautiful.'
Transformation: Simple 'In spite of the rain, they marched' → Complex 'Although it rained, they marched'.
tv-8.summary: Idioms are fixed expressions with non-literal meanings — must be memorised. Common ones: beat around the bush, hit the nail on the head, spill the beans, burning midnight oil, once in a blue moon. Sentence transformation changes grammatical form while keeping meaning: degree conversion (superlative→comparative→positive), affirmative↔negative, exclamatory↔assertive, simple↔compound↔complex, active↔passive, direct↔indirect speech.

questions.question: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means something that happens very rarely or almost never.

questions.question: Transform: 'What a courageous soldier he is!' → Assertive:
options: He is not a courageous soldier.
He is a very courageous soldier.
questions.explanation: Exclamatory → Assertive: Replace 'What a...' with 'very' and restructure as a statement.

questions.question: Transform to positive degree: 'Iron is the hardest of all metals.'
options: Iron is harder than most metals.
No other metal is as hard as iron.
Iron is one of the hardest metals.
All metals are not as hard as iron.
questions.explanation: Superlative → Positive: 'No other + noun + is as + adjective + as + subject'.

questions.question: 'He spilled the beans.' This idiom means:
questions.explanation: 'Spill the beans' means to accidentally or deliberately reveal a secret or confidential information.

questions.question: Transform: 'Although he was injured, he continued fighting.' → Simple sentence:
options: He was injured but continued fighting.
In spite of his injury, he continued fighting.
He was injured so he continued.
questions.explanation: Complex sentence → Simple: Replace 'although' clause with 'in spite of + noun/gerund'.

questions.question: What does 'cost an arm and a leg' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Cost an arm and a leg' is an idiom meaning something is extremely expensive.

questions.question: Transform: 'Everyone respected him.' → Negative:
options: There was no one who did not respect him.
He was not respected by anyone.
questions.explanation: The correct negative transformation of 'everyone' uses 'there is/was no one who did not'.

questions.question: Transform to passive: 'The Navy awarded the officer a medal.'
options: The officer was awarded a medal by the Navy.
A medal awarded the officer by the Navy.
The Navy was awarded by the officer.
The officer awarded the medal by the Navy.
questions.explanation: Active → Passive: object (officer) becomes subject + was awarded + by the Navy.

questions.question: 'Under the weather' means:
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' is an idiom meaning to feel ill or unwell.

questions.question: Which is the correct transformation of 'Rohit is the best student'?
options: Rohit is better than any other student.
No other student is as good as Rohit.
Both A and B are correct.
Neither A nor B is correct.
questions.explanation: Both comparative ('better than any other') and positive ('no other is as good as') are valid transformations of the superlative.

questions.question: Transform to complex: 'He ran fast and still missed the bus.'
options: Although he ran fast, he missed the bus.
Because he ran fast, he missed the bus.
He ran fast so he missed the bus.
If he ran fast, he would miss the bus.
questions.explanation: The 'still' in the original indicates contrast/concession — use 'Although' for the complex transformation.

questions.question: 'Burning the midnight oil' means:
questions.explanation: 'Burning the midnight oil' = working or studying very late into the night.

questions.question: Transform: 'He is too weak to lift the box.' → 'So...that' form:
options: He is so weak that he cannot lift the box.
He is so weak so he cannot lift.
Too weak is he that he can't lift.
He is weak therefore he cannot lift.
questions.explanation: 'Too...to' → 'so...that...cannot': 'too weak to lift' = 'so weak that he cannot lift'.

questions.question: What does 'hit the books' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' is an informal idiom meaning to start studying or to study hard.

questions.question: Transform to indirect speech: She said, 'I am learning trigonometry.'
options: She said that she is learning trigonometry.
She said that she was learning trigonometry.
She said that I was learning trigonometry.
She said that she had learned trigonometry.
questions.explanation: Present continuous → Past continuous in indirect speech: 'am learning' → 'was learning'. Pronoun 'I' changes to 'she'.

ag-2.title: Gap Filling and Dialogue Completion
ag-2.notes:
Gap filling and dialogue completion test your ability to select the correct word, phrase, or grammatical form to complete a sentence or conversation. These questions directly test grammar, vocabulary, and context understanding.

GAP FILLING — TYPES OF GAPS:

1. Articles (a/an/the):
'A' before consonant sounds: a book, a university (u sounds like 'you').
'An' before vowel sounds: an hour (h is silent), an apple, an honest man.
'The' for specific/unique things: the Sun, the Prime Minister, the book I mentioned.
No article: uncountable nouns in general sense (Water is essential), plural nouns in general (Dogs are loyal).

2. Auxiliary verbs (is/are/was/were/has/have/had/will/would/can/could/should/must):
Match the auxiliary to the tense context.

3. Prepositions (see tv-5 rules).

4. Pronouns (I/me, he/him, who/whom, whose, which, that):
'Who' is the subject; 'whom' is the object. 'Whose' shows possession.

5. Connectors (however, therefore, moreover, although, unless, since, etc.):
'However' = contrast. 'Therefore/Thus/Hence' = result. 'Moreover/Furthermore' = addition. 'Nevertheless' = contrast despite.

DIALOGUE COMPLETION:
A dialogue has social functions: greeting, requesting, apologising, agreeing, disagreeing, offering, thanking.

Functions and common expressions:
Greeting: 'How do you do?' → 'How do you do?' (formal) / 'Fine, thank you. And you?'
Requesting politely: 'Could you please...?', 'Would you mind...?', 'May I...?'
Apologising: 'I am sorry for...', 'I apologise for...', 'Please forgive me.'
Agreeing: 'I agree with you.', 'Absolutely.', 'That's right.', 'Exactly.'
Disagreeing politely: 'I'm afraid I disagree.', 'With due respect, I think...'
Offering: 'Shall I help you?', 'Would you like...?', 'Can I get you...?'
Thanking: 'Thank you very much.', 'I'm grateful to you.', 'Much obliged.'
Accepting an offer: 'Yes, please.', 'That would be great.'
Refusing an offer: 'No, thank you.', 'That's very kind, but I'm fine.'

STRATEGY for gap filling:
1. Read the whole sentence first for context.
2. Identify what grammatical category the gap requires (verb, article, preposition, connector).
3. Consider the tense and logical flow.
4. Eliminate options that are grammatically wrong.
5. Select the option that fits both grammar AND meaning.
points: Articles: 'a' before consonant sound, 'an' before vowel sound, 'the' for specific items.
No article before uncountable nouns in general sense (Water is life).
'An hour', 'an honest man' — use 'an' when the word begins with a silent consonant.
Who (subject) vs Whom (object): 'Who did this?' / 'To whom did you speak?'
Connectors: However=contrast, Therefore=result, Moreover=addition, Unless=if not.
Dialogue: match the response to the function (greeting, request, apology, etc.).
Polite requests: 'Could you please...?' / 'Would you mind...?'
Agreement: 'Absolutely', 'Exactly', 'I agree'. Disagreement: 'I'm afraid I disagree'.
Strategy: read whole sentence, identify gap type, check grammar + meaning.
Tense consistency: ensure the auxiliary and main verb match the timeline.
examples: Fill: '___ honest man always speaks truth.' → An (honest begins with vowel sound /ɒ/)
Fill: 'He left ___ I arrived.' → before/after/when — context gives 'before' (he left first).
Dialogue: A: 'Could you lend me your notes?' B: '___' → 'Sure, here you go.' / 'I'm sorry, I need them.'
Fill: 'She is ___ best student in the class.' → the (specific, unique — best student)
Connector: 'He studied hard; ___, he failed.' → However (contrast — studied but failed)
ag-2.summary: Gap filling tests articles (a/an/the), prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, and connectors. Use 'an' before vowel sounds (an hour, an honest man). 'The' before specific/unique items. Connectors: However (contrast), Therefore (result), Moreover (addition). Dialogue completion requires matching the social function of the conversation — greetings, requests, apologies, agreement. Always read the full context before choosing.

questions.question: Fill in: '___ European country I visited was France.'
questions.explanation: 'The' is used because we are referring to a specific European country the speaker visited.

questions.question: 'He studied hard. ___, he scored full marks.' Choose the best connector.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' introduces a result/conclusion. He studied → therefore he scored full marks.

questions.question: Fill: '___ honest person never betrays his friends.'
questions.explanation: 'An' is used before words beginning with a vowel sound. 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h', so the vowel sound is /ɒ/ — use 'an'.

questions.question: A: 'Would you like some tea?' B: '___ '
questions.explanation: The polite and natural response to an offer is 'Yes, please.' or 'No, thank you.'

questions.question: Fill: '___ whom did you submit the report?'
questions.explanation: 'To whom' — the report is submitted TO someone. 'Whom' is the object form of 'who'.

questions.question: Fill: 'I have been waiting here ___ two hours.'
questions.explanation: 'For' is used with a duration of time. 'Since' is used with a point in time.

questions.question: A: 'I'm sorry for being late.' B: '___'
questions.explanation: The appropriate response to an apology is acceptance: 'Never mind, it's alright' or 'That's okay.'

questions.question: Fill: 'She is ___ tallest girl in the team.'
questions.explanation: Superlatives always take 'the' — 'the tallest', 'the best', 'the most intelligent'.

questions.question: Fill: 'He spoke to the officer ___ was in charge.'
questions.explanation: 'Who' is used for people as the subject of the relative clause ('who was in charge').

questions.question: 'He is poor. ___, he is happy.' Best connector:
questions.explanation: 'However' introduces a contrast — he is poor (bad) BUT happy (surprising positive).

questions.question: A: 'May I come in, sir?' B: '___'
questions.explanation: The natural, polite response to a permission request is 'Yes, please come in.'

questions.question: Fill: '___ milk in the glass is fresh.'
questions.explanation: 'The' is used for specific milk — the milk that is in the glass (specific reference).

questions.question: Fill: 'She has known him ___ childhood.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time. Childhood is a specific point/period from which the duration begins.

questions.question: A: 'Could you help me with this problem?' B: '___'
options: Yes, of course! What do you need?
questions.explanation: The natural response to a polite request is agreeable and helpful: 'Yes, of course! What do you need?'

questions.question: Fill: 'He is ___ only person ___ can solve this.'
questions.explanation: 'The only' — specific and unique reference. 'Who' for people as subject of relative clause.

ag-3.title: Sentence Transformation and Changing Narration
ag-3.notes:
Sentence transformation rewrites a sentence in a different grammatical form while preserving its meaning. Changing narration (direct↔indirect speech) is the most important transformation tested in NEA.

CHANGING NARRATION — DIRECT TO INDIRECT:

The GOLDEN RULES:
1. Tense backshift (when reporting verb is past — said/told/asked):
Present Simple → Past Simple
Present Continuous → Past Continuous
Present Perfect → Past Perfect
Past Simple → Past Perfect
Future (will) → would
Can → could, May → might, Must → had to

2. Pronoun changes:
1st person (I, me, my, we, us, our) → changes based on subject of reporting verb.
2nd person (you, your) → changes based on object of reporting verb.
3rd person (he, she, they) → no change.

3. Time and place word changes:
now → then / at that time
today → that day
yesterday → the previous day / the day before
tomorrow → the next day / the following day
here → there
this → that
these → those
last week → the previous week
next year → the following year
ago → before

4. Punctuation: Remove inverted commas. Add 'that' after said/told.

STATEMENTS: He said, 'I am happy.' → He said that he was happy.

QUESTIONS:
Yes/No questions: Use 'if' or 'whether'. Auxiliary goes after subject.
He asked, 'Are you ready?' → He asked if I was ready.
Wh-questions: Use the question word. No inversion.
She asked, 'Where do you live?' → She asked where I lived.

COMMANDS/REQUESTS:
Affirmative: 'told/asked/ordered + object + to + verb'.
He said, 'Sit down.' → He told me to sit down.
Negative: 'told/asked + object + not to + verb'.
She said, 'Don't make noise.' → She told them not to make noise.

EXCLAMATIONS:
'What a beautiful day!' → He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful day.

INDIRECT TO DIRECT: Reverse all the above changes.
points: Tense backshift: Present→Past, Continuous→Past Continuous, Perfect→Past Perfect, will→would.
Pronouns: 1st person changes; 3rd person (he/she/they) stays the same.
Time words: now→then, today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there.
Statements: add 'that' after reporting verb; remove inverted commas.
Yes/No questions: use 'if/whether' + statement word order (no inversion).
Wh-questions: use question word + statement order (no auxiliary inversion).
Commands: told/asked/ordered + object + to-infinitive.
Negative commands: told/asked + object + not to + infinitive.
Exclamations: use 'exclaimed that' + very/great in the statement.
No tense change when reporting verb is present tense (says/tells) or the fact is universal.
examples: He said, 'I will come tomorrow.' → He said that he would come the next day.
She asked, 'Have you eaten?' → She asked if I had eaten.
He said, 'Where is the captain?' → He asked where the captain was.
She said to him, 'Please open the window.' → She requested him to open the window.
He said, 'What a brave soldier you are!' → He exclaimed that I was a very brave soldier.
ag-3.summary: Direct speech quotes exact words; indirect speech reports them with changes. Key changes: tense backshift (present→past, will→would), pronoun shift (I→he/she), time words (today→that day, tomorrow→the next day). Statements add 'that'. Yes/No questions use 'if/whether' + statement order. Wh-questions keep the question word + statement order. Commands use 'told/asked + to-infinitive'. No tense change if reporting verb is present tense.

questions.question: Change to indirect: He said, 'I am a naval officer.'
options: He said that he is a naval officer.
He said that he was a naval officer.
He told that he was a naval officer.
He said that I was a naval officer.
questions.explanation: 'Said' is past tense → tense backshifts: 'am' → 'was'. No comma or inverted commas. 'I' → 'he'.

questions.question: Change to indirect: She asked, 'Do you play chess?'
options: She asked if I play chess.
She asked if I played chess.
She asked whether do I play chess.
She asked that I played chess.
questions.explanation: Yes/No question → if/whether + statement order + tense backshift. 'Do you play' → 'if I played'.

questions.question: Change to indirect: 'Where are you going?' he asked.
options: He asked me where are you going.
He asked me where I am going.
He asked me where I was going.
He asked where was I going.
questions.explanation: Wh-question in indirect speech: question word + statement order + tense backshift. 'are you' → 'I was'.

questions.question: Change to indirect: The officer said, 'Attention!'
options: The officer commanded them to stand at attention.
questions.explanation: Commands use 'commanded/ordered/told + object + to-infinitive'.

questions.question: Change to direct: He said that he had finished the work.
options: He said, 'I have finished the work.'
He said, 'I had finished the work.'
questions.explanation: Indirect → Direct reverses tense backshift: Past Perfect 'had finished' → Present Perfect 'have finished'.

questions.question: Change to indirect: She said, 'Don't run in the corridor.'
options: She said not to run in the corridor.
She told them not to run in the corridor.
She told them to not run.
questions.explanation: Negative command: 'told + object + not to + infinitive'. Object 'them' is required.

questions.question: Which time word change is correct in indirect speech?
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' or 'the following day' in indirect speech.

questions.question: Change to indirect: He said, 'I will visit you tomorrow.'
options: He said he will visit me tomorrow.
He said he would visit me the next day.
He said he would visit you the next day.
He said he shall visit me next day.
questions.explanation: Will→would, tomorrow→the next day, you→me (object of reporting verb changes).

questions.question: Change to indirect: They said, 'We are happy here.'
options: They said that they are happy there.
They said that they were happy there.
They said that we were happy here.
They said that they were happy here.
questions.explanation: Tense backshift: are→were. Pronoun: we→they. Place: here→there.

questions.question: Change to indirect: She asked me, 'Can you swim?'
options: She asked me if I can swim.
She asked me if I could swim.
She asked me whether can I swim.
She asked me that I could swim.
questions.explanation: Can→could in indirect speech. Yes/No question uses 'if/whether' + statement order.

questions.question: Change to indirect: He said, 'How beautiful this garden is!'
options: He said that this garden is beautiful.
He exclaimed that the garden was very beautiful.
He said how beautiful this garden is.
He exclaimed how beautiful was the garden.
questions.explanation: Exclamation in indirect speech: 'exclaimed that + very/great'. 'this' → 'the', 'is' → 'was'.

questions.question: The teacher said, 'The Earth revolves around the Sun.' → Indirect:
options: The teacher said that the Earth revolved around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
The teacher told that Earth revolves.
The teacher said Earth had revolved.
questions.explanation: Universal truths do not change tense in indirect speech: 'The Earth revolves' stays as is.

questions.question: Change to indirect: 'Please help me,' she said to him.
options: She told him to help her.
She requested him to help her.
She said him to help her.
questions.explanation: Polite request with 'please' → 'requested + object + to-infinitive'.

questions.question: In indirect speech, 'last week' becomes:
questions.explanation: Time word change in indirect speech: 'last week' → 'the previous week' or 'the week before'.

questions.question: Change to indirect: He asked, 'Who broke the window?'
options: He asked who broke the window.
He asked who had broken the window.
He asked who did break the window.
He asked that who broke the window.
questions.explanation: Wh-question in indirect: question word + statement order + tense backshift. 'broke' → 'had broken'.

ag-4.title: Reordering of Words and Sentences
ag-4.notes:
Reordering (also called rearrangement) tests your knowledge of correct English word order and sentence structure. You are given jumbled words or sentences and must arrange them logically.

BASIC ENGLISH SENTENCE STRUCTURE:
The standard word order is: Subject + Verb + Object + Complement + Adverb (SVOCA).
Example: She (S) gave (V) him (O) a book (C) yesterday (A).

RULES FOR WORD ORDER:

1. ADJECTIVES before nouns: 'a brave young soldier' — Opinion→Size→Age→Shape→Colour→Origin→Material.

2. ADVERBS of frequency come:
Before the main verb: She always comes on time.
After 'be' verbs: He is always punctual.
Between auxiliary and main verb: He has never lied.

3. ADVERBS of manner usually come after the verb or object: He spoke softly. She completed the task quickly.

4. ADVERBS of time usually come at the end of the sentence or at the beginning: He arrived yesterday. Yesterday, he arrived.

5. PLACE before TIME at end: She went to the market (place) at noon (time).

6. QUESTIONS — invert subject and auxiliary: Normal: He is tired. Question: Is he tired?

7. INDIRECT QUESTIONS — do NOT invert: 'Tell me where he lives.' (NOT 'Tell me where does he live.')

8. NEGATIVE sentences: Place 'not' after the first auxiliary: He does not play cricket. She cannot come.

9. EMPHATIC order (for emphasis, inversion is used): 'Never have I seen such bravery.' (inversion after negative adverbs)

STRATEGY FOR JUMBLED SENTENCES:
1. Find the SUBJECT first (who/what the sentence is about).
2. Find the MAIN VERB next.
3. Connect the object and complement.
4. Place adjectives before nouns and adverbs in their correct positions.
5. Read the complete sentence aloud to check if it sounds natural.
points: Basic order: Subject + Verb + Object + Complement + Adverb (SVOCA).
Adjectives come before the noun they modify.
Adjective order: Opinion→Size→Age→Shape→Colour→Origin→Material.
Adverbs of frequency: before main verb, after 'be' verb, between auxiliary and main verb.
Adverbs of manner: after verb or object.
Time and place: place comes before time at the end of a sentence.
Questions: auxiliary verb before subject (Is he...? Did she...?).
Indirect questions do NOT invert: 'Tell me where he lives' (not 'where does he live').
Negative adverbs (never, rarely, hardly) at the start require inversion.
Strategy: find subject first, then verb, then add other elements in correct order.
examples: Jumbled: always / she / on time / arrives → She always arrives on time.
Jumbled: brave / young / a / soldier → a brave young soldier (opinion before age).
Jumbled: yesterday / the market / she / went / to → She went to the market yesterday.
Indirect: Tell me where does he live. ✗ → Tell me where he lives. ✓
Inversion: Never I have seen such courage. ✗ → Never have I seen such courage. ✓
ag-4.summary: English follows SVOCA word order. Adjectives come before nouns in order: opinion→size→age→colour→origin→material. Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb or after 'be'. Place comes before time at sentence end. Questions invert subject and auxiliary. Indirect questions keep statement order. Negative adverbs at sentence start require subject-auxiliary inversion. Strategy: find subject first, then verb, then arrange the rest.

questions.question: Arrange: always / she / is / late / for work
options: She is always late for work.
Always she is late for work.
She always is late for work.
She is late always for work.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency go after 'be' verbs. Correct: She is always late.

questions.question: Arrange: the / brave / young / a / officer
questions.explanation: Adjective order: opinion (brave) before age (young) before noun. 'A brave young officer'.

questions.question: Arrange: to / Delhi / went / yesterday / she
questions.explanation: Basic order: Subject (she) + Verb (went) + Place (to Delhi) + Time (yesterday).

questions.question: Which is correctly ordered?
options: Tell me where does he live.
questions.explanation: Indirect questions use statement order: 'where he lives' (not 'where does he live').

questions.question: Arrange: has / he / never / to me / lied
options: He has never lied to me.
Never he has lied to me.
He never has lied to me.
He has lied never to me.
questions.explanation: Adverb 'never' goes between auxiliary (has) and main verb (lied).

questions.question: Arrange: carefully / the / she / read / instructions
questions.explanation: Adverbs of manner usually come after the object: 'read the instructions carefully'.

questions.question: Arrange: never / such / I / have / bravery / seen
options: I have never seen such bravery.
Never have I seen such bravery.
Never I have seen such bravery.
Both A and B are correct.
questions.explanation: Both are correct. When 'never' is at the start (emphatic), inversion occurs: 'Never have I seen'.

questions.question: Which sentence has the correct word order for an adjective?
questions.explanation: Adjective order: Opinion (beautiful) → Age (old) → Origin (Italian) → Noun (village).

questions.question: Arrange: she / hard / has / been / working / all day
options: She has been working hard all day.
She hard has been working all day.
She has been hard working all day.
All day she hard has been working.
questions.explanation: SVOCA order: Subject + Present Perfect Continuous + Adverb of manner + Time adverb.

questions.question: Arrange: asked / where / the / he / gone / had / captain
options: He asked where the captain had gone.
He asked where had the captain gone.
He asked the captain where had gone.
He asked where gone the captain had.
questions.explanation: Indirect question: question word + statement order. 'Where the captain had gone' (not 'where had the captain gone').

questions.question: Which sentence is correctly arranged?
options: He gave to me a letter yesterday.
He gave me a letter yesterday.
He gave yesterday me a letter.
Yesterday a letter he gave me.
questions.explanation: When 'give' has two objects: S + V + Indirect Object + Direct Object + Time. 'He gave me a letter yesterday.'

questions.question: Arrange: plays / sometimes / the / guitar / he
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency (sometimes) go before the main verb: 'He sometimes plays the guitar'.

questions.question: Choose the correctly ordered sentence:
options: She quickly ran to school in the morning.
She ran to school quickly in the morning.
She ran quickly to school in the morning.
Quickly she ran in the morning to school.
questions.explanation: Manner (quickly) comes after verb, then Place (to school), then Time (in the morning).

questions.question: Arrange: the / who / soldier / medal / won / the
options: The soldier who won the medal.
Who won the medal the soldier.
questions.explanation: Subject (the soldier) + Verb (won) + Object (the medal). This is the complete sentence.

questions.question: Which question is correctly formed?
questions.explanation: Direct question: auxiliary + subject + main verb. 'Where is she going?' — auxiliary 'is' before subject 'she'.

ag-5.title: Editing and Error Correction of Words and Sentences
ag-5.notes:
Editing and error correction questions present a passage or sentences with grammatical errors. You must identify and correct them. This tests thorough knowledge of grammar rules.

COMMON TYPES OF ERRORS:

1. SUBJECT-VERB AGREEMENT ERRORS:
Wrong: The news are shocking. ✗ → The news is shocking. ✓ (news = singular)
Wrong: Each of the students have passed. ✗ → Each of the students has passed. ✓ (each = singular)
Wrong: Mathematics are difficult. ✗ → Mathematics is difficult. ✓ (subject that looks plural but is singular)
Wrong: Neither of them are ready. ✗ → Neither of them is ready. ✓

2. TENSE ERRORS:
Wrong: Yesterday I go to school. ✗ → Yesterday I went to school. ✓
Wrong: She has gone to Delhi yesterday. ✗ → She went to Delhi yesterday. ✓ (Present perfect + specific past time = error)
Wrong: He is working here since 2010. ✗ → He has been working here since 2010. ✓

3. ARTICLE ERRORS:
Wrong: She is best student in the class. ✗ → She is the best student. ✓
Wrong: He is an university student. ✗ → He is a university student. ✓ (u = 'you' sound, consonant)
Wrong: The gold is precious. ✗ → Gold is precious. ✓ (general reference, no article)

4. PREPOSITION ERRORS (see tv-5).

5. PRONOUN ERRORS:
Wrong: Me and him went to school. ✗ → He and I went to school. ✓ (subject case)
Wrong: Between you and I. ✗ → Between you and me. ✓ (object after preposition)
Wrong: Everyone must do their duty. ✓ (acceptable with gender-neutral plural pronoun)

6. DOUBLE NEGATIVE:
Wrong: I didn't see nobody. ✗ → I didn't see anybody. ✓

7. REDUNDANCY (repetition of meaning):
Wrong: Return back ✗ → Return ✓. Revert back ✗ → Revert ✓. Repeat again ✗ → Repeat ✓.
Wrong: Free gift ✗ → Gift ✓. Advance warning ✗ → Warning ✓.

8. WRONG WORD FORM:
Wrong: He gave a suggestion. ✗ (suggest is a verb) → He made a suggestion. ✓
Wrong: Please make a try. ✗ → Please make an attempt / try. ✓

9. ADJECTIVE vs ADVERB:
Wrong: He ran very quick. ✗ → He ran very quickly. ✓ (modify verb with adverb)
Wrong: She feels badly about it. ✗ → She feels bad about it. ✓ (after linking verb, use adjective)
points: News, mathematics, physics, economics, ethics — take singular verb.
Each, everyone, everyone, nobody, someone — take singular verb.
Present perfect cannot be used with specific past time words (yesterday, last year).
Since 2010/childhood + have been doing (present perfect continuous for ongoing action).
Superlatives always need 'the': the best, the tallest, the most intelligent.
'A university', 'a European' — vowel letter but consonant sound → use 'a'.
Double negatives: replace second negative with positive equivalent (any, anyone, anything).
Redundancies: return back, repeat again, revert back, free gift — avoid.
Pronouns in subject position: He and I went. Object position: between you and me.
After linking verbs (feel, seem, look, sound, taste): use adjective, not adverb.
examples: Error: The committee have decided. ✗ → The committee has decided. ✓ (collective noun, singular)
Error: She has visited Paris last year. ✗ → She visited Paris last year. ✓
Error: He ran very quick. ✗ → He ran very quickly. ✓ (adverb needed)
Error: Return back the book. ✗ → Return the book. ✓ ('back' is redundant)
Error: Me and my friend went. ✗ → My friend and I went. ✓ (subject case, I before me)
ag-5.summary: Error correction tests subject-verb agreement (news/each/mathematics = singular), tense consistency (no present perfect with specific past time), articles (a/an/the rules), pronoun case (I for subject, me for object), double negatives (use 'any' not 'no' after negation), redundancy (return back, repeat again), and adjective vs adverb use. Identify the error type, then apply the correct rule.

questions.question: Correct the error: 'The news are very shocking.'
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun — always takes a singular verb: 'is'.

questions.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
questions.explanation: Present perfect cannot be used with specific past time 'yesterday'. Use simple past: 'met'.

questions.question: Correct: 'He is an university professor.'
questions.explanation: 'University' starts with the sound /j/ (like 'you') — a consonant sound. So use 'a', not 'an'.

questions.question: Correct: 'I didn't see nobody at the gate.'
options: I didn't see anybody at the gate.
I didn't see no one at the gate.
I saw nobody at the gate. (both options correct)
Both A and C are correct.
questions.explanation: Both 'I didn't see anybody' and 'I saw nobody' are correct — avoid using two negatives together.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'Return back the library books by Friday.'
questions.explanation: 'Return back' is redundant. 'Return' already means to go/give back. Drop 'back'.

questions.question: Correct: 'She feels badly about the news.'
options: She feels bad about the news.
She feels more badly about the news.
She is feeling badly about the news.
questions.explanation: After linking verb 'feels', use adjective 'bad' not adverb 'badly'. She feels bad.

questions.question: Correct: 'Each of the cadets have completed the drill.'
options: Each of the cadets has completed the drill.
Each of the cadet have completed.
questions.explanation: 'Each' always takes a singular verb. 'Each of the cadets has completed'.

questions.question: Correct: 'He is working here since five years.'
options: He is working here for five years.
He has been working here for five years.
He was working here since five years.
He works here since five years.
questions.explanation: Ongoing action from the past to now: present perfect continuous + 'for' (duration). 'Has been working for five years.'

questions.question: Correct: 'Me and him went to the parade.'
options: I and him went to the parade.
Me and he went to the parade.
He and I went to the parade.
Me and he went to the parade.
questions.explanation: Subject pronouns required: 'He and I'. Also, by convention, put the first person (I) last.

questions.question: Which sentence has NO error?
questions.explanation: Mathematics (and other -ics subjects: physics, economics) takes a singular verb.

questions.question: Correct: 'She gave a very good suggestion.'
options: She made a very good suggestion.
She did a very good suggestion.
She told a very good suggestion.
questions.explanation: Collocations: 'make a suggestion' (not 'give a suggestion'). Fixed English verb collocations.

questions.question: Identify the error: 'He is one of the best student in the class.'
options: 'one of the best' should be 'the one best'
'student' should be 'students' — 'one of' takes plural noun
questions.explanation: 'One of the best' is followed by a plural noun: 'one of the best students'.

questions.question: Correct: 'Between you and I, this is wrong.'
options: Between you and me, this is wrong.
Between you and myself, this is wrong.
Between I and you, this is wrong.
questions.explanation: Prepositions take object case: 'between you and me' (not 'I'). 'I' is subject; 'me' is object.

questions.question: Correct: 'The gold is the most precious metal.'
options: A gold is most precious metal.
Gold is the most precious metal.
The gold is most precious metal.
questions.explanation: No article before material nouns used in general sense. 'Gold is the most precious metal.' ('The' before superlative is correct.)

questions.question: Correct: 'Neither of the candidates are qualified.'
options: Neither of the candidates is qualified.
Neither of the candidates were qualified.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is singular and takes a singular verb: 'is qualified'.

ag-6.title: Synonyms and Antonyms
ag-6.notes:
Synonyms are words that have the same or similar meanings. Antonyms are words that have opposite meanings. Both are heavily tested in NEA to check vocabulary range.

KEY SYNONYM PAIRS:
Abundant = plentiful, ample, copious, profuse.
Audacious = bold, daring, fearless, intrepid.
Benevolent = kind, charitable, generous, philanthropic.
Brave = courageous, valiant, intrepid, gallant, dauntless.
Calm = tranquil, serene, placid, composed.
Diligent = hardworking, industrious, assiduous, painstaking.
Elated = joyful, ecstatic, jubilant, exhilarated.
Eminent = distinguished, renowned, prominent, notable.
Fervent = passionate, ardent, zealous, vehement.
Genuine = authentic, real, sincere, bona fide.
Humble = modest, meek, unassuming, unpretentious.
Ignorant = unaware, uninformed, oblivious.
Lethargic = sluggish, listless, languid, torpid.
Mournful = sorrowful, grieving, lamenting, doleful.
Novel = new, original, innovative, unprecedented.
Obstinate = stubborn, headstrong, tenacious, unyielding.
Pacify = calm, appease, placate, soothe.
Rapid = swift, fast, speedy, brisk, hasty.
Superfluous = unnecessary, redundant, excess, surplus.
Vigorous = energetic, robust, dynamic, strenuous.

KEY ANTONYM PAIRS:
Abundant ↔ Scarce. Brave ↔ Cowardly. Calm ↔ Agitated. Diligent ↔ Lazy. Eminent ↔ Obscure. Fervent ↔ Indifferent. Genuine ↔ Fake/Counterfeit. Humble ↔ Arrogant. Innocent ↔ Guilty. Joyful ↔ Sorrowful. Kind ↔ Cruel. Lethargic ↔ Energetic. Modest ↔ Conceited. Optimistic ↔ Pessimistic. Patient ↔ Impatient. Rigid ↔ Flexible. Sincere ↔ Insincere. Timid ↔ Bold. Transparent ↔ Opaque. Virtuous ↔ Corrupt.

PREFIX ANTONYMS:
Happy ↔ Unhappy. Honest ↔ Dishonest. Legal ↔ Illegal. Possible ↔ Impossible. Responsible ↔ Irresponsible. Regular ↔ Irregular. Mature ↔ Immature. Literate ↔ Illiterate. Fortunate ↔ Unfortunate. Visible ↔ Invisible.

TRICKY PAIRS (commonly confused):
Aloof (distant) ≠ Close. Benign (harmless/kind) ≠ Malignant. Candid (frank) = Frank. Fastidious (very fussy) ≈ Meticulous. Prodigal (wasteful) ≠ Thrifty.
points: Synonyms have similar meanings; antonyms have opposite meanings.
Brave synonyms: courageous, valiant, intrepid, gallant, dauntless.
Diligent synonyms: hardworking, industrious, assiduous, painstaking.
Genuine synonyms: authentic, real, sincere, bona fide.
Transparent ↔ Opaque; Humble ↔ Arrogant; Lethargic ↔ Energetic.
Prefix un-: unhappy, uncertain, unofficial, unusual.
Prefix dis-: dishonest, disagree, disloyal, discourage.
Prefix in-/im-/ir-/il-: incorrect, impossible, irregular, illegal.
Abundant ↔ Scarce; Eminent ↔ Obscure; Genuine ↔ Counterfeit.
Context matters: some words have multiple synonyms but only one fits a specific sentence.
examples: Synonym: The valiant (= brave) soldier received the medal.
Antonym: He is eminent (famous) in his field. ↔ She is obscure (unknown).
Prefix antonym: The plan is feasible. ↔ The plan is infeasible/unfeasible.
Synonym in context: She is an industrious (= diligent) student who never wastes time.
Antonym: The river was abundant with fish last year; now it is scarce.
ag-6.summary: Synonyms share meanings (brave = courageous = valiant); antonyms are opposites (brave ↔ cowardly). Key antonym prefixes: un- (unhappy), dis- (dishonest), in-/im-/ir-/il- (incorrect/impossible/irregular/illegal). Important pairs for NEA: genuine/fake, humble/arrogant, diligent/lazy, transparent/opaque, abundant/scarce, eminent/obscure, lethargic/energetic. Always check context — choose the synonym that fits the meaning of the sentence.

ip-2.title: Phrases and Their Usage in Sentences
ip-2.notes:
A phrase is a group of words that functions as a single unit in a sentence. Unlike a clause, a phrase does not contain both a subject and a finite verb. Understanding different types of phrases and important phrasal verbs is essential for NEA.

TYPES OF PHRASES:

1. NOUN PHRASE: a noun plus its modifiers. Functions as subject, object, or complement.
Example: 'The brave naval officer' received the medal.

2. VERB PHRASE: the main verb plus auxiliaries.
Example: She has been working all day.

3. ADJECTIVE PHRASE: an adjective plus its modifiers.
Example: He is very tall (very tall = adjective phrase).

4. ADVERB PHRASE: an adverb plus modifiers.
Example: She speaks quite fluently.

5. PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE: preposition + noun/pronoun.
Example: He sat on the deck of the ship.

IMPORTANT PHRASAL VERBS:
Break down = stop functioning / have an emotional collapse. The car broke down on the highway.
Bring up = raise (a child) / mention a topic. He was brought up by his grandfather.
Call off = cancel. The exercise was called off due to rain.
Carry on = continue. Carry on with your training.
Come across = find unexpectedly. I came across an interesting article.
Drop off = leave someone somewhere. He dropped off the cadets at the base.
Fall back on = rely on when other options fail. Always have a backup plan to fall back on.
Give up = stop trying / quit. Never give up on your dreams.
Go through = experience / examine carefully. He went through a difficult time.
Hold on = wait. Hold on, I'll be right there.
Look into = investigate. The committee will look into the matter.
Make up = invent / reconcile. Don't make up excuses. They made up after the argument.
Put off = postpone. The meeting was put off to next week.
Run out of = exhaust supply. We ran out of fuel.
Set up = establish. The Navy set up a new base.
Take off = remove / depart (plane) / become successful. The aircraft took off at dawn.
Turn down = refuse / lower volume. He turned down the offer. Turn down the volume.
Work out = exercise / solve a problem. Work out the equation carefully.
points: A phrase is a group of words with no finite verb — it functions as one unit.
Noun phrase = noun + modifiers. Verb phrase = main verb + auxiliaries.
Prepositional phrase = preposition + noun (on the deck, in the room).
Phrasal verbs: verb + preposition/adverb with a new idiomatic meaning.
Break down = stop working/collapse; Bring up = raise a child/mention topic.
Call off = cancel; Carry on = continue; Come across = find unexpectedly.
Give up = quit; Look into = investigate; Put off = postpone.
Run out of = exhaust supply; Take off = depart/become successful.
Turn down = refuse; Work out = exercise/solve.
Context determines the meaning of phrasal verbs — same verb, different particles, different meanings.
examples: Phrasal verb: The match was called off (= cancelled) due to bad weather.
Phrasal verb: She came across (= found unexpectedly) an old letter in the drawer.
Phrasal verb: He turned down (= refused) the promotion to stay near his family.
Prepositional phrase: The flag was hoisted at the top of the mast.
Noun phrase: The young naval cadet from Kerala was selected for the mission.
ip-2.summary: Phrases are word groups that function as one unit without a finite verb. Types: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase, prepositional phrase. Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a preposition/adverb to create new meanings: break down (stop working), call off (cancel), give up (quit), look into (investigate), put off (postpone), run out of (exhaust), turn down (refuse), come across (find unexpectedly). Meanings change with different particles.

voc-2.title: One-Word Substitution
voc-2.notes:
One-word substitution replaces a descriptive phrase with a single precise word. These questions test vocabulary precision and are a regular feature in NEA English.

CATEGORY 1 — PEOPLE AND PROFESSIONS:
One who can speak two languages = Bilingual.
One who can speak many languages = Polyglot.
One who looks on the bright side = Optimist.
One who looks on the dark side = Pessimist.
One who believes in God = Theist.
One who does not believe in God = Atheist.
One who questions God's existence = Agnostic.
One who eats both plants and animals = Omnivore.
One who eats only plants = Herbivore.
One who eats only meat = Carnivore.
One who is 100 years old = Centenarian.
One who lives to a very old age = Nonagenarian (90s).
One who treats mental illness = Psychiatrist.
One who treats eye disorders = Ophthalmologist.
One who studies stars = Astronomer.
One who studies rocks/earth = Geologist.
One who studies insects = Entomologist.
One who studies birds = Ornithologist.
One who studies ancient things = Archaeologist.
One who performs operations = Surgeon.
One who makes/sells spectacles = Optician.

CATEGORY 2 — PLACES AND THINGS:
A place where animals are kept = Zoo.
A place where bees are kept = Apiary.
A place where fish are kept = Aquarium.
A place where bread is baked = Bakery.
A place where medicines are sold = Pharmacy/Chemist.
A building where aircraft are kept = Hangar.
A place where soldiers are stationed = Barracks.
A building where monks live = Monastery.
A place where paintings are exhibited = Gallery.

CATEGORY 3 — ACTIONS AND STATES:
To look at someone with longing = Yearn.
A sudden, violent storm = Squall.
Fear of water = Hydrophobia.
Fear of heights = Acrophobia.
Fear of closed spaces = Claustrophobia.
Fear of open spaces = Agoraphobia.
The killing of a king = Regicide.
The killing of one's father = Patricide.
The killing of one's mother = Matricide.
The killing of one's brother = Fratricide.
The killing of one's self = Suicide.
Killing of human beings = Homicide.

CATEGORY 4 — GROUPS:
A group of fish = Shoal.
A group of cattle = Herd.
A group of sheep = Flock.
A group of lions = Pride.
A group of wolves = Pack.
A group of soldiers = Troop/Battalion.
A group of sailors = Crew.
points: Polyglot = speaks many languages; Bilingual = speaks two.
Atheist = no belief in God; Theist = believes in God; Agnostic = uncertain.
Astronomer = studies stars; Geologist = studies earth; Entomologist = insects.
Omnivore = eats both; Herbivore = only plants; Carnivore = only meat.
Apiary = bees; Aquarium = fish; Hangar = aircraft; Barracks = soldiers.
Hydrophobia = fear of water; Acrophobia = heights; Claustrophobia = closed spaces.
Regicide = killing a king; Patricide = father; Matricide = mother; Fratricide = brother.
Shoal = group of fish; Herd = cattle; Flock = sheep; Pride = lions; Pack = wolves.
Ophthalmologist = eye doctor; Psychiatrist = mental health; Optician = spectacles.
Centenarian = 100 years old; Archaeologist = studies ancient things.
examples: One word: 'A person who speaks many languages' = Polyglot.
One word: 'A place where aircraft are housed' = Hangar.
One word: 'The killing of one's own father' = Patricide.
One word: 'Fear of closed spaces' = Claustrophobia.
One word: 'A group of sheep' = Flock.
voc-2.summary: One-word substitution replaces a phrase with a single precise word. Key categories: people (polyglot, atheist, omnivore, astronomer), places (apiary, aquarium, hangar, barracks), phobias (hydrophobia, acrophobia, claustrophobia), murders (regicide, patricide, matricide, fratricide), and group names (shoal, herd, flock, pride, pack). Memorise these by category for easy recall in exams.
