questions.explanation: F₂ = F₁ × (A₂/A₁) = 100 F₁. Output force is 100 times input force.

mfw-3.title: Surface Tension and Viscosity
mfw-3.notes:
Surface tension and viscosity are important fluid properties with many real-world applications.

SURFACE TENSION:
The tendency of a liquid surface to minimize its area, behaving like a stretched elastic membrane.
Cause: Cohesive forces between liquid molecules. Surface molecules experience net inward pull.
Unit: N/m (force per unit length) or J/m² (energy per unit area)
Symbol: T or γ or S

EFFECTS OF SURFACE TENSION:
Spherical shape of droplets (minimum surface area).
Capillary rise/fall.
Insects walking on water (water strider).
Needle floating on water.
Meniscus in glass tubes.

CAPILLARY ACTION:
Rise in narrow tubes due to surface tension.
h = 2T cosθ / (ρgr)
where T=surface tension, θ=contact angle, ρ=density, r=tube radius
Water (concave meniscus, θ<90°): rises in glass.
Mercury (convex meniscus, θ>90°): falls in glass.

EXCESS PRESSURE:
Inside a liquid drop: ΔP = 2T/r
Inside a soap bubble (two surfaces): ΔP = 4T/r

FACTORS AFFECTING SURFACE TENSION:
Decreases with temperature increase.
Decreases with addition of surfactant (soap, detergent).
Contaminants reduce surface tension.

VISCOSITY:
Internal resistance of fluid to flow. 'Fluid friction'.
Symbol: η (eta). Unit: Pa·s or N·s/m² or Poise (1 P = 0.1 Pa·s)

STOKES' LAW:
Drag force on sphere moving slowly through viscous fluid:
F = 6πηrv
where η=viscosity, r=radius, v=velocity

TERMINAL VELOCITY:
When drag force + buoyancy = weight:
vt = 2r²(ρ-σ)g / 9η
where ρ=density of sphere, σ=density of fluid

Factors: Increases with r², decreases with η.
points: Surface tension: inward cohesive force at surface. Unit: N/m.
Drops are spherical: minimum surface area for given volume.
Capillary rise: h=2Tcosθ/ρgr. Water rises; mercury falls in glass.
Excess pressure in drop: 2T/r. In soap bubble: 4T/r (two surfaces).
Surface tension decreases with temperature and with soap/detergent.
Viscosity: fluid's internal resistance to flow. Unit: Pa·s.
Stokes' Law: drag F=6πηrv on sphere in viscous fluid.
Terminal velocity: vt=2r²(ρ-σ)g/9η. When drag+buoyancy=weight.
Higher viscosity → slower flow. Honey > water > air.
Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids; increases for gases.
examples: Soap bubble r=2cm, T=0.03N/m: excess pressure=4T/r=4×0.03/0.02=6 Pa
Water drops spherical due to minimum surface area principle
Rain drop reaches terminal velocity when weight=drag+buoyancy
Motor oil more viscous than water → engine parts glide smoothly
Capillary rise: water in 0.1mm radius tube: h=2×0.073×1/(1000×10×0.0001)≈0.146m
mfw-3.summary: Surface tension (N/m): inward cohesive force minimises surface area. Drops spherical; water rises in capillary (h=2Tcosθ/ρgr). Excess pressure: drop=2T/r; bubble=4T/r. Decreases with temp and soap. Viscosity (Pa·s): fluid friction opposing flow. Stokes' drag F=6πηrv. Terminal velocity vt=2r²(ρ-σ)g/9η when forces balance.

questions.question: Surface tension unit is:
questions.explanation: Surface tension is force per unit length: N/m, equivalently energy per unit area: J/m².

questions.question: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius r:
questions.explanation: Soap bubble has two surfaces (inner and outer), so excess pressure = 2×(2T/r) = 4T/r.

questions.question: Water rises in capillary because:
questions.explanation: Water-glass adhesion > water-water cohesion → contact angle < 90° → concave meniscus → capillary rise.

questions.question: Surface tension of liquid decreases when:
questions.explanation: Soap/detergent molecules reduce intermolecular forces at surface → decreases surface tension.

questions.question: Drops are spherical because:
options: Sphere has minimum surface area for given volume
questions.explanation: Surface tension minimises surface area. For a given volume, sphere has the minimum surface area.

questions.question: Viscosity is:
questions.explanation: Viscosity is the measure of a fluid's internal resistance to flow — its 'thickness' or internal friction.

questions.question: Stokes' Law: drag force F = ?
questions.explanation: Stokes' Law: F = 6πηrv for a sphere of radius r moving at velocity v in fluid of viscosity η.

questions.question: Terminal velocity is reached when:
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity: net downward force = 0. Weight = Drag force + Buoyant force. After this, acceleration = 0.

questions.question: Mercury in glass capillary:
questions.explanation: Mercury-glass contact angle > 90° (convex meniscus) → mercury is depressed (falls) in glass capillary.

questions.question: Viscosity of liquids with increasing temperature:
questions.explanation: For liquids, viscosity decreases with temperature (molecules move faster, reducing intermolecular resistance).

questions.question: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop of radius r:
questions.explanation: Liquid drop has ONE surface, so excess pressure = 2T/r (unlike soap bubble which has 4T/r).

questions.question: Terminal velocity is proportional to:
questions.explanation: vt = 2r²(ρ-σ)g/9η. Terminal velocity ∝ r². Larger sphere → much higher terminal velocity.

questions.question: SI unit of viscosity:
questions.explanation: SI unit of dynamic viscosity is Pa·s (Pascal-second) = N·s/m² = kg/(m·s).

questions.question: Why does a needle float on water despite being denser?
questions.explanation: The needle rests on the water surface, supported by surface tension (the stretched membrane of water surface).

questions.question: Capillary rise h is proportional to:
questions.explanation: h = 2Tcosθ/ρgr. Height of capillary rise is inversely proportional to tube radius: h ∝ 1/r.

mfw-4.title: Elasticity — Stress, Strain and Hooke's Law
mfw-4.notes:
Elasticity is the property of a material to regain its original shape after deforming forces are removed.

DEFINITIONS:
Stress: restoring force per unit area = F/A. Unit: Pa (N/m²)
Strain: fractional change in dimension (dimensionless)
Longitudinal strain = ΔL/L
Volumetric strain = ΔV/V
Shear strain = x/L (lateral displacement/original length) = tan φ

HOOKE'S LAW:
Within elastic limit: Stress ∝ Strain
Stress = E × Strain (E = elastic modulus)

ELASTIC MODULI:

1. YOUNG'S MODULUS (Y):
For longitudinal stress and strain:
Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL)
Unit: Pa
For steel: Y ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa
For rubber: Y ≈ 10⁷ Pa

2. BULK MODULUS (B):
For volumetric stress and strain:
B = -P/(ΔV/V) = -PV/ΔV
Negative sign: volume decreases when pressure increases.
Compressibility K = 1/B
Gases have much lower B than solids.

3. MODULUS OF RIGIDITY (SHEAR MODULUS, G):
For shear stress and strain:
G = (F/A)/(x/L) = FL/(Ax)

POISSON'S RATIO (ν):
ν = lateral strain / longitudinal strain = -(ΔD/D)/(ΔL/L)
Range: -1 < ν < 0.5 for most materials
For rubber: ν ≈ 0.5
For steel: ν ≈ 0.3

ELASTIC POTENTIAL ENERGY:
Energy stored per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain = stress²/2E
Total energy stored in wire: U = ½ × F × ΔL

ELASTIC LIMIT: Maximum stress beyond which material does not return to original shape.
PLASTIC DEFORMATION: Permanent change beyond elastic limit.
FRACTURE POINT: Material breaks.
points: Stress = F/A (Pa). Strain = change/original (dimensionless).
Hooke's Law: Stress ∝ Strain within elastic limit. E = Stress/Strain.
Young's modulus Y = FL/(AΔL). For longitudinal deformation.
Bulk modulus B = -PV/ΔV. For volumetric compression.
Shear modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. For shape change.
Elastic potential energy per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain.
Elastic limit: material returns to original. Beyond it: plastic deformation.
Poisson's ratio ν = lateral strain/longitudinal strain ≈ 0.3 (steel), 0.5 (rubber).
Steel has high Young's modulus (stiff). Rubber has low Y (flexible).
Compressibility K = 1/B. Gases highly compressible (low B).
examples: Steel wire L=2m, A=10⁻⁶m², F=100N: ΔL=FL/YA=100×2/(2×10¹¹×10⁻⁶)=10⁻³m=1mm
Elastic PE: wire stretched by ΔL=1mm with F=100N: U=½×100×10⁻³=0.05J
Bulk modulus: pressure 10⁵ Pa reduces water volume by 0.005%: B=10⁵/0.00005=2×10⁹ Pa
Young's modulus Y: steel(2×10¹¹) > aluminium(7×10¹⁰) > glass(7×10¹⁰) > rubber(~10⁷)
Shear: cube of side L displaced by x under force F: G=FL/(Ax)
mfw-4.summary: Elasticity: material returns to original shape. Stress=F/A; strain=ΔL/L. Hooke's Law: stress∝strain up to elastic limit. Young's modulus Y=FL/(AΔL) — longitudinal. Bulk modulus B=-PV/ΔV — volumetric. Shear modulus G — shape change. Elastic PE per volume=½×stress×strain. Beyond elastic limit: plastic deformation. Fracture = breaking point.

questions.question: Stress is defined as:
questions.explanation: Stress = F/A = restoring force per unit cross-sectional area. Unit: Pascal (Pa).

questions.question: Strain is:
questions.explanation: Strain = ΔL/L is a dimensionless ratio. It has no units.

questions.question: Hooke's Law is valid:
questions.explanation: Hooke's Law (stress ∝ strain) is valid only within the elastic limit of the material.

questions.question: Young's Modulus Y = ?
questions.explanation: Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). F=force, L=original length, A=area, ΔL=extension.

questions.question: Bulk modulus relates to:
questions.explanation: Bulk modulus B = -P/(ΔV/V) relates hydrostatic pressure to volumetric strain.

questions.question: Elastic potential energy stored in stretched wire:
questions.explanation: Elastic PE = ½ × Force × Extension = ½FΔL (analogous to ½kx² for spring).

questions.question: Material with highest Young's modulus is most:
questions.explanation: High Young's modulus = high stress for given strain = stiff material. Steel is stiffer than rubber.

questions.question: Compressibility K of a fluid:
questions.explanation: Compressibility K = 1/B (reciprocal of bulk modulus). High K means easy to compress.

questions.question: Beyond elastic limit, material shows:
questions.explanation: Beyond elastic limit, material does not return to original shape — permanent (plastic) deformation occurs.

questions.question: Shear modulus G applies to:
questions.explanation: Shear (rigidity) modulus G = shear stress/shear strain. It resists change in shape at constant volume.

questions.question: Poisson's ratio is:
questions.explanation: Poisson's ratio ν = -lateral strain/longitudinal strain. Negative sign because lateral contracts when longitudinal extends.

questions.question: Young's modulus of steel is approximately:
questions.explanation: Young's modulus of steel ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa (200 GPa) — much stiffer than rubber (≈10⁷ Pa).

questions.question: Stress has the same units as:
questions.explanation: Stress = F/A has units N/m² = Pa, same as pressure.

questions.question: Energy stored per unit volume = ?
questions.explanation: Elastic energy density = ½ × stress × strain = stress²/2E = E×strain²/2.

questions.question: Rubber has a low Young's modulus. This means:
questions.explanation: Low Y means small stress (force/area) produces large strain (extension) — rubber deforms easily with small force.

grav-1.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
grav-1.notes:
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation describes the attractive force between any two masses.

NEWTON'S LAW OF UNIVERSAL GRAVITATION:
'Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force that is:
- Directly proportional to the product of their masses
- Inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them'

MATHEMATICALLY:
F = G m₁m₂/r²

where:
G = Universal Gravitational Constant = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
m₁, m₂ = masses of two objects
r = distance between their centres

PROPERTIES:
Always attractive (never repulsive)
Acts along the line joining the two masses
Long-range force (infinite range, but decreases with r²)
Weakest of four fundamental forces
Acts between ALL objects with mass
Independent of medium (acts in vacuum too)

GRAVITATIONAL FIELD:
Region around a mass where gravitational force is experienced.
g = F/m = GM/r² (gravitational field intensity)
Unit: N/kg or m/s²

GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL:
Work done per unit mass to bring test mass from infinity to that point:
V = -GM/r (negative, as gravity is attractive)
Unit: J/kg

GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY:
U = -Gm₁m₂/r
Negative: bound state
U = 0 at r = ∞ (reference point)

ACCELERATION DUE TO GRAVITY (on Earth surface):
g = GM_E/R_E²
G=6.67×10⁻¹¹, M_E=6×10²⁴kg, R_E=6.4×10⁶m → g≈9.8 m/s²
points: F = Gm₁m₂/r². G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².
Gravity: always attractive, acts along line joining masses, infinite range.
Gravity is the weakest fundamental force.
Gravitational field intensity g = GM/r². Unit: N/kg = m/s².
Gravitational potential V = -GM/r (negative). Unit: J/kg.
Gravitational PE: U = -Gm₁m₂/r. Negative = bound state.
U=0 at infinity (reference). Bound objects have negative U.
g on Earth surface = GM_E/R_E² ≈ 9.8 m/s².
F ∝ m₁m₂ (directly). F ∝ 1/r² (inverse square law).
Works in vacuum — independent of medium.
examples: Two 1kg masses 1m apart: F=6.67×10⁻¹¹ N (extremely small!)
At height h above Earth: g'=GM/(R+h)²=g×R²/(R+h)²
Moon orbits Earth: gravitational force provides centripetal force
Gravitational PE of satellite at height h: U=-GM_E×m/(R+h)
grav-1.summary: Newton's Gravitation: F=Gm₁m₂/r², G=6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Always attractive, inverse square law, weakest force, infinite range. Gravitational field g=GM/r². Potential V=-GM/r. PE=-Gm₁m₂/r (negative=bound). Earth's surface g=9.8 m/s²=GM_E/R_E². Force decreases as 1/r² with distance.

questions.question: Universal Gravitational Constant G value:
questions.explanation: G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² — measured by Cavendish experiment (1798).

questions.question: Gravitational force F ∝ ?
questions.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Force is directly proportional to product of masses and inversely to square of distance.

questions.question: Gravitational force is always:
questions.explanation: Gravitational force is always attractive — it pulls masses toward each other, never pushes them apart.

questions.question: If distance between two masses doubles, force becomes:
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². If r doubles: F ∝ 1/(2r)² = 1/4r². Force becomes 1/4th.

questions.question: g = GM_E/R_E² is acceleration due to gravity:
questions.explanation: g = GM_E/R_E² gives the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of Earth ≈ 9.8 m/s².

questions.question: Gravitational potential V = ?
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential V = -GM/r. Negative sign indicates that potential increases (becomes less negative) with distance.

questions.question: Gravitational PE is negative because:
options: It is less than kinetic energy
It represents a bound state (work needed to separate)
questions.explanation: Negative PE means energy must be supplied to separate the masses (they are bound). U=0 at infinity (free state).

questions.question: Newton's law of gravitation is an:
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1/r² is called the inverse square law. Gravity weakens with the square of distance.

questions.question: Range of gravitational force:
questions.explanation: Gravitational force has infinite range — it acts between any two masses at any distance, though it weakens with r².

questions.question: Gravitational field intensity g at height h above Earth:
questions.explanation: g' = GM/(R+h)² = g×R²/(R+h)². Field decreases with square of distance from Earth's centre.

questions.question: Among four fundamental forces, gravity is:
questions.explanation: Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, roughly 10³⁸ times weaker than strong nuclear force.

questions.question: Gravitational force between two masses is independent of:
questions.explanation: Gravitational force is independent of the medium between the objects — it acts through vacuum equally.

questions.question: Cavendish experiment measured:
questions.explanation: Henry Cavendish (1798) measured G using a torsion balance with lead spheres.

questions.question: If mass of one object doubles and distance halves, force:
questions.explanation: F∝m₁m₂/r². m₁→2m₁ (×2), r→r/2 (r²→r²/4, so ×4). Total: F×2×4=8F.

questions.question: Gravitational PE is maximum (least negative) when:
questions.explanation: U = -Gm₁m₂/r. As r→∞, U→0. Maximum value is 0 (least negative), the reference point.

grav-3.title: Satellites and Orbital Mechanics
grav-3.notes:
A satellite is any object that orbits a larger body. Natural satellites (Moon) and artificial satellites (ISS, GPS) follow the same physics.

ORBITAL VELOCITY:
For circular orbit at radius r from Earth's centre:
Gravity provides centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r
Orbital velocity: v₀ = √(GM/r)

At surface (r=R): v₀ = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s
Orbital speed decreases as orbital radius increases.

ORBITAL PERIOD:
T = 2πr/v₀ = 2π√(r³/GM)
T² ∝ r³ (Kepler's Third Law for circular orbits)

GEOSTATIONARY SATELLITE:
Orbits over equator.
Orbital period T = 24 hours (synchronous with Earth's rotation).
Orbital radius: r ≈ 42,000 km (about 6.6 Earth radii).
Height above surface: h ≈ 36,000 km.
Appears stationary relative to Earth's surface.
Used for: TV broadcasting, weather monitoring, communication.
India's INSAT, GSAT series are geostationary.

GEOPOLAR/SUN-SYNCHRONOUS ORBIT:
Passes over poles. Lower altitude (~500-900 km). Used for remote sensing.

ESCAPE VELOCITY:
Minimum speed to escape Earth's gravity:
vₑ = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s
vₑ = √2 × v₀ (orbital velocity at surface)

WEIGHTLESSNESS:
In orbit, both astronaut and satellite fall freely toward Earth (free fall).
Apparent weight = 0 (weightlessness).
Actual weight (mg) still exists — they are in constant free fall.

ENERGY OF ORBITING SATELLITE:
KE = GMm/2r
PE = -GMm/r
Total E = KE + PE = -GMm/2r (negative = bound orbit)

For higher orbit: more PE (less negative), less KE, less total energy.
points: Orbital velocity v₀=√(GM/r)=√(gR²/r). At surface≈7.9 km/s.
Escape velocity vₑ=√(2gR)≈11.2 km/s. vₑ=√2×v₀.
Orbital period T=2π√(r³/GM). T²∝r³ (Kepler's 3rd Law).
Geostationary: T=24h, r≈42,000km, h≈36,000km, over equator.
Geostationary used for communication, TV, weather.
Weightlessness in orbit = free fall condition (not absence of gravity).
Total orbital energy = -GMm/2r (negative = bound).
KE=GMm/2r; PE=-GMm/r; Total E=-GMm/2r.
As r increases: v₀ decreases, T increases, KE decreases.
Sun-synchronous/polar orbit: passes over poles, used for remote sensing.
examples: At surface: v₀=√(gR)=√(9.8×6.4×10⁶)≈7.9 km/s
Escape velocity: vₑ=√(2×9.8×6.4×10⁶)≈11.2 km/s=√2×7.9
GPS satellites at ~20,200km: T≈12 hours
ISS at ~400km: v₀≈7.66 km/s, T≈90 minutes
Geostationary: T=24h, from T²=4π²r³/GM: r≈42,164km
grav-3.summary: Orbital velocity v₀=√(GM/r); at Earth surface≈7.9 km/s. Escape velocity vₑ=√(2GM/R)≈11.2 km/s=√2×v₀. Period T∝r^(3/2). Geostationary: T=24h, h≈36,000km, over equator — used for communications. Weightlessness = free fall. Total orbital energy=-GMm/2r (negative=bound). Higher orbit: slower speed, longer period, higher PE.

Escape velocity is approximately:

questions.question: Weightlessness in orbit is because:

Gravity is cancelled by centrifugal force
questions.explanation: In orbit, the satellite and astronaut are both in continuous free fall toward Earth — apparent weight = 0 (weightlessness).

questions.explanation: vₑ=√(2gR)=√2×√(gR)=√2×v₀. Escape velocity is √2 times orbital velocity.

questions.question: Total energy of satellite in circular orbit:
questions.explanation: Total E = KE + PE = GMm/2r - GMm/r = -GMm/2r. Negative means satellite is bound to Earth.

questions.question: Geostationary satellite orbit height above Earth:
questions.explanation: Geostationary height above surface ≈ 36,000 km (total radius from centre ≈ 42,164 km).

questions.question: As orbital radius increases, orbital speed:
questions.explanation: v₀=√(GM/r). As r increases, v₀ decreases — satellites in higher orbits move slower.

questions.question: Kepler's Third Law: T² ∝ ?
questions.explanation: T²=4π²r³/GM. So T²∝r³ (square of period proportional to cube of orbital radius).

questions.question: Which orbit is used for TV broadcasting/communication:
questions.explanation: Geostationary satellites appear fixed over one point — ideal for TV, telephone, and communication broadcasting.

questions.question: Orbital period of ISS (height ~400km):
questions.explanation: ISS orbits at ~400km altitude at ~7.66 km/s, completing one orbit in approximately 90 minutes.

questions.question: For object to escape Earth, it needs speed ≥ ?
questions.explanation: Escape velocity from Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s. At this speed, kinetic energy equals gravitational PE (½mv²=GMm/R).

questions.explanation: KE = ½mv₀² = ½m×GM/r = GMm/2r. (Positive, since kinetic energy is always positive.)

questions.question: Geostationary satellite is always above:
questions.explanation: Geostationary satellites must orbit in the equatorial plane to appear stationary relative to Earth's surface.

questions.question: Moon is a natural satellite of Earth. It stays in orbit because:
options: There is no atmosphere to slow it
questions.explanation: Earth's gravitational pull on the Moon provides the centripetal force needed for its circular orbit.

grav-4.title: Variation of g with Altitude, Depth and Rotation
grav-4.notes:
The acceleration due to gravity (g) is not constant — it varies with altitude, depth, latitude, and Earth's rotation.

g AT SURFACE: g = GM_E/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s²

VARIATION WITH ALTITUDE (h above surface):
g_h = GM/(R+h)² = g[R/(R+h)]² = g(1 - 2h/R) for h<<R
→ g decreases with altitude
→ g_h < g always

VARIATION WITH DEPTH (d below surface):
Inside Earth, only inner sphere contributes:
g_d = g(1 - d/R)
→ g decreases linearly with depth
→ At centre (d=R): g_d = 0

VARIATION WITH LATITUDE (λ):
Due to Earth's rotation and non-spherical shape:
g_λ = g - ω²R cos²λ
where ω = Earth's angular velocity
At equator (λ=0): g is minimum (rotation effect maximum)
At poles (λ=90°): g is maximum (no rotation effect, also closer to centre)
g_pole > g_equator by ≈ 0.05 m/s²

EFFECT OF EARTH'S ROTATION:
At equator, centrifugal pseudo-force reduces apparent g.
Effective g_equator = g - ω²R ≈ 9.78 m/s²
Effective g_pole ≈ 9.83 m/s²

NOTE:
g ∝ 1/(R+h)² for altitude → decreases faster
g ∝ (1-d/R) for depth → decreases linearly
g = 0 at Earth's centre

WEIGHT VARIATION:
Weight W = mg → varies with g
You weigh slightly more at poles than at equator.
points: g = GM/R² ≈ 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface.
With altitude: g_h = g[R/(R+h)]² decreases as 1/(R+h)².
With depth: g_d = g(1-d/R) decreases linearly. g=0 at centre.
With latitude: g minimum at equator, maximum at poles.
g at equator < g at poles (rotation + shape effects).
Earth's rotation reduces effective g at equator by ω²R.
Weight = mg varies wherever g varies.
For h<<R: g_h ≈ g(1-2h/R) (approximate formula).
At depth = R (centre): g = 0.
g_poles > g_equator by approximately 0.05 m/s².
examples: At h=R (height equal to Earth's radius): g_h=g×R²/(2R)²=g/4
At depth d=R/2: g_d=g(1-0.5)=g/2
At Earth's centre: g=0 (weight=0, but mass unchanged)
g at equator≈9.78, at poles≈9.83 m/s²
grav-4.summary: g varies: with altitude g_h=g[R/(R+h)]² (decreases inverse square); with depth g_d=g(1-d/R) (decreases linearly, zero at centre); with latitude (minimum at equator, maximum at poles due to rotation and shape). Approximate: g_h≈g(1-2h/R) for small h. Weight varies with g — heavier at poles, lighter at equator and higher altitudes.

questions.question: g at the centre of Earth is:
questions.explanation: At Earth's centre, symmetrical pull from all sides cancels out. Net g = 0.

questions.question: g at height h above surface (exact formula):
questions.explanation: g_h = GM/(R+h)² = g×R²/(R+h)²

questions.question: g is maximum at:
questions.explanation: At poles: no centrifugal effect, closer to Earth's centre → g is maximum ≈ 9.83 m/s².

questions.question: At depth d, g_d = ?
questions.explanation: g_d = g(1 - d/R). At surface (d=0): g_d=g. At centre (d=R): g_d=0.

questions.question: At height equal to Earth's radius R, g becomes:
questions.explanation: g_h = g×R²/(R+R)² = g×R²/4R² = g/4

questions.question: g is minimum at:
questions.explanation: At equator: maximum centrifugal effect + slightly larger radius → g is minimum among surface points.

questions.question: Weight of a person increases when they:
questions.explanation: Moving from equator to poles: g increases → Weight = mg increases.

questions.question: Approximate formula for g at small altitude h (h<<R):
questions.explanation: Using binomial approximation: g_h = g[R/(R+h)]² ≈ g(1-2h/R) for h<<R.

questions.question: g variation with depth is:
questions.explanation: g_d = g(1-d/R) — linear relationship. g decreases linearly as depth increases.

questions.question: Why is g less at equator than poles?
options: Earth rotates and bulges at equator
questions.explanation: Two effects: (1) Earth's rotation creates centrifugal effect reducing g; (2) Earth bulges at equator (larger R) → less g.

questions.question: Mass of object changes with g?
questions.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic property — it does NOT change with location. Weight = mg changes because g changes.

questions.question: g at height h = R above surface:
questions.explanation: g_h = gR²/(R+R)² = gR²/4R² = g/4

questions.question: Earth's rotation affects g most at:
questions.explanation: Centrifugal effect is ω²R cos²λ. Maximum at equator (λ=0, cos0°=1), zero at poles (cos90°=0).

questions.question: g at surface compared to at depth R/2:
questions.explanation: g_d=g(1-R/2/R)=g/2. So g_surface/g_depth = g/(g/2) = 2. Surface is double.

grav-5.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Binding Energy
grav-5.notes:
Gravitational potential energy and binding energy are fundamental concepts in orbital mechanics and space science.

GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY:
U = -GMm/r
Negative: bound state (energy needed to separate)
U = 0 at r = ∞ (reference)
U decreases (becomes more negative) as r decreases
Change in PE: ΔU = GMm(1/r₁ - 1/r₂)

Near Earth's surface:
ΔU = mgh (for small height changes, h<<R)

GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL:
V = -GM/r (potential at point due to mass M)
Potential energy U = mV
Potential at Earth's surface: V₀ = -GM/R = -gR

WORK DONE AGAINST GRAVITY:
To lift mass m from r₁ to r₂ (r₂>r₁):
W = GMm(1/r₁ - 1/r₂) = U₂ - U₁ = ΔU

BINDING ENERGY:
Energy required to free a body from gravitational field.
For satellite in orbit: BE = -E_total = GMm/2r
For body on Earth's surface: BE = ½mv_e² = GMm/R

ESCAPE VELOCITY FROM ENERGY:
½mv_e² = GMm/R → v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR)

ORBITAL ENERGY:
KE = GMm/2r (positive)
PE = -GMm/r (negative)
Total E = -GMm/2r (negative → bound)
Binding Energy = |Total E| = GMm/2r

TO SHIFT ORBIT:
Energy to move satellite from r₁ to r₂:
ΔE = GMm/2 × (1/r₁ - 1/r₂)
For higher orbit (r₂>r₁): ΔE > 0 (energy must be added)
points: U = -GMm/r. Negative = bound. U=0 at infinity.
ΔU = GMm(1/r₁ - 1/r₂) = work done against gravity.
Near surface: ΔU = mgh (approximate).
Gravitational potential V = -GM/r. U = mV.
Binding energy = energy to completely free body from gravity.
Binding energy of satellite = GMm/2r = |Total orbital energy|.
Escape velocity: ½mv² = GMm/R → v=√(2gR)≈11.2 km/s.
Total orbital energy = KE + PE = GMm/2r - GMm/r = -GMm/2r.
More negative total energy = more tightly bound orbit.
Energy to raise orbit: ΔE = GMm/2(1/r₁-1/r₂) > 0 for higher orbit.
examples: Total orbital energy at surface orbit: E=-GMm/2R=-½mgR
Binding energy at surface: BE=GMm/R=mgR=100×9.8×6.4×10⁶≈6.3×10⁹J
grav-5.summary: Gravitational PE: U=-GMm/r (negative=bound, zero at infinity). Work lifting m from r₁ to r₂: W=GMm(1/r₁-1/r₂). Near surface: ΔU≈mgh. Potential V=-GM/r. Orbital energy: KE=GMm/2r, PE=-GMm/r, Total=-GMm/2r. Binding energy=GMm/2r. Escape: ½mv²=GMm/R → v=√(2gR). More negative energy = more tightly bound.

questions.question: Gravitational PE U = ?
questions.explanation: Gravitational PE U = -GMm/r. Negative sign because gravity is attractive and reference is at infinity.

questions.question: U = 0 at:
questions.explanation: Gravitational PE is zero at infinity (r=∞). This is the reference point; all bound objects have negative PE.

questions.question: Work done to lift mass m by height h (near surface):
questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface: W = ΔU = mgh (work done against gravity = gain in gravitational PE).

questions.question: Total orbital energy of satellite = ?
questions.explanation: Total E = KE + PE = GMm/2r - GMm/r = -GMm/2r. Negative means satellite is bound.

questions.question: Binding energy of satellite in orbit at radius r:
questions.explanation: Binding energy = |Total energy| = |-(-GMm/2r)| = GMm/2r.

questions.question: Escape velocity is derived from:
questions.explanation: Escape: KE = magnitude of PE → ½mv² = GMm/R → v = √(2GM/R).

questions.question: Gravitational potential at Earth's surface V₀ = ?
questions.explanation: V₀ = -GM/R. Since g = GM/R², GM = gR². So V₀ = -gR²/R = -gR.

questions.question: To move satellite to higher orbit, energy must be:
questions.explanation: Higher orbit has higher PE (less negative), less KE, but the total energy is less negative → more energy needed.

questions.question: KE of satellite in circular orbit = ?
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv₀² = ½m×GM/r = GMm/2r. (Always positive.)

questions.question: PE is more negative in a ___ orbit:
questions.explanation: PE = -GMm/r. Smaller r → more negative PE. Lower orbit has smaller r → more negative PE.

questions.question: Binding energy of object on Earth's surface:
questions.explanation: On surface: binding energy = GMm/R (energy needed to completely escape Earth's gravity).

questions.question: If orbital radius doubles, binding energy:
questions.explanation: BE = GMm/2r. If r doubles: BE = GMm/4r = half. Binding energy halves.

questions.question: PE change when satellite moves from r₁ to r₂>r₁:
questions.explanation: As r increases, -GMm/r becomes less negative (increases toward zero). PE increases.

questions.question: A tightly bound satellite has total energy that is:
questions.explanation: More negative total energy = more tightly bound. E = -GMm/2r: smaller r → larger magnitude → more negative.

questions.question: Gravitational potential energy near surface: which formula applies?
questions.explanation: For small h (h<<R): mgh ≈ GMm/R - GMm/(R+h) = -ΔU. Both formulas give same result for small heights.

ow-1.title: Simple Harmonic Motion — Basics
ow-1.notes:
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is the most fundamental type of oscillatory motion.

DEFINITION:
SHM is a periodic motion in which the restoring force is proportional to and directed opposite to the displacement from equilibrium.
F = -kx (Hooke's Law type)
The negative sign shows force opposes displacement.

EQUATION OF MOTION:
ma = -kx
a = -(k/m)x = -ω²x
where ω = √(k/m) = angular frequency

DISPLACEMENT:
x = A sin(ωt + φ) or x = A cos(ωt + φ)
A = amplitude (maximum displacement)
φ = phase constant (depends on initial conditions)

VELOCITY:
v = dx/dt = Aω cos(ωt + φ)
v = ω√(A² - x²)
Maximum velocity: v_max = Aω (at x=0, equilibrium)
Minimum velocity: v = 0 (at x=±A, extreme positions)

ACCELERATION:
a = -ω²x
Maximum acceleration: a_max = ω²A (at extremes, x=±A)
Zero acceleration at equilibrium (x=0)

PERIOD AND FREQUENCY:
T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k)
f = 1/T = ω/2π

ENERGY IN SHM:
KE = ½mω²(A²-x²) = ½k(A²-x²)
PE = ½kx² = ½mω²x²
Total E = KE + PE = ½kA² = ½mω²A² (constant)
At extremes: E = PE (all potential), KE = 0
At equilibrium: E = KE (all kinetic), PE = 0
points: SHM: F = -kx. Restoring force proportional to and opposite displacement.
a = -ω²x. Acceleration proportional to displacement, directed toward equilibrium.
x = A sin(ωt+φ). A=amplitude. ω=angular frequency. φ=phase.
v = ω√(A²-x²). Max v = Aω at x=0. Zero v at x=±A.
a_max = ω²A at extremes. a=0 at equilibrium.
Total energy = ½kA² = constant (conserved).
At extremes: all PE, zero KE. At equilibrium: all KE, zero PE.
ω = √(k/m). Higher spring constant or lower mass → higher ω.
SHM is projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter.
examples: Spring k=100 N/m, m=1kg: ω=√100=10 rad/s, T=2π/10≈0.63s
A=0.1m: v_max=Aω=1 m/s. PE_max=½×100×0.01=0.5J=Total E
a at x=0.05m: a=-100×0.05=−5 m/s² (directed toward centre)
SHM example: pendulum, spring-mass, LC circuit, tides
ow-1.summary: SHM: F=-kx, a=-ω²x. Displacement x=Asin(ωt+φ). Velocity v=ω√(A²-x²): max=Aω at centre, zero at extremes. Acceleration: max=ω²A at extremes, zero at centre. Period T=2π√(m/k). Total energy=½kA²=constant. Energy oscillates between KE and PE. ω=√(k/m).

questions.question: In SHM, restoring force is:
questions.explanation: F = -kx. The negative sign means force is directed opposite to displacement — always toward equilibrium.

questions.question: Acceleration in SHM:
questions.explanation: a = -ω²x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium (negative).

questions.question: Maximum velocity in SHM occurs at:
questions.explanation: v = ω√(A²-x²). Maximum when x=0 (equilibrium): v_max = Aω.

questions.question: At extreme positions in SHM:
options: v is max, a is zero
v is zero, a is maximum
Both v and a are zero
Both v and a are maximum
questions.explanation: At x = ±A: v = ω√(A²-A²) = 0. a = -ω²(±A) = ±ω²A = maximum. So v=0, a=maximum.

questions.question: Total energy in SHM = ?
options: Both B and C are same
questions.explanation: Total E = ½kA² = ½mω²A² (since k=mω²). Both B and C are equivalent expressions.

questions.question: At equilibrium in SHM:
questions.explanation: At x=0 (equilibrium): PE=½k(0)²=0. KE=Total E. All energy is kinetic.

questions.question: ω (angular frequency) of spring-mass SHM = ?
questions.explanation: ω = √(k/m). Higher spring constant k → higher ω. Higher mass m → lower ω.

questions.question: SHM displacement: x = A sin(ωt + φ). Here φ is:
questions.explanation: φ is the phase constant (initial phase), determined by initial conditions (position and velocity at t=0).

questions.question: KE in SHM at displacement x:
questions.explanation: KE = Total E - PE = ½kA² - ½kx² = ½k(A²-x²).

questions.question: PE in SHM at displacement x:
questions.explanation: PE = ½kx² = ½mω²x². Maximum at extremes (x=±A), zero at equilibrium.

questions.question: Spring k=400N/m, m=4kg. Angular frequency ω:
In SHM, when PE = KE:
questions.explanation: PE=KE: ½kx²=½k(A²-x²) → x²=A²-x² → 2x²=A² → x=A/√2

questions.question: SHM is an example of:
questions.explanation: SHM is periodic (repeats after time T) and oscillatory (moves back and forth around equilibrium).

questions.question: If amplitude doubles in SHM (same ω), total energy:
questions.explanation: E = ½kA². If A doubles: E = ½k(2A)² = 4×½kA². Energy quadruples.

ow-2.title: Simple Pendulum and Spring Systems
ow-2.notes:
The simple pendulum and spring-mass system are two fundamental examples of SHM.

SIMPLE PENDULUM:
A mass (bob) on a light, inextensible string swinging under gravity.
For small oscillations (θ < 15°): SHM
Restoring force: F = -mg sinθ ≈ -mgθ (for small θ)
ω = √(g/L)
Time period: T = 2π√(L/g)

KEY FEATURES:
T depends only on L and g — independent of mass and amplitude (for small angles)
T increases with length L
T decreases with higher g (shorter period on higher gravity planet)
On Moon (g_moon = g/6): T_moon = √6 × T_earth

SECONDS PENDULUM:
T = 2 seconds. Length L = g/π² ≈ 1 m on Earth

INFLUENCE OF FACTORS:
Temperature: L increases with T (thermal expansion) → T increases
Altitude: g decreases → T increases
Acceleration: in accelerating elevator, effective g changes
In free fall: effective g = 0 → pendulum doesn't oscillate

SPRING-MASS SYSTEM:
Mass m attached to spring of constant k.
T = 2π√(m/k)
ω = √(k/m)

SERIES SPRINGS: k_eff = k₁k₂/(k₁+k₂) [less stiff]
PARALLEL SPRINGS: k_eff = k₁ + k₂ [more stiff]

SPRINGS IN SERIES: 1/k_eff = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
SPRINGS IN PARALLEL: k_eff = k₁ + k₂

LOADED SPRING: If spring stretched by x₀ under weight mg at equilibrium:
mg = kx₀
Time period same as unloaded: T = 2π√(m/k)
points: Pendulum period: T = 2π√(L/g). Independent of mass and amplitude (small angles).
T increases with L (longer pendulum → slower). T decreases with g (stronger gravity → faster).
Seconds pendulum: T=2s, L≈1m on Earth.
Spring period: T = 2π√(m/k). Increases with mass, decreases with k.
Series springs: 1/k_eff=1/k₁+1/k₂ (softer). Parallel: k_eff=k₁+k₂ (stiffer).
On Moon (g=g_E/6): T_pendulum=√6×T_Earth.
In free fall: effective g=0, pendulum doesn't oscillate.
Temperature increases L → increases T (pendulum slows).
Altitude increases → g decreases → pendulum period increases.
Spring-mass: ω=√(k/m). Higher k or lower m → higher ω → shorter period.
examples: Pendulum L=1m on Earth: T=2π√(1/9.8)≈2s (seconds pendulum)
L=4m: T=2π√(4/9.8)=2π×0.639≈4s (double length → double period)
Two springs k₁=k₂=100N/m in series: k_eff=50N/m, T increases
Two springs in parallel: k_eff=200N/m, T decreases
ow-2.summary: Simple pendulum T=2π√(L/g): depends only on L and g, not mass/amplitude. Seconds pendulum: T=2s, L≈1m. Spring-mass T=2π√(m/k). Series springs: 1/k_eff=sum of 1/k. Parallel: k_eff=sum of k. On Moon: pendulum period=√6 times Earth value. In free fall: pendulum doesn't work.

questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g). Period increases with length L and decreases with g.

questions.question: Two springs k₁=k₂=k in parallel. Effective spring constant:

questions.question: At higher altitude, pendulum clock:
questions.explanation: Higher altitude → g decreases → T = 2π√(L/g) increases → pendulum slower → clock loses time.

questions.explanation: T=2π√(1/100)=2π/10=π/5 s. Both A and B are equivalent expressions.

questions.explanation: T∝1/√k. If k→3k: T→T/√3. Period decreases by factor √3.

questions.question: Simple pendulum amplitude is doubled (still small angle). Period:
questions.explanation: For small oscillations, T = 2π√(L/g) is independent of amplitude. Period unchanged.

ow-3.title: Wave Motion — Properties and Types
ow-3.notes:
A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy through a medium (or vacuum) without transferring matter.

TYPES OF WAVES:

1. MECHANICAL WAVES: Require a medium.
- Transverse: particles oscillate ⊥ to wave direction. E.g., water waves, string waves, EM waves.
- Longitudinal: particles oscillate ∥ to wave direction. E.g., sound waves, compression waves.

2. ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES: Don't need medium. Travel at c=3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma ray.

3. MATTER WAVES (de Broglie): λ = h/mv

KEY TERMS:
Amplitude (A): maximum displacement of particle.
Wavelength (λ): distance between two consecutive points in same phase.
Frequency (f): oscillations per second. Unit: Hz.
Time period (T): time for one complete oscillation.
Wave speed (v): v = fλ = λ/T
Angular frequency: ω = 2πf
Wave number: k = 2π/λ

WAVE EQUATION:
y(x,t) = A sin(ωt - kx + φ) [travelling in +x direction]
y(x,t) = A sin(ωt + kx + φ) [travelling in -x direction]

SPEED OF WAVES:
On string: v = √(T/μ) where T=tension, μ=mass per unit length
Sound in medium: v = √(B/ρ) where B=bulk modulus, ρ=density
Sound in air ≈ 332-340 m/s at room temperature
Sound faster in solids > liquids > gases

INTENSITY:
I ∝ A² (proportional to square of amplitude)
I ∝ f² (proportional to square of frequency)
points: Wave transfers energy, not matter.
Transverse: particle motion ⊥ to wave. Longitudinal: ∥ to wave.
Mechanical waves need medium; EM waves do not.
v = fλ = λ/T. Angular frequency ω=2πf. Wave number k=2π/λ.
Wave equation: y=A sin(ωt-kx) for +x direction.
Sound: faster in solids > liquids > gases.
Sound speed in air ≈ 332-340 m/s at room temperature.
Speed on string: v=√(T/μ). Tension up → speed up.
Intensity ∝ A² ∝ f².
EM waves: radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma (increasing frequency).
examples: EM spectrum: visible light λ=400-700nm, f≈4×10¹⁴-7×10¹⁴ Hz
Wave y=0.2sin(100t-5x): A=0.2m, ω=100 rad/s, k=5 m⁻¹, v=ω/k=20 m/s
Intensity doubles when amplitude increases by √2
ow-3.summary: Waves transfer energy not matter. Transverse (⊥): string, EM waves. Longitudinal (∥): sound. v=fλ. Sound: solids>liquids>gases; in air≈340 m/s. String speed v=√(T/μ). Wave equation y=Asin(ωt-kx). ω=2πf; k=2π/λ; v=ω/k. Intensity∝A². EM waves need no medium, travel at c=3×10⁸ m/s.

questions.question: Transverse waves have particle motion:
questions.explanation: In transverse waves, particles oscillate perpendicular (⊥) to the direction of wave propagation.

questions.question: Sound is a ___ wave:
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave — air molecules compress and rarefy along the direction of sound propagation.

questions.question: Wave speed v = ?
questions.explanation: v = fλ (wave speed = frequency × wavelength).

questions.question: EM waves travel fastest in:
questions.explanation: EM waves travel at maximum speed c = 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum. They slow down in media.

questions.question: Intensity of a wave is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Wave intensity I ∝ A² (square of amplitude). Doubling amplitude quadruples intensity.

questions.question: Speed of sound is greatest in:
questions.explanation: Sound speed: solids > liquids > gases. Steel ≈ 5000 m/s >> water ≈ 1500 m/s >> air ≈ 340 m/s.

questions.question: Wave number k = ?
questions.explanation: Wave number k = 2π/λ. Unit: rad/m. (Not to be confused with spring constant k.)

questions.question: For wave y=A sin(ωt-kx): wave travels in direction:
questions.explanation: y = Asin(ωt - kx) represents a wave moving in the +x direction. y=Asin(ωt+kx) travels in -x.

questions.question: Mechanical waves require:
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves (sound, water waves) require a material medium for propagation — they cannot travel in vacuum.

questions.question: If frequency doubles (same speed), wavelength:
questions.explanation: v = fλ = constant. If f doubles: λ = v/f → halves.

questions.question: Speed on string v = √(T/μ). If tension quadruples:
questions.explanation: v∝√T. If T→4T: v→√4×v=2v. Speed doubles.

questions.question: Wavelength is distance between:
options: Two consecutive points in same phase
questions.explanation: Wavelength λ = distance between two consecutive points that are in the same phase of oscillation.

questions.question: Period T and frequency f: T = ?
questions.explanation: T = 1/f. Period and frequency are reciprocals.

questions.question: Sound cannot travel in:
questions.explanation: Sound requires a medium (mechanical wave). It cannot travel in vacuum — no particles to vibrate.

questions.question: EM wave with highest frequency:
questions.explanation: EM spectrum ordered by increasing frequency: Radio < Microwave < IR < Visible < UV < X-ray < Gamma rays.

ow-4.title: Superposition and Interference of Waves
ow-4.notes:
When two or more waves meet at a point, the principle of superposition determines the resultant.

PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION:
The resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of displacements of all individual waves:
y = y₁ + y₂ + y₃ + ...

INTERFERENCE:
When two coherent waves superpose:
Constructive interference: waves in phase (path difference = nλ)
Destructive interference: waves out of phase (path difference = (2n+1)λ/2)

For two waves y₁=A sinωt and y₂=A sin(ωt+φ):
Resultant amplitude: R = 2A cos(φ/2)
Resultant intensity: I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2)

Constructive (φ=0, 2π, 4π...): R=2A, I=4I₀ (maximum)
Destructive (φ=π, 3π...): R=0, I=0 (minimum)

BEATS:
When two sounds of nearly equal frequencies f₁ and f₂ superpose:
Beat frequency = |f₁ - f₂|
The amplitude oscillates at beat frequency.
Beats used to tune musical instruments.

STATIONARY (STANDING) WAVES:
Formed when two waves of same amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions.
y = 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt)
NODES: points of zero displacement. At x = 0, λ/2, λ, 3λ/2...
ANTINODES: points of maximum displacement. At x = λ/4, 3λ/4...
Distance between consecutive nodes = λ/2
Distance between consecutive antinodes = λ/2
Distance node to adjacent antinode = λ/4

VIBRATION OF STRINGS:
Fundamental frequency: f₁ = v/2L = (1/2L)√(T/μ)
Harmonics: fₙ = nf₁
String fixed at both ends: nodes at both ends.
Overtones: 2nd harmonic = 1st overtone, etc.
points: Superposition: y = y₁ + y₂ (algebraic sum of displacements).
Constructive interference: path difference = nλ. Amplitude=2A, I=4I₀.
Destructive interference: path difference=(2n+1)λ/2. Amplitude=0, I=0.
Beats: frequency=|f₁-f₂|. Two slightly different frequencies.
Standing waves: two opposite waves. Nodes (zero) and antinodes (max).
Node-to-node distance = λ/2. Node-to-antinode = λ/4.
Standing wave: y=2Asin(kx)cos(ωt). No energy transfer.
String fundamental: f₁=v/2L=(1/2L)√(T/μ).
Harmonics: fₙ=nf₁. nth harmonic = (n-1)th overtone.
Coherent sources needed for stable interference pattern.
examples: Beats: f₁=440Hz, f₂=443Hz: 3 beats/second
Standing wave L=1m string: λ=2m for fundamental, f=v/2
String 2m, tension 100N, μ=0.1kg/m: v=√1000≈31.6m/s, f₁=31.6/4≈7.9Hz
Constructive: two speakers 2m apart, wavelength 2m: path difference=0 → loud
Node-antinode in standing wave: water in Chladni patterns
ow-4.summary: Superposition: displacements add algebraically. Constructive interference: path diff=nλ, amplitude=2A. Destructive: path diff=(2n+1)λ/2, amplitude=0. Beats=|f₁-f₂|. Standing waves: nodes (zero, every λ/2) and antinodes (max, every λ/2 starting at λ/4). String fundamental f₁=v/2L. Harmonics fₙ=nf₁.

questions.question: Principle of superposition states:
options: Waves cannot pass through each other
Resultant = algebraic sum of individual displacements
Only same frequency waves can superpose
questions.explanation: Superposition: resultant displacement = algebraic sum (y₁+y₂). Waves pass through each other unchanged.

questions.question: Constructive interference occurs when path difference =
questions.explanation: Constructive interference: waves arrive in phase → path difference = nλ (integer multiple of wavelength).

questions.explanation: Standing waves form when two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose.

questions.explanation: Nodes are fixed points of zero displacement in a standing wave. Antinodes are points of maximum displacement.

questions.explanation: Node to adjacent antinode = λ/4 (quarter wavelength).

questions.question: Standing wave equation y = 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt). This represents:
options: Standing wave with no energy transfer
questions.explanation: y=2Asin(kx)cos(ωt) is a standing wave. Position (kx) and time (ωt) are separated — no net energy transfer.

questions.question: Coherent sources must have:

questions.explanation: Coherent sources: same frequency and a constant phase difference. Required for stable interference patterns.

questions.explanation: Constructive: R=2A, I∝A²→(2A)²=4A². So I=4I₀ (four times individual intensity).

ow-5.title: Sound Waves — Characteristics and Doppler Effect
ow-5.notes:
Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave requiring a medium. It cannot travel in vacuum.

CHARACTERISTICS OF SOUND:
Loudness: related to intensity (I ∝ A²). Measured in decibels (dB).
dB scale: L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) where I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² (threshold of hearing)

Pitch: related to frequency. Higher frequency = higher pitch.
Quality/Timbre: due to harmonics present. Different instruments at same pitch have different quality.

SPEED OF SOUND:
In ideal gas: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M)
γ = adiabatic index (1.4 for diatomic like air)
At 0°C: v₀ ≈ 332 m/s. At temperature T°C: v = v₀ + 0.6T m/s
At room temp (27°C): v ≈ 332 + 0.6×27 ≈ 348 m/s

RESONANCE:
Frequency of forced oscillation matches natural frequency → maximum amplitude.
Resonance column experiment confirms sound wavelength.

DOPPLER EFFECT:
Apparent change in frequency when source and/or observer are in relative motion.

FORMULA:
f_observed = f_source × [(v + v_observer)/(v - v_source)]

Conventions (take +ve toward each other, -ve away):
- Observer moving toward source: v_o = +v_o
- Observer moving away from source: v_o = -v_o
- Source moving toward observer: v_s = +v_s (denominator uses -)
- Source moving away: v_s = -v_s (denominator uses +)

Simplified:
Source approaching observer: f' = f(v+v_o)/(v-v_s) [f' > f]
Source receding: f' = f(v-v_o)/(v+v_s) [f' < f]

APPLICATIONS:
Ambulance siren (higher pitch as approaching, lower as receding)
RADAR speed guns (microwave Doppler)
SONAR (ultrasound Doppler in submarines)
Astronomy: redshift/blueshift of stars
Weather radar (Doppler weather radar)
points: Loudness ∝ Intensity ∝ A². Measured in dB.
Pitch ∝ frequency. Quality depends on harmonics.
Speed in air: v≈332 m/s at 0°C. Increases by 0.6 m/s per °C.
v=√(γP/ρ)=√(γRT/M) for ideal gas.
Doppler effect: relative motion between source and observer changes apparent frequency.
Source approaching: f'>f (higher pitch). Receding: f'<f (lower pitch).
Formula: f'=f[(v+v_o)/(v-v_s)] with sign convention.
SONAR, RADAR, ambulance siren, red/blueshift — all Doppler applications.
Resonance: forced frequency = natural frequency → maximum amplitude.
Threshold of hearing: I₀=10⁻¹² W/m². dB = 10 log(I/I₀).
examples: dB of sound I=10⁻¹⁰W/m²: L=10log(10⁻¹⁰/10⁻¹²)=10log100=20dB
Redshift in astronomy: galaxy moving away → sound (EM) waves stretched → longer wavelength
ow-5.summary: Sound: longitudinal wave, needs medium. Loudness∝I∝A²; pitch∝f; quality=harmonic content. Speed in air=332 m/s at 0°C; increases 0.6 m/s per °C. Doppler: f'=f(v±v_o)/(v∓v_s). Approaching→higher f; receding→lower f. Applications: SONAR, RADAR, ambulance, astronomical redshift. Resonance: forced frequency=natural frequency.

questions.question: Sound waves are:
questions.explanation: Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves — air molecules vibrate parallel to wave direction.

questions.question: Pitch of sound depends on:
questions.explanation: Pitch is the subjective perception of frequency. Higher frequency → higher pitch.

questions.question: Speed of sound in air at 0°C ≈
questions.explanation: Speed of sound in air at 0°C ≈ 332 m/s. At 27°C: ≈ 348 m/s.

questions.question: Doppler effect: ambulance siren sounds higher pitched when:
questions.explanation: When source moves toward observer, sound waves compress → wavelength decreases → frequency (pitch) increases.

questions.question: Sound cannot travel in:
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a medium. Vacuum has no particles to vibrate → sound cannot propagate.

questions.question: Loudness of sound depends on:
questions.explanation: Loudness is related to intensity I ∝ A². Greater amplitude → higher intensity → louder sound.

questions.question: Doppler formula when both source and observer are stationary:
questions.explanation: No relative motion → no Doppler shift → f' = f (observed frequency = source frequency).

questions.question: SONAR uses Doppler effect with:
questions.explanation: SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) uses ultrasonic sound waves. Doppler shift detects speed of objects like submarines.

questions.question: Speed of sound increases with:
questions.explanation: v = √(γRT/M). Speed increases with temperature T. At constant temperature: speed independent of pressure.

questions.question: dB scale: sound level L = ?
questions.explanation: Sound level in decibels: L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) dB, where I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m².

questions.question: Resonance occurs when:
questions.explanation: Resonance: when forcing frequency matches natural frequency → maximum amplitude response.

questions.question: Which is NOT an application of Doppler effect?
questions.explanation: Reflection of sound is echo — not Doppler. Doppler requires relative motion between source and observer.

questions.question: Source moving away from stationary observer: apparent frequency:
questions.explanation: Source moving away → waves stretch → longer wavelength → lower frequency → lower pitch.

questions.question: Threshold of hearing intensity I₀ =
questions.explanation: I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the threshold of hearing — the faintest sound a human can detect. This corresponds to 0 dB.

questions.question: Quality (timbre) of musical sound depends on:

questions.explanation: Timbre is determined by the harmonics (overtones) present along with the fundamental — why violin and flute sound different at same pitch.

ow-6.title: Reflection and Refraction of Waves
ow-6.notes:
Waves undergo reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference — behaviours that define wave nature.

REFLECTION:
Wave bounces off a boundary.
Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection.
Speed and wavelength unchanged. Frequency unchanged.
Phase change: at fixed (rigid) boundary → 180° phase reversal. At free boundary → no phase change.
Echo: reflection of sound from a surface. Minimum distance for echo ≈ 17m (to hear separately).

REFRACTION:
Wave passes from one medium to another, changing speed.
Frequency unchanged. Speed and wavelength change.
Snell's Law (for waves): v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂ = sin i/sin r
Wave bends toward normal when entering slower medium.
Sound refracts upward in daytime (warm ground makes sound faster below) and downward at night.

DIFFRACTION:
Waves bend around obstacles or through openings.
Significant when λ ≈ obstacle/opening size.
Light diffracts less than sound (λ_light << λ_sound).

LAWS OF REFLECTION:
1. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal are in same plane.
2. Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (i = r).

SPECULAR vs DIFFUSE REFLECTION:
Specular: smooth surface, parallel rays remain parallel.
Diffuse: rough surface, rays scatter in many directions.

TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (TIR):
Occurs when light travels from denser to rarer medium at angle ≥ critical angle.
Critical angle θ_c: sin θ_c = n₂/n₁ = 1/n (n = refractive index of denser medium)
Applications: optical fibres, diamonds, mirages, binoculars.
points: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Speed unchanged.
Fixed boundary: 180° phase change. Free boundary: no phase change.
Refraction: frequency constant, speed and wavelength change.
Snell's Law: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂ = n₂/n₁.
Diffraction: bending around obstacles. Significant when λ ≈ obstacle size.
Sound diffracts more than light (longer wavelength).
Total Internal Reflection: denser→rarer, angle≥critical angle.
Critical angle: sinθ_c=1/n (n=refractive index of denser medium).
TIR applications: optical fibres, endoscope, mirages, diamonds.
Echo: sound reflection. Minimum 17m distance to hear separate echo.
examples: Echo: stand 20m from wall. Time = 2×20/340 = 0.118s > 0.1s → echo heard
TIR: glass n=1.5: sinθ_c=1/1.5=2/3 → θ_c=41.8°. Angles>41.8°: TIR
Refraction: light from air to glass (n=1.5): bends toward normal
Diffraction: sound bends around corners (λ≈1m) but light doesn't (λ≈500nm)
Diamond: high n→small critical angle→TIR makes it sparkle
ow-6.summary: Reflection: i=r, frequency and speed unchanged. Fixed boundary: 180° phase change. Refraction: speed and λ change, frequency constant. Snell's Law: sini/sinr=n₂/n₁. Diffraction: bending around obstacles, significant when λ≈obstacle. TIR: denser→rarer at angle≥critical angle (sinθ_c=1/n). Applications: optical fibres, diamonds, mirages.

questions.question: In reflection, which quantity remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: In reflection, both speed and frequency are unchanged. Wavelength = v/f → also unchanged. Only direction changes.

questions.question: Angle of incidence = 40°. Angle of reflection =
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 40°.

questions.question: In refraction, which quantity remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: During refraction, frequency remains constant. Speed and wavelength change when wave enters different medium.

questions.question: Snell's Law: sin i/sin r = ?
questions.explanation: Snell's Law: sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁. (Ratio of speeds or ratio of refractive indices.)

questions.question: Total Internal Reflection occurs when:
options: Light goes from rarer to denser medium
Light goes from denser to rarer at angle ≥ critical angle
Angle of incidence is less than critical angle
questions.explanation: TIR: light traveling from optically denser to rarer medium at angle of incidence ≥ critical angle → complete reflection.

questions.question: Optical fibres work on the principle of:
questions.explanation: Optical fibres use TIR to guide light along the fibre without loss — light bounces repeatedly off the inner walls.

questions.question: Sound diffracts around corners because:
questions.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when wavelength ≈ obstacle size. Sound λ ≈ 1m matches everyday obstacles well.

questions.question: Phase change at fixed boundary reflection:
questions.explanation: At a fixed (rigid) boundary, reflected wave undergoes 180° phase reversal. Free boundary: no phase change.

questions.question: For echo to be heard distinctly, minimum distance from reflecting wall:
questions.explanation: Minimum time to hear echo = 0.1s (persistence of hearing). Distance = v×t/2 = 340×0.1/2 = 17m.

questions.question: Light bends toward normal when entering:
questions.explanation: When light enters a denser medium (higher n), it slows down and bends toward the normal.

questions.question: Mirage is caused by:
options: Total Internal Reflection in hot air layers
questions.explanation: Mirage: hot air near ground has lower refractive index. Light undergoes TIR in temperature gradient layers.

questions.question: In specular reflection (smooth mirror):
options: Parallel rays remain parallel after reflection
questions.explanation: Specular (mirror-like) reflection: smooth surface reflects parallel rays as parallel rays.

questions.question: Diffraction is maximum when wavelength:
questions.explanation: Diffraction effects are most pronounced when wavelength ≈ size of the obstacle or opening.

questions.question: Which phenomenon explains why we can hear around corners?
questions.explanation: Sound diffracts (bends) around corners because its wavelength (~1m) is comparable to everyday obstacle sizes.

ow-7.title: Vibration of Air Columns
ow-7.notes:
Musical instruments work by setting up standing waves in strings or air columns.

OPEN PIPE (open at both ends):
Antinodes at both ends (free boundaries).
Fundamental (1st harmonic): λ₁ = 2L, f₁ = v/2L
2nd harmonic: λ₂ = L, f₂ = v/L = 2f₁
3rd harmonic: f₃ = 3v/2L = 3f₁
All harmonics present: f_n = nv/2L = nf₁ (n = 1,2,3...)

CLOSED PIPE (closed at one end):
Node at closed end, antinode at open end.
Fundamental: λ₁ = 4L, f₁ = v/4L
3rd harmonic: f₃ = 3v/4L = 3f₁
5th harmonic: f₅ = 5v/4L = 5f₁
Only ODD harmonics present: f_n = nv/4L (n = 1,3,5...)
Closed pipe fundamental = half that of open pipe of same length.

COMPARISON:
Open pipe at same length: f₁_open = v/2L = 2 × f₁_closed
Open pipe gives richer sound (all harmonics).
Closed pipe gives mellower sound (only odd harmonics).

END CORRECTION:
Actual antinode forms slightly outside open end.
Effective length L_eff = L + e (e = end correction ≈ 0.6r for radius r)

RESONANCE IN AIR COLUMN:
When tuning fork held over air column: resonance when column length = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4... (closed pipe)
Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2.

MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS:
Flute, clarinet: open/closed air columns
Organ pipes: open or closed
Frequency tuned by changing effective air column length (valves, finger holes)
points: Open pipe: antinodes at both ends. Fundamental f₁=v/2L. ALL harmonics present.
Closed pipe: node at closed, antinode at open end. Fundamental f₁=v/4L. ODD harmonics only.
Open pipe fundamental = 2 × closed pipe fundamental (same length).
Open pipe harmonics: f₁,2f₁,3f₁,... Closed: f₁,3f₁,5f₁,...
Resonance in closed column at lengths λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4...
Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2.
End correction: effective length slightly more than actual.
Closed pipe gives mellower tone; open pipe gives richer tone.
All harmonics = overtones. nth harmonic = (n-1)th overtone.
Speed v=fλ. At resonance: use resonance length to find λ, then v.
examples: Open pipe L=0.5m, v=340m/s: f₁=340/1=340Hz. 2nd harmonic=680Hz
Closed pipe L=0.5m: f₁=340/2=170Hz. 3rd harmonic=510Hz (only odd)
Resonance at 17cm then 51cm: λ/4=17cm→λ=68cm, f=340/0.68=500Hz
Open pipe sounds richer: flute has all harmonics → fuller sound
Clarinet (cylindrical, closed at reed): mostly odd harmonics → hollow sound
ow-7.summary: Open pipe (both ends open): f_n=nv/2L, all harmonics. Closed pipe (one end): f_n=nv/4L for odd n only. Same length: f₁_open=2f₁_closed. Resonance in closed pipe at lengths λ/4, 3λ/4, etc. Consecutive resonance lengths differ by λ/2. End correction adds slightly to effective length. Open→richer sound; closed→mellower.

questions.explanation: f₁_open=v/2L; f₁_closed=v/4L. So f₁_open/f₁_closed=2. Open pipe fundamental is twice closed pipe's.

questions.question: Successive resonance lengths in closed pipe differ by:
questions.explanation: Resonance at λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4... Difference = 3λ/4-λ/4 = λ/2.

Closed pipe L=0.85m, v=340m/s. Fundamental frequency:
questions.explanation: f₁=v/4L=340/(4×0.85)=340/3.4=100Hz (half that of open pipe)

questions.explanation: A pipe open at both ends = open pipe. Closed at one end = stopped pipe or closed pipe.

questions.explanation: End correction: the antinode forms slightly outside the open end. Effective length = L + e where e ≈ 0.6r.

questions.explanation: 3rd harmonic = 3f₁. For closed pipe: this is the 1st overtone (since 2nd harmonic doesn't exist in closed pipe).

questions.explanation: Difference=75-25=50cm=λ/2. So λ=100cm=1m.

questions.question: Flute is an example of:
questions.explanation: Flute is an open pipe instrument — open at both ends. All harmonics are present, giving its rich tone.

questions.question: Open pipe gives richer sound than closed pipe because:
questions.explanation: Open pipe produces all harmonics (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) giving a complex, richer waveform compared to closed pipe (odd only).

questions.explanation: At first resonance: L=λ/4 → λ=4×17cm=68cm=0.68m. v=fλ=500×0.68=340 m/s.

opt-1.title: Reflection of Light — Plane and Spherical Mirrors
opt-1.notes:
Reflection of light follows two simple laws and forms the basis of mirror optics.

LAWS OF REFLECTION:
1. Angle of incidence (i) = Angle of reflection (r)
2. Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal are in the same plane.

PLANE MIRROR:
Image is virtual, erect, same size as object.
Image distance = Object distance (behind mirror).
Lateral inversion: left-right reversal.
Minimum mirror length to see full image = half the height of person.

SPHERICAL MIRRORS:
Concave mirror: reflecting surface curves inward (like a cave).
Convex mirror: reflecting surface curves outward.

KEY TERMS:
Pole (P): midpoint of mirror.
Centre of Curvature (C): centre of the sphere of which mirror is part.
Radius of Curvature (R): radius of that sphere.
Principal Focus (F): where parallel rays converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex).
Focal Length (f): distance PF. f = R/2.
Principal Axis: line through P and C.

SIGN CONVENTION (New Cartesian):
Distances measured from Pole (P).
Distances in direction of incident light: positive (+).
Distances opposite to incident light: negative (−).
Object always placed on left → object distance u always negative.

MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f = 2/R
MAGNIFICATION: m = −v/u = h'/h

IMAGE NATURE by Magnification:
m positive: virtual, erect image.
m negative: real, inverted image.
|m| > 1: enlarged. |m| < 1: diminished. |m| = 1: same size.

CONCAVE MIRROR uses: searchlights, headlights, shaving/makeup mirrors, solar cookers, ophthalmoscopes.
CONVEX MIRROR uses: rear-view mirrors, security mirrors (wide field of view).
points: Laws of reflection: i=r; incident ray, reflected ray, normal coplanar.
Plane mirror: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted, image distance=object distance.
Spherical mirror: f=R/2. Mirror formula: 1/v+1/u=1/f.
Magnification m=−v/u=h'/h. Positive m→virtual erect; negative→real inverted.
Sign convention: distances from pole, +ve in incident light direction.
Object distance u always negative (object on left).
Concave: converging mirror. Convex: diverging mirror.
Convex mirror: always virtual, erect, diminished image. Used as rear-view mirror.
Concave mirror: image nature depends on object position.
Minimum mirror for full self-view = half your height.
examples: Object 30cm from concave mirror f=20cm: 1/v=1/f−1/u=1/20−1/(−30)=3/60+2/60=5/60→v=12cm (virtual)
m=−v/u=−(−60)/(−30)=−2 (real, inverted, magnified 2×)
Convex mirror: always positive v, so image always virtual, erect, behind mirror
Shaving mirror (concave, f=30cm), face at 10cm: v=−f×u/(u+f)=30×10/(10−30)=−15cm (virtual, upright, magnified)
opt-1.summary: Laws of reflection: i=r. Plane mirror: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted. Mirror formula: 1/v+1/u=1/f; f=R/2. Sign convention: all from pole, incident direction positive. m=−v/u; positive=virtual erect; negative=real inverted. Concave=converging (uses: headlights, solar cookers); Convex=diverging, always virtual (uses: rear-view mirror).

questions.question: Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals:
questions.explanation: First law of reflection: angle of incidence (i) = angle of reflection (r), measured from the normal.

questions.question: Focal length of spherical mirror with radius of curvature 30cm:
Mirror formula is:
questions.explanation: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. This relates image distance (v), object distance (u), and focal length (f).

questions.question: Convex mirror always forms:
questions.explanation: Convex mirror always produces a virtual, erect, and diminished image — regardless of object position.

questions.question: Rear-view mirrors in vehicles are:
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors give a wide field of view with a virtual, diminished image — ideal for rear-view mirrors.

questions.question: Magnification m = −v/u. If m = −2, image is:
questions.explanation: Negative m means real and inverted. |m|=2 means magnified 2 times.

questions.question: In sign convention, object distance u for object placed left of mirror:
questions.explanation: Object is always to the left of mirror (opposite to incident light direction) → u is always negative.

questions.question: Plane mirror image is:
questions.explanation: Plane mirror always forms a virtual (behind mirror), erect (upright), and same-size image.

questions.question: Shaving/makeup mirrors use:
questions.explanation: Concave mirrors form a magnified, erect image when object is between F and P — used as shaving/makeup mirrors.

questions.question: If object is at centre of curvature of concave mirror, image is:
questions.explanation: Object at C (u=R=2f): mirror formula gives v=2f=R. Image forms at C itself — same size, real, inverted.

questions.question: Lateral inversion in plane mirror means:
questions.explanation: Lateral inversion: the left side of object appears as right side of image (left-right reversal). Writing appears mirror-reversed.

questions.question: Minimum length of plane mirror to see your full image:
questions.explanation: A plane mirror half your height is sufficient to see your complete reflection, when hung at the right height.

questions.question: Concave mirror is used in solar cookers because:
options: It converges parallel rays at focus — producing high temperature
questions.explanation: Concave mirror converges parallel sunrays at focus, concentrating heat energy to a point — used in solar cookers.

questions.question: Object at focus of concave mirror. Image forms:
questions.explanation: Object at F: rays after reflection go parallel (never converge) → image at infinity.

questions.question: Magnification of convex mirror is always:
questions.explanation: Convex mirror: v is positive (small), u is negative (large). m=−v/u = positive and less than 1 → diminished virtual image.

opt-2.title: Refraction of Light — Snell's Law and Lenses
opt-2.notes:
Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another due to change in speed.

SNELL'S LAW:
n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
OR: sin i / sin r = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂

REFRACTIVE INDEX (n):
n = c/v (ratio of speed in vacuum to speed in medium)
n of air ≈ 1. n of glass ≈ 1.5. n of water ≈ 1.33.

REFRACTION RULES:
Light entering denser medium (higher n): bends toward normal.
Light entering rarer medium (lower n): bends away from normal.

LENSES:
Convex (converging) lens: thicker at centre.
Concave (diverging) lens: thinner at centre.

KEY TERMS (same as mirrors):
Optical centre (O), Principal focus (F), Focal length (f).
For convex lens: f is positive. For concave: f is negative.

LENS FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
(Note: different sign from mirror formula — minus not plus)

MAGNIFICATION: m = v/u = h'/h
(Note: m = +v/u for lenses, not −v/u like mirrors)

LENS MAKER'S FORMULA:
1/f = (n−1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂]

POWER OF LENS:
P = 1/f (in metres). Unit: Dioptre (D).
Convex lens: P positive. Concave: P negative.
Combined: P = P₁ + P₂ + P₃...

APPLICATIONS:
Convex lens: cameras, projectors, magnifying glass, spectacles for hypermetropia (farsightedness).
Concave lens: spectacles for myopia (nearsightedness).
points: Snell's Law: n₁sini=n₂sinr. n=c/v.
Denser medium: bends toward normal. Rarer: away from normal.
Lens formula: 1/v−1/u=1/f (minus, not plus like mirror).
Magnification for lens: m=v/u (positive, not −v/u).
Convex lens: f positive, converging. Concave: f negative, diverging.
Power P=1/f(m). Unit: Dioptre(D). Convex=+ve, Concave=−ve.
Combined power: P=P₁+P₂.
Myopia: concave lens. Hypermetropia: convex lens.
n_glass≈1.5, n_water≈1.33, n_air≈1.0.
Critical angle: sinθc=1/n. TIR when angle≥critical angle.
examples: Convex lens f=20cm, u=−30cm: 1/v=1/20+1/(−30)=3/60−2/60=1/60→v=60cm (real, inverted)
m=v/u=60/(−30)=−2 (real, inverted, magnified)
Power of concave lens f=−25cm=−0.25m: P=1/(−0.25)=−4D
Combined: P₁=+5D, P₂=−2D: P=+3D, f=1/3≈33cm
Snell's Law: light from air(n=1) to glass(n=1.5) at 30°: sinr=sin30°/1.5=0.5/1.5=1/3→r=19.47°
opt-2.summary: Refraction: n₁sini=n₂sinr (Snell's Law). n=c/v. Denser medium→bends toward normal. Lens formula: 1/v−1/u=1/f. Magnification m=v/u. Power P=1/f(D). Convex (+): hypermetropia. Concave (−): myopia. Combined power=P₁+P₂. n_glass=1.5, n_water=1.33.

questions.question: Snell's Law states:
questions.explanation: Snell's Law: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r. The product n×sinθ is conserved across an interface.

questions.question: Refractive index n = ?
questions.explanation: n = c/v where c = speed of light in vacuum, v = speed in medium. n≥1 always.

questions.question: Lens formula is:
questions.explanation: Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Note the minus sign, unlike mirror formula (1/v+1/u=1/f).

questions.question: Power of lens with f=50cm:
questions.explanation: P=1/f(metres)=1/0.5=2D (Dioptres)

questions.question: Concave lens is used to correct:
questions.explanation: Concave (diverging) lens diverges light rays, pushing the image back onto the retina — corrects myopia.

questions.question: For convex lens, focal length is:
questions.explanation: Convex lens is converging — focal length is positive by sign convention.

questions.question: Light going from glass(n=1.5) to air(n=1) at 30°. It bends:
questions.explanation: Going from denser(glass) to rarer(air) medium → bends away from normal → refracted angle > incident angle.

questions.question: Magnification for lens m=v/u. Real inverted image has m:
questions.explanation: For lens: m=v/u. Real images form on opposite side (v positive), object on left (u negative) → m=v/u is negative.

questions.question: Combined power of +3D and −1D lenses:
questions.explanation: P_total = P₁+P₂ = +3+(−1) = +2D

questions.question: n_water=1.33 means light travels in water at:
questions.explanation: n=c/v → v=c/n=c/1.33 ≈ 0.75c. Light is slower in water than in vacuum.

questions.question: Convex lens, object beyond 2F. Image is:
questions.explanation: Object beyond 2F: image forms between F and 2F on other side — real, inverted, diminished.

questions.question: Dioptre is unit of:
questions.explanation: Dioptre (D) is the SI unit of power of a lens. 1D = 1m⁻¹.

questions.question: Object at focus of convex lens. Image:
questions.explanation: Object at F: refracted rays go parallel → image at infinity (cannot be formed on screen).

questions.question: Hypermetropia (farsightedness) corrected by:
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia: eyeball too short, image forms behind retina. Convex (converging) lens brings image forward onto retina.

questions.question: Lens maker's formula involves:
options: Radii of curvature and refractive index
questions.explanation: Lens maker's formula: 1/f=(n−1)[1/R₁−1/R₂]. It uses the refractive index n and both radii of curvature.

opt-3.title: Dispersion and Scattering of Light
opt-3.notes:
White light is composed of seven colours (VIBGYOR). Dispersion separates them; scattering explains why the sky is blue.

DISPERSION:
Splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism or diffraction grating.
Cause: refractive index of glass varies with wavelength (colour).
Violet light: highest n, bends most. Red light: lowest n, bends least.
Order of deviation: Violet > Indigo > Blue > Green > Yellow > Orange > Red (VIBGYOR)

PRISM:
Light enters and refracts at both surfaces.
Angle of prism A. Angle of deviation δ.
Minimum deviation D: occurs when ray passes symmetrically through prism.
At minimum deviation: n = sin[(A+D)/2] / sin(A/2)

RAINBOW:
Formed by dispersion and total internal reflection in water droplets.
Primary rainbow: red outside, violet inside (one TIR).
Secondary rainbow: colours reversed (two TIR, less bright).

SCATTERING OF LIGHT (Rayleigh Scattering):
Light scattered by particles much smaller than its wavelength.
Scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ (inversely proportional to 4th power of wavelength)
Blue light (short λ) scatters much more than red light (long λ).

APPLICATIONS OF SCATTERING:
Blue sky: sunlight scattered by air molecules. Blue (short λ) scatters most → sky appears blue.
Red sunrise/sunset: sunlight travels long path through atmosphere → blue scattered away → red/orange remaining.
White clouds: water droplets (larger than λ) scatter all wavelengths equally → white.
Danger signals are red: red light scatters least → travels furthest → visible from far away.
points: Dispersion: white light splits into VIBGYOR (violet to red) by prism.
Violet bends most (highest n); red bends least (lowest n).
Rayleigh scattering: I∝1/λ⁴. Blue scatters most, red least.
Blue sky: blue light scattered most by atmosphere.
Red sunset: blue scattered away, red/orange light remains.
Rainbow: dispersion + TIR in water droplets.
Primary rainbow: red outside, violet inside.
White clouds: large droplets scatter all colours equally.
Danger signals red: least scattered, travels furthest.
Minimum deviation formula: n=sin[(A+D)/2]/sin(A/2).
examples: Blue sky: nitrogen and oxygen molecules (size<<λ) scatter blue 5.5× more than red
Tyndall effect: beam visible in colloidal solution (like car headlights in fog)
Sunset: light travels through 300km atmosphere → blue scattered away → red/orange sky
Rainbow angle: primary at ~42°, secondary at ~51°
opt-3.summary: Dispersion: prism splits white light into VIBGYOR. Violet (highest n) deviates most; red least. Rayleigh scattering: I∝1/λ⁴ → blue sky (blue scatters most), red sunset (blue scattered away). Rainbow: dispersion+TIR in water droplets; primary has red outside. Danger signals red (least scattered). Tyndall effect: scattering in colloidal suspensions.

questions.question: In dispersion by prism, which colour deviates most?
questions.explanation: Violet has the highest refractive index in glass → bends/deviates most. Red has lowest n → deviates least.

questions.question: Sky appears blue because:
options: Blue light scatters most by air molecules
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering: I∝1/λ⁴. Blue light (short λ) scatters ~10 times more than red → sky appears blue.

questions.question: Rayleigh scattering intensity ∝:
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering: I ∝ 1/λ⁴. Shorter wavelengths scatter much more intensely.

questions.question: Red sunset occurs because:
options: Red light is emitted more at dusk
Blue light scattered away by long atmosphere path
questions.explanation: At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere. Blue scattered away; longer-wavelength red/orange remains.

questions.question: Order of colours in VIBGYOR (from most to least deviation by prism):
questions.explanation: Deviation order from most to least: Violet>Indigo>Blue>Green>Yellow>Orange>Red.

questions.question: Primary rainbow has:
questions.explanation: Primary rainbow: single TIR in raindrops. Red appears on outside (~42°), violet on inside.

questions.question: White clouds appear white because:
options: Large water droplets scatter all wavelengths equally
questions.explanation: Cloud water droplets are much larger than light wavelength → scatter all colours equally → clouds appear white.

questions.question: Danger/stop signals are RED because:
options: Red is most visible in daylight
Red light scatters least, travels furthest
Red light is cheapest to produce
questions.explanation: Red has longest wavelength → scatters least (I∝1/λ⁴) → penetrates fog and distance best → danger signals use red.

questions.question: Tyndall effect is scattering of light by:
questions.explanation: Tyndall effect: scattering of light by colloidal particles (size comparable to light wavelength). Makes beam visible in fog/milk.

questions.question: Dispersion of white light occurs because:
options: Speed of all colours is different in prism
questions.explanation: Different colours have different speeds (and refractive indices) in glass → different bending → dispersion.

questions.question: In secondary rainbow compared to primary:
questions.explanation: Secondary rainbow: two TIR inside droplets → dimmer (more light lost), and colours are reversed (violet outside, red inside).

questions.question: Which scatters more: blue light or red light?
questions.explanation: Blue (λ≈450nm) scatters ~(700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.5 times more than red (λ≈700nm). I∝1/λ⁴.

questions.question: At minimum deviation in prism, the ray inside:
questions.explanation: At minimum deviation, the refracted ray inside the prism travels parallel to the base (symmetric path through prism).

questions.question: Spectral colours in order of increasing wavelength:
options: ROYGBIV and VIBGYOR are same reversed
questions.explanation: Increasing wavelength: Violet(~400nm)<Indigo<Blue<Green<Yellow<Orange<Red(~700nm). ROYGBIV = Red to Violet in increasing order.

questions.question: Newton showed white light is composed of:
questions.explanation: Newton used a prism to split white light into 7 colours (VIBGYOR) and showed it is a mixture of all colours.

opt-4.title: The Human Eye and Optical Instruments
opt-4.notes:
The human eye is the natural optical instrument. Understanding it helps design corrective lenses and optical devices.

HUMAN EYE:
Cornea: transparent front surface, most refraction occurs here.
Iris: controls pupil size (regulates light).
Pupil: opening for light entry (2–8mm diameter).
Lens: fine focusing (flexible, crystalline).
Retina: screen with rods (dim light, no colour) and cones (colour, detail).
Fovea: most sensitive region, maximum cone density.
Optic nerve: transmits signals to brain.

ACCOMMODATION:
Ability of eye lens to adjust focal length by changing curvature (via ciliary muscles).
Far point: farthest point seen clearly = infinity (normal eye).
Near point: closest point seen clearly = 25cm (normal adult eye).
Range of accommodation: near point to far point.

DEFECTS OF VISION:

1. MYOPIA (Nearsightedness):
Eyeball too long, or lens too converging.
Image forms in FRONT of retina.
Can see near but not far.
Correction: CONCAVE lens.

2. HYPERMETROPIA (Farsightedness):
Eyeball too short, or lens not converging enough.
Image forms BEHIND retina.
Can see far but not near clearly.
Correction: CONVEX lens.

3. PRESBYOPIA:
