Age-related loss of accommodation (ciliary muscles weaken).
Near point moves farther → needs reading glasses (convex lens).

4. ASTIGMATISM:
Cornea/lens not uniformly curved → blurred vision at all distances.
Correction: cylindrical lens.

MAGNIFYING GLASS: Simple convex lens.
Magnifying power M = D/f (object at focus)
M = 1 + D/f (object at near point)
D = 25cm (least distance of distinct vision).

COMPOUND MICROSCOPE:
Objective lens (small focal length) + Eyepiece (moderate f).
Magnification M = m_objective × m_eyepiece = (L/f_o) × (D/f_e)

TELESCOPE:
Astronomical: objective (large f) + eyepiece (small f).
Magnification = f_objective/f_eyepiece.
points: Cornea provides main refraction; lens provides fine accommodation.
Near point=25cm (normal). Far point=infinity (normal).
Myopia: image in front of retina. Correction: concave lens.
Hypermetropia: image behind retina. Correction: convex lens.
Presbyopia: age-related loss of accommodation. Concave/convex readers.
Astigmatism: cylindrical lens correction.
Magnifying glass: M=D/f or 1+D/f. D=25cm.
Compound microscope: M=(L/f_o)×(D/f_e).
Telescope magnification: M=f_o/f_e.
Rods: dim light (no colour). Cones: colour and detail.
examples: Magnifying glass f=5cm: M=25/5=5× (object at focus)
Microscope f_o=1cm, f_e=5cm, L=20cm: M=(20/1)×(25/5)=100×
Telescope f_o=200cm, f_e=4cm: M=200/4=50×
Myopia: person sees clearly up to 1m. Needs concave lens P=−1D
Hypermetropia: near point at 1m. Needs convex lens to bring to 25cm
opt-4.summary: Eye: cornea+lens focuses on retina. Near point=25cm; far point=∞. Myopia (front of retina) → concave lens. Hypermetropia (behind retina) → convex lens. Presbyopia (aging) → reading glasses. Astigmatism → cylindrical lens. Magnifying glass M=D/f. Microscope M=(L/f_o)×(D/f_e). Telescope M=f_o/f_e.

questions.question: Normal near point of human eye:
questions.explanation: The near point (least distance of distinct vision) for a normal adult eye is 25 cm.

questions.question: Myopia is corrected by:
questions.explanation: Myopia: image forms in front of retina. Concave (diverging) lens diverges rays, shifting image back onto retina.

questions.question: In myopic eye, image forms:
questions.explanation: Myopia: eyeball too long or lens too powerful → image converges before retina (in front of it).

questions.question: Accommodation of eye means:
options: Changing focal length of lens to see at different distances
questions.explanation: Accommodation: ciliary muscles change lens curvature → focal length adjusts → clear vision at different distances.

questions.question: Magnifying power of simple magnifier M=D/f. Here D=:
questions.explanation: D = 25cm = least distance of distinct vision (near point of normal eye). Standard value used in magnification formulas.

questions.question: Astigmatism is corrected by:
questions.explanation: Astigmatism: non-uniform corneal curvature. Corrected by cylindrical lenses that compensate in specific direction.

questions.question: Compound microscope uses:
options: Two lenses: short focal length objective + eyepiece
questions.explanation: Compound microscope: short f objective creates magnified real image; eyepiece acts as magnifier for that image.

questions.question: Telescope magnification M = ?
questions.explanation: Astronomical telescope: M = f_objective/f_eyepiece. Large objective focal length + small eyepiece = high magnification.

questions.question: Presbyopia is due to:
options: Weakening of ciliary muscles with age
questions.explanation: Presbyopia: ciliary muscles weaken with age → lens loses flexibility → near point recedes → difficulty reading.

questions.question: Retinal cells responsible for colour vision:
questions.explanation: Cone cells (concentrated in fovea) detect colour and fine detail in bright light. Rods work in dim light but don't detect colour.

questions.question: Function of iris in eye:
options: Control amount of light entering (pupil size)
questions.explanation: Iris muscles contract/relax to change pupil diameter (2-8mm), controlling the amount of light entering the eye.

questions.question: Hypermetropic person has near point at 1m. Power of corrective lens:
questions.explanation: Need lens to form virtual image of object at 25cm at near point 1m. 1/v=1/1, 1/u=1/0.25. P=1/v−1/u=1−4=−3D. Actually: object at u=25cm=0.25m, image at v=1m=100cm. P=1/1−1/0.25=1−4=−3... Hmm, sign convention needed. For hypermetropia correcting lens: P=1/f where f brings 25cm object to appear at 100cm. 1/f=1/(−1)−1/(−0.25)=−1+4=+3D.

questions.question: Far point of myopic person is 2m. Power of corrective lens:
questions.explanation: Concave lens to bring ∞ to 2m: f=−2m. P=1/f=1/(−2)=−0.5D

questions.question: In compound microscope, to increase magnification:
questions.explanation: M=(L/f_o)×(D/f_e). To increase M: increase tube length L, decrease f_o, or decrease f_e.

questions.question: Main refraction of light entering eye occurs at:
questions.explanation: About 2/3 of total eye refraction occurs at the cornea (air-cornea interface). The lens provides fine adjustable focusing.

opt-5.title: Wave Nature of Light — Interference and Diffraction
opt-5.notes:
Light exhibits wave nature through interference and diffraction phenomena.

EVIDENCE FOR WAVE NATURE:
Interference (Young's double slit), Diffraction, Polarisation.
Particle nature: Photoelectric effect, Compton scattering.
Light shows wave-particle duality.

YOUNG'S DOUBLE SLIT EXPERIMENT (YDSE):
Setup: light through two slits S₁ and S₂ separated by d, screen at distance D.
Path difference: Δ = d sinθ ≈ dy/D (for small θ, y = position on screen)
Bright fringes (constructive): Δ = nλ, y_n = nλD/d
Dark fringes (destructive): Δ = (2n+1)λ/2, y_n = (2n+1)λD/2d
Fringe width β = λD/d (spacing between adjacent bright or dark fringes)

CONDITIONS:
Coherent sources (constant phase difference).
Narrow slits.
Monochromatic light for clear fringes.

INTENSITY:
I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2), where φ = phase difference = 2πΔ/λ
Bright: I_max = 4I₀. Dark: I_min = 0.

DIFFRACTION:
Bending of light around obstacles/slits.
Significant when λ ≈ slit width.

SINGLE SLIT DIFFRACTION:
Central maximum: wide and bright.
Minima: a sinθ = nλ (a = slit width, n = 1,2,3...)
Width of central maximum = 2λD/a

DIFFRACTION GRATING:
Many slits. Sharp principal maxima.
Condition: d sinθ = nλ (d = grating element)

POLARISATION:
Light is transverse → can be polarised.
Polaroid filters block one plane of vibration.
Brewster's Law: tan θ_B = n (polarising angle).
Malus' Law: I = I₀cos²θ.
points: YDSE: fringe width β=λD/d. Bright fringes at y=nλD/d.
Constructive: path diff=nλ. Destructive: path diff=(2n+1)λ/2.
Coherent monochromatic sources needed for clear interference.
I=4I₀cos²(φ/2). Max=4I₀, Min=0.
Single slit: central max width=2λD/a. Minima at asinθ=nλ.
Diffraction grating: dsinθ=nλ. Sharp maxima.
Polarisation proves transverse nature of light.
Brewster's angle: tanθ_B=n. At this angle, reflected light fully polarised.
Malus' Law: I=I₀cos²θ (intensity through analyser at angle θ).
β=λD/d: fringe width increases with λ, D; decreases with d.
examples: If slit separation d doubles: fringe width β halves
Single slit a=1mm, D=1m, λ=500nm: central max width=2×500×10⁻⁹×1/10⁻³=1mm
Grating 5000 lines/cm: d=1/5000cm=2×10⁻⁶m. 1st order: sinθ=λ/d=500nm/2000nm=0.25→θ=14.5°
Brewster's angle for glass n=1.5: tanθ=1.5→θ=56.3°
opt-5.summary: YDSE proves wave nature: fringe width β=λD/d. Bright fringes: path diff=nλ. Dark: (2n+1)λ/2. I=4I₀cos²(φ/2). Single slit diffraction: central max width=2λD/a. Diffraction grating: dsinθ=nλ. Polarisation: Malus' Law I=I₀cos²θ; Brewster's angle tanθ=n. Light is transverse wave (shown by polarisation).

questions.question: In YDSE, fringe width β = ?
questions.explanation: Fringe width β = λD/d where λ=wavelength, D=screen distance, d=slit separation.

questions.question: Condition for bright fringe in YDSE:
questions.explanation: Constructive interference (bright fringe): path difference = nλ (n=0,1,2...) → waves arrive in phase.

questions.question: If slit separation d in YDSE doubles, fringe width:
questions.explanation: β=λD/d. If d doubles: β=λD/2d = β/2. Fringe width halves.

questions.question: Maximum intensity in YDSE interference = ?
questions.explanation: At constructive interference: R=2A, I∝(2A)²=4A². So I_max=4I₀.

questions.question: Polarisation proves light is:
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised (vibration in one plane). Polarisation of light proves it is a transverse wave.

questions.question: Malus' Law: I = ?
questions.explanation: Malus' Law: I = I₀cos²θ where θ = angle between polariser and analyser transmission axes.

questions.question: Single slit diffraction: first minimum condition:
questions.explanation: Single slit minima: a sinθ = nλ (n=1,2,3...). First minimum: a sinθ = λ.

questions.question: YDSE requires coherent sources because:
options: Stable interference pattern needs constant phase difference
Only coherent sources can be narrow
questions.explanation: Coherent sources maintain constant phase difference → stable interference pattern. Incoherent → pattern changes randomly → no visible fringes.

questions.question: Width of central maximum in single slit = ?
questions.explanation: Width of central maximum = 2λD/a (twice the distance to first minimum on either side).

questions.question: Diffraction grating condition for principal maximum:
questions.explanation: Diffraction grating: d sinθ = nλ where d = grating element (spacing), n = order of maximum.

questions.question: Brewster's Law: tanθ_B = n. At Brewster's angle, reflected light is:
questions.explanation: At Brewster's angle, reflected light is completely plane-polarised (vibrating perpendicular to plane of incidence).

questions.question: In YDSE, if wavelength of light increases, fringe width:
questions.explanation: β=λD/d. Fringe width directly proportional to λ. Longer wavelength → wider fringes.

questions.question: Zero order bright fringe in YDSE is at:
questions.explanation: Zero-order (n=0) bright fringe: Δ=0, y=0. Located at the centre of the screen where path difference=0. Both statements are same.

questions.question: Young's double slit experiment was first performed by:
questions.explanation: Thomas Young performed this experiment in 1801, providing definitive evidence for the wave nature of light.

questions.question: Fringe width β=1mm in YDSE. If screen distance D doubles:
questions.explanation: β=λD/d. If D doubles: β=2λD/d=2mm. Fringe width doubles.

ce-2.title: Ohm's Law, Resistance and Circuits
ce-2.notes:
Ohm's Law relates voltage, current, and resistance — the foundation of circuit analysis.

OHM'S LAW:
V = IR
V = voltage (Volts, V), I = current (Amperes, A), R = resistance (Ohms, Ω)
Ohmic conductors: R is constant (independent of V and I).
Non-ohmic: R changes (diodes, thermistors, light bulbs).

RESISTANCE:
R = ρL/A
ρ = resistivity (Ω·m), L = length, A = cross-sectional area.
Resistivity depends on material and temperature.
ρ increases with temperature for metals (positive temperature coefficient).
ρ decreases with temperature for semiconductors (negative temperature coefficient).

RESISTORS IN SERIES:
R_eff = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...
Same current through all. Voltage divides.

RESISTORS IN PARALLEL:
1/R_eff = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ...
Same voltage across all. Current divides.
For two in parallel: R_eff = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂)

ELECTRICAL POWER:
P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Unit: Watt (W)

ELECTRICAL ENERGY:
E = Pt = VIt = I²Rt
Unit: Joule (J) or kWh
1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J

KIRCHHOFF'S LAWS:
1. KCL (Junction Rule): Sum of currents entering junction = Sum leaving.
   ΣI_in = ΣI_out (Conservation of charge)
2. KVL (Loop Rule): Sum of all EMFs and voltage drops around any closed loop = 0.
   ΣV = 0 (Conservation of energy)

INTERNAL RESISTANCE:
Real battery: EMF (ε) with internal resistance (r).
Terminal voltage: V = ε - Ir
Short circuit current: I_sc = ε/r
points: V=IR. R=ρL/A. Resistivity ρ: metals increase with T; semiconductors decrease.
Series: R_eff=R₁+R₂. Same current, voltage divides.
Parallel: 1/R_eff=1/R₁+1/R₂. Same voltage, current divides.
Power P=VI=I²R=V²/R. Energy E=Pt.
KCL: currents at junction balance. KVL: voltages in loop sum to zero.
Terminal voltage V=ε−Ir. Internal resistance reduces terminal voltage.
Parallel combination always smaller than smallest individual resistor.
Series combination always larger than largest individual resistor.
Non-ohmic devices: V-I graph is not straight line (diodes, LEDs, filament bulbs).
examples: V=12V, R=4Ω: I=V/R=3A
R₁=6Ω, R₂=3Ω in parallel: R_eff=6×3/(6+3)=2Ω
Power in 10Ω resistor with 2A: P=I²R=4×10=40W
Battery ε=6V, r=1Ω, external R=5Ω: I=6/6=1A, V=6−1=5V
Resistivity of copper ≈1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m; germanium ≈0.46 Ω·m
ce-2.summary: Ohm's Law: V=IR. R=ρL/A. Series: R_eff=sum. Parallel: 1/R_eff=sum of 1/R. Power P=VI=I²R=V²/R. KCL: currents at junction balance. KVL: voltage sum in loop=0. Internal resistance: V=ε−Ir. 1 kWh=3.6×10⁶J. Metals: ρ increases with T; semiconductors: ρ decreases with T.

questions.question: V=IR is Ohm's Law. If V=12V and I=3A, R=?
Resistance R=ρL/A. If length doubles and area halves:
questions.explanation: R=ρL/A. New R=ρ(2L)/(A/2)=4ρL/A=4R. Resistance becomes 4 times.

questions.question: Three 6Ω resistors in parallel. Equivalent resistance:
Power P=V²/R. If voltage doubles (same R):
questions.explanation: P=V²/R. If V→2V: P=(2V)²/R=4V²/R=4P. Power quadruples.

questions.question: KCL (Kirchhoff's Current Law) is based on:
questions.explanation: KCL: sum of currents at a junction = 0. This follows from conservation of electric charge.

questions.question: Battery EMF=9V, internal resistance r=1Ω, external R=8Ω. Current:
Terminal voltage of battery (ε=9V, r=1Ω, I=1A):
questions.explanation: Terminal voltage V=ε−Ir=9−1×1=8V

questions.question: Resistors in series: which is same for all?
questions.explanation: In series: same current flows through all resistors. Voltage drops vary (V=IR, so higher R→higher V drop).

questions.question: Resistors in parallel: which is same for all?
questions.explanation: In parallel: same voltage across all resistors. Current divides (more current through lower resistance).

questions.question: Equivalent resistance of 4Ω and 12Ω in parallel:
For metals, as temperature increases, resistivity:
questions.explanation: Metals: positive temperature coefficient. Increased temperature → more ion vibrations → more electron scattering → higher resistivity.

questions.question: KVL (Loop Rule) is based on:
questions.explanation: KVL: algebraic sum of EMFs and potential drops around any closed loop = 0. Based on conservation of energy.

questions.question: Ohmic conductor has V-I graph that is:
questions.explanation: Ohmic conductors follow V=IR with constant R → V-I graph is a straight line through the origin.

questions.question: Power dissipated in resistor R with current I:
questions.explanation: P=I²R. Power is proportional to I² and R. Also P=V²/R=VI.

ce-4.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Current
ce-4.notes:
Electromagnetic induction is the production of EMF by changing magnetic flux — the basis of generators and transformers.

FARADAY'S LAWS:
1. An EMF is induced in a conductor when magnetic flux through it changes.
2. The magnitude of induced EMF = rate of change of magnetic flux:
   ε = −dΦ/dt = −N×dΦ/dt (N = number of turns)

LENZ'S LAW:
Induced current direction is such that it opposes the change causing it.
(Negative sign in Faraday's law represents Lenz's Law)

MAGNETIC FLUX:
Φ = BA cosθ
B = magnetic field, A = area, θ = angle between B and normal to area.
Unit: Weber (Wb) = V·s = kg·m²·s⁻²·A⁻¹

MOTIONAL EMF:
Conductor of length L moving at velocity v in field B:
ε = BvL (when v, B, L mutually perpendicular)

SELF INDUCTION:
EMF induced in a coil due to change in its own current.
ε = −L(dI/dt), L = self-inductance (Henry, H)

MUTUAL INDUCTION:
EMF induced in one coil due to change in current in nearby coil.
ε₂ = −M(dI₁/dt), M = mutual inductance (H)

TRANSFORMER:
Changes AC voltage using mutual induction.
V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ = I₁/I₂ (ideal transformer)
Step-up: N₂>N₁, V₂>V₁.
Step-down: N₂<N₁, V₂<V₁.
Power: P₁=P₂ (ideal); V₁I₁=V₂I₂

ALTERNATING CURRENT:
I = I₀ sin(ωt), V = V₀ sin(ωt)
RMS values: I_rms = I₀/√2 ≈ 0.707I₀
V_rms = V₀/√2
Peak/maximum values: I₀, V₀.
Frequency in India: 50 Hz. Period: T=0.02s.
RMS used for power calculations: P=V_rms×I_rms.
points: Faraday's Law: ε=−NdΦ/dt. Flux Φ=BAcosθ.
Lenz's Law: induced current opposes change in flux.
Motional EMF: ε=BvL.
Self-inductance: ε=−L(dI/dt). Unit: Henry(H).
Transformer: V₂/V₁=N₂/N₁. Step-up: N₂>N₁. Step-down: N₂<N₁.
Ideal transformer: V₁I₁=V₂I₂ (power conserved).
AC: I=I₀sin(ωt). RMS: I_rms=I₀/√2.
India AC: 50Hz, 220V RMS. Peak voltage=220√2≈311V.
Power in AC: P=V_rms×I_rms×cosφ (cosφ=power factor).
Eddy currents: induced in metal objects in changing B field; cause heating.
examples: Flux changes from 2Wb to 6Wb in 0.1s: ε=ΔΦ/Δt=4/0.1=40V
Transformer: V₁=220V, N₁=100, N₂=1000: V₂=220×10=2200V (step-up)
India 220V supply: V_rms=220V, V₀=220√2≈311V
Motional EMF: L=0.5m, v=10m/s, B=0.2T: ε=0.2×10×0.5=1V
100W light bulb at 220V: I=P/V=100/220≈0.45A RMS
ce-4.summary: Faraday: ε=−NdΦ/dt. Lenz's Law: opposes change. Motional EMF=BvL. Transformer: V₂/V₁=N₂/N₁, V₁I₁=V₂I₂. AC: V_rms=V₀/√2, I_rms=I₀/√2. India: 50Hz, 220V rms (peak≈311V). Power=V_rms×I_rms. Self-inductance: ε=−L×dI/dt. Eddy currents: heating in metals in changing B fields.

questions.question: Faraday's Law of induction states: ε = ?
questions.explanation: Faraday's Law: ε = −N×dΦ/dt. Induced EMF equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux.

questions.question: Lenz's Law states induced current:
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law: induced current direction is such that it opposes the cause (change in flux) — negative sign in Faraday's law.

questions.question: Magnetic flux Φ = ?
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cosθ where θ is angle between B and the normal to area A. Unit: Weber (Wb).

questions.question: Unit of self-inductance:
questions.explanation: Self-inductance is measured in Henry (H). 1H = 1 V·s/A.

questions.question: Transformer V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁. Step-up transformer has:
questions.explanation: Step-up transformer: secondary turns N₂ > primary turns N₁ → V₂ > V₁ (voltage steps up).

questions.question: Ideal transformer: V₁=100V, I₁=5A, V₂=500V. Current I₂:
questions.explanation: Power conserved: V₁I₁=V₂I₂. 100×5=500×I₂. I₂=500/500=1A

questions.question: RMS value of AC current I=I₀sinωt:
questions.explanation: I_rms = I₀/√2 ≈ 0.707×I₀. This is the effective value used for power calculations.

questions.question: India's AC supply frequency is:
questions.explanation: India uses 50 Hz AC supply (same as most of Asia, Europe, Africa). USA uses 60 Hz.

questions.question: Motional EMF in conductor: ε = ?
questions.explanation: Motional EMF: ε = BvL when B, v, L are mutually perpendicular. B=field, v=velocity, L=length.

questions.question: Eddy currents are induced in:
options: Metal conductors in changing magnetic field
questions.explanation: Eddy currents are circulating induced currents in bulk metal conductors placed in changing magnetic fields.

questions.question: Self-inductance EMF: ε = ?
questions.explanation: Self-induced EMF: ε = −L×dI/dt. The negative sign reflects Lenz's law — it opposes the change in current.

questions.question: India 220V AC supply. Peak voltage V₀ = ?
questions.explanation: V₀ = V_rms × √2 = 220 × 1.414 ≈ 311V. The 220V is the RMS value; peak is about 311V.

questions.question: Power in AC circuit P = ?
questions.explanation: AC power P = V_rms × I_rms × cosφ where cosφ = power factor. For purely resistive circuit: cosφ=1, P=V_rms×I_rms.

questions.question: Transformer works on:
questions.explanation: Transformer requires changing (AC) current to produce changing flux for mutual induction. It does NOT work with steady DC.

questions.question: Principle of generator is:
questions.explanation: Electric generators use Faraday's Law — mechanical rotation changes magnetic flux through coil → induces EMF.

heat-1.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection, Radiation
heat-1.notes:
Heat transfers from higher to lower temperature by three methods: conduction, convection, and radiation.

CONDUCTION:
Heat transfer through a material without bulk movement of matter.
Occurs mainly in solids.
Fourier's Law: Q/t = kA(T₁−T₂)/L
k = thermal conductivity (W/m·K)
Metals: high k (good conductors). Non-metals: low k (insulators).
Thermal resistance: R_th = L/(kA)

CONVECTION:
Heat transfer by bulk movement of fluid (liquid or gas).
Natural convection: due to density differences (hot fluid rises, cold sinks).
Forced convection: fluid moved by fan/pump.
Examples: sea breeze, land breeze, air conditioning, boiling water.

RADIATION:
Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (infrared) — no medium required.
All bodies emit thermal radiation.
Stefan-Boltzmann Law: P = σεAT⁴
σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴ (Stefan's constant)
ε = emissivity (0 to 1; blackbody ε=1)
Blackbody: perfect absorber and emitter.
Wien's Displacement Law: λ_max × T = b = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K
Hotter body: shorter peak wavelength.

NEWTON'S LAW OF COOLING:
dT/dt = −k(T−T₀)
Rate of cooling proportional to temperature difference with surroundings.
For small excess temperature: valid approximation.

THERMAL EXPANSION:
Linear: ΔL = αLΔT (α = linear expansion coefficient)
Area: ΔA = 2αAΔT
Volume: ΔV = γVΔT = 3αVΔT
For water: density maximum at 4°C.
points: Conduction: heat through material, no bulk movement. Q/t=kA(T₁−T₂)/L.
Convection: heat by bulk fluid movement. Natural=density difference; forced=fan/pump.
Radiation: electromagnetic waves, needs no medium. P=σεAT⁴.
Stefan-Boltzmann Law: P=σεAT⁴. σ=5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴.
Wien's Law: λ_max×T=constant=2.898×10⁻³ m·K. Hotter→shorter λ.
Newton's Law of Cooling: rate ∝ temperature excess.
Blackbody: ε=1. Perfect absorber and emitter.
Thermal conductivity k: metals high, non-metals/insulators low.
Linear expansion: ΔL=αLΔT. Volume: ΔV=3αVΔT.
Water: maximum density at 4°C (anomalous expansion).
examples: Steel rod L=1m, A=1cm², T₁=100°C, T₂=20°C, k=50W/mK: Q/t=50×10⁻⁴×80/1=0.4W
Sun's surface T≈5778K: λ_max=2898/5778≈0.5μm (visible light — explains why sunlight is mostly visible)
Body T=37°C=310K: λ_max=2898/310≈9.35μm (infrared — thermal imaging cameras)
Blackbody emitting at 1000K: P=5.67×10⁻⁸×1×1×10¹²≈56.7kW/m²
Steel expands 12×10⁻⁶/°C. Railway gap: ΔL=12×10⁻⁶×10×40=0.0048m=4.8mm per 10m rail for 40°C change
heat-1.summary: Three heat transfer methods: conduction (Q/t=kAΔT/L, solids, no bulk movement), convection (fluids, bulk movement), radiation (EM waves, P=σεAT⁴, no medium needed). Stefan-Boltzmann: P∝T⁴. Wien's Law: λ_max×T=constant (hotter→shorter λ). Newton's cooling: rate∝ΔT. Blackbody ε=1. Water density max at 4°C.

questions.question: Fourier's Law: rate of heat flow = ?
questions.explanation: Q/t = kA(T₁−T₂)/L where k=thermal conductivity, A=area, L=length, T₁−T₂=temperature difference.

questions.question: Convection requires:
questions.explanation: Convection involves bulk movement of fluid particles carrying heat — requires a fluid (liquid or gas) medium.

questions.question: Stefan-Boltzmann Law: P = σεAT⁴. If temperature doubles:
questions.explanation: P∝T⁴. If T→2T: P→(2T)⁴=16T⁴. Power increases 16 times.

questions.question: Wien's Law: λ_max × T = constant means:
options: Hotter bodies emit shorter peak wavelength
questions.explanation: Wien's Law: as temperature increases, peak emission wavelength decreases. Sun (hot) → visible. Human body (cool) → infrared.

questions.question: Blackbody emissivity ε = ?
questions.explanation: A perfect blackbody has emissivity ε=1 — it is a perfect absorber and emitter of radiation.

questions.question: Which method of heat transfer needs no medium?
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves — needs no medium. It works in vacuum (how Sun heats Earth).

questions.question: Sea breeze occurs because:
options: Sea water is hotter than land
Land heats faster → hot air rises → sea air moves in
questions.explanation: Daytime: land heats faster than sea → land air rises (convection) → cooler sea air moves to land = sea breeze.

questions.question: Good thermal conductors are:
questions.explanation: Metals have high thermal conductivity (copper ≈ 400 W/m·K, silver ≈ 420 W/m·K). They're excellent heat conductors.

questions.question: Newton's Law of Cooling states rate of cooling ∝:
questions.explanation: Newton's Law of Cooling: dT/dt = −k(T−T₀). Rate of cooling proportional to excess temperature above surroundings.

questions.question: Linear thermal expansion: ΔL = ?
questions.explanation: Linear expansion: ΔL = αLΔT where α = linear expansion coefficient, L = original length, ΔT = temperature change.

questions.question: Water has maximum density at:
questions.explanation: Water shows anomalous expansion — maximum density at 4°C. Below 4°C, water expands as it cools (why ice floats).

questions.question: Stefan's constant σ ≈
questions.explanation: Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ ≈ 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴. Used in P=σεAT⁴.

questions.question: Volume expansion coefficient γ in terms of linear coefficient α:
questions.explanation: γ = 3α. Volume expands in three dimensions, so volume coefficient = 3 × linear coefficient.

questions.question: Infrared radiation from human body detected by:
questions.explanation: Human body at ~37°C emits infrared radiation (λ_max≈9μm). Thermal/infrared cameras detect this for medical, security use.

questions.question: Thermal conductivity is highest for:
questions.explanation: Silver has the highest thermal conductivity (~420 W/m·K) of common materials. Copper (~400) is close. Air has very low k≈0.025.

heat-2.title: Laws of Thermodynamics
heat-2.notes:
Thermodynamics studies heat, work, and energy transformations.

SYSTEM AND SURROUNDINGS:
System: region under study. Surroundings: everything else.
Closed system: exchanges energy not matter. Open: both. Isolated: neither.

ZEROTH LAW:
If A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C.
This is the basis of temperature measurement.

FIRST LAW (Conservation of Energy):
ΔU = Q − W
Q = heat added to system, W = work done BY system, ΔU = change in internal energy.
Alternatively: Q = ΔU + W (energy input = increase in internal energy + work done)
Internal energy U is a state function; Q and W are path-dependent.

THERMODYNAMIC PROCESSES:
Isothermal: constant temperature. ΔU=0, Q=W. (For ideal gas)
Adiabatic: no heat exchange. Q=0, ΔU=−W.
Isochoric (Constant Volume): W=0, Q=ΔU.
Isobaric (Constant Pressure): W=PΔV.

SECOND LAW:
Kelvin-Planck: No heat engine can convert all heat to work in a cycle.
Clausius: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot body.
Entropy (S): measure of disorder. ΔS≥0 for any spontaneous process.
Natural processes: entropy always increases.

CARNOT ENGINE:
Most efficient reversible heat engine working between T_H and T_L:
Efficiency η = 1 − T_L/T_H = (T_H−T_L)/T_H
No real engine can exceed Carnot efficiency.

REFRIGERAT0R:
Moves heat from cold to hot — requires work input.
Coefficient of Performance (COP) = Q_L/W = T_L/(T_H−T_L)

THIRD LAW:
As temperature approaches absolute zero (0K), entropy approaches zero.
points: Zeroth Law: defines temperature and thermometry.
First Law: ΔU=Q−W. Energy conservation. ΔU is state function.
Isothermal: ΔT=0, ΔU=0, Q=W. Adiabatic: Q=0, ΔU=−W.
Isochoric: W=0, Q=ΔU. Isobaric: W=PΔV.
Second Law: entropy increases in natural processes. Heat: hot→cold spontaneously.
Carnot efficiency η=1−T_L/T_H. Maximum possible for given temperatures.
No engine more efficient than Carnot (working between same temperatures).
Refrigerator COP=Q_L/W=T_L/(T_H−T_L).
Third Law: entropy→0 as T→0K.
Entropy: measure of disorder/randomness. ΔS≥0 for spontaneous process.
examples: System absorbs 500J heat, does 200J work: ΔU=500−200=300J
Adiabatic compression: Q=0, work done ON gas=+200J: ΔU=−(−200)=+200J (temperature rises)
Real engine can never achieve 40% Carnot efficiency
heat-2.summary: Zeroth Law: thermal equilibrium is transitive (defines temperature). First Law: ΔU=Q−W (energy conservation). Processes: isothermal (ΔU=0), adiabatic (Q=0), isochoric (W=0), isobaric (W=PΔV). Second Law: entropy increases; Carnot efficiency η=1−T_L/T_H is maximum. Third Law: entropy→0 at T→0K.

questions.question: First Law of Thermodynamics: ΔU = ?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q − W. Internal energy change = heat added − work done by system. (Some books write Q=ΔU+W; same thing.)

questions.question: In isothermal process for ideal gas:
questions.explanation: Isothermal: temperature constant → internal energy constant (for ideal gas: U depends only on T) → ΔU=0.

questions.question: In adiabatic process:
questions.explanation: Adiabatic: Q=0 (no heat exchange with surroundings). First Law: ΔU=−W (work done at expense of internal energy).

questions.question: Carnot engine efficiency η = ?
questions.explanation: Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_L/T_H = (T_H−T_L)/T_H. Maximum possible efficiency for given source and sink temperatures.

questions.question: Second Law (Clausius statement): Heat flows spontaneously:
questions.explanation: Clausius: heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter one. Hot→Cold is the natural direction.

questions.question: Entropy in natural processes:
questions.explanation: Second Law: entropy of universe always increases in any natural (irreversible) process. ΔS_universe ≥ 0.

questions.question: Isochoric process has:
questions.explanation: Isochoric = constant volume. ΔV=0 → W=PΔV=0. All heat goes to internal energy: Q=ΔU.

questions.question: Zeroth Law of thermodynamics establishes:
questions.explanation: Zeroth Law: if A↔B and B↔C thermally, then A↔C. This establishes temperature as a valid measurable property.

questions.question: Refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot by:
questions.explanation: Clausius: heat cannot flow cold→hot spontaneously. Refrigerator does this by consuming external work (electricity).

questions.question: In adiabatic compression, temperature of gas:
questions.explanation: Adiabatic compression: Q=0, work done ON gas (W<0 for system). ΔU=Q−W=0−(negative)=positive → T increases.

questions.question: Isobaric process: work done W = ?
questions.explanation: Isobaric = constant pressure. W = PΔV (work = pressure × volume change).

questions.question: Third Law states entropy approaches zero as:
questions.explanation: Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero (0K), entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero.

questions.question: Heat engine efficiency can never be 100% because:
options: Second Law requires heat rejection to cold reservoir
questions.explanation: Second Law (Kelvin-Planck): no heat engine can convert all input heat to work in a cycle — some must be rejected to a cold sink.

questions.question: System receives 1000J heat and does 600J work. ΔU = ?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q − W = 1000 − 600 = 400J. Internal energy increases by 400J.

mag-2.title: Magnetic Force on Current and Moving Charges
mag-2.notes:
A magnetic field exerts force on moving charges and current-carrying conductors.

FORCE ON A MOVING CHARGE:
F = q(v × B) = qvB sinθ
q = charge, v = velocity, B = magnetic field, θ = angle between v and B
Direction: right-hand rule (or Fleming's left-hand rule for conventional current)
Maximum force when v ⊥ B (θ=90°): F = qvB
Zero force when v ∥ B (θ=0°): F = 0
SI unit of B: Tesla (T). 1T = 1 N/(A·m)

CIRCULAR MOTION IN MAGNETIC FIELD:
Charged particle moving perpendicular to uniform B:
magnetic force = centripetal force → qvB = mv²/r
Radius: r = mv/(qB)
Period: T = 2πm/(qB) — independent of speed!
Cyclotron frequency: f = qB/(2πm)

FORCE ON CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR:
F = IL × B (vector form)
|F| = BIL sinθ
I = current, L = length of conductor
Direction: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (FBI rule)

FLEMING'S LEFT-HAND RULE:
Stretch thumb, index, middle finger mutually perpendicular:
Index → Field (B)
Middle → Current (I)
Thumb → Force (thrust/motion)

TORQUE ON CURRENT LOOP:
τ = NIAB sinθ
N = turns, I = current, A = area, B = field, θ = angle between B and plane of loop.
Maximum torque: τ_max = NIAB (when B in plane of loop, θ=90°)
This is the principle of electric motors.

MAGNETIC MOMENT:
m = NIA (unit: A·m²)
Direction: perpendicular to plane of loop (right-hand rule).
points: F=qvBsinθ on moving charge. Max when v⊥B; zero when v∥B.
Circular motion: r=mv/(qB). Period T=2πm/qB (independent of speed).
Force on conductor: F=BILsinθ. Direction: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.
Fleming's LHR: index=Field, middle=Current, thumb=Force.
Torque on loop: τ=NIABsinθ. Principle of electric motor.
Magnetic moment m=NIA.
1 Tesla = 1 N/(A·m).
Cyclotron uses circular motion of charges in B field.
Lorentz force = electric + magnetic: F=q(E+v×B).
Neutral particle (q=0): no magnetic force.
examples: Electron v=10⁶m/s, B=0.1T, perpendicular: F=1.6×10⁻¹⁹×10⁶×0.1=1.6×10⁻¹⁴N
Circular radius: r=mv/qB=9.1×10⁻³¹×10⁶/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹×0.1)=0.057m=5.7cm
Wire L=0.5m, I=3A, B=0.4T, perpendicular: F=0.4×3×0.5=0.6N
Motor coil: 100 turns, area 50cm²=5×10⁻³m², I=2A, B=0.5T: τ=100×2×5×10⁻³×0.5=0.5N·m
Cyclotron frequency independent of speed: f=qB/2πm
mag-2.summary: Force on charge: F=qvBsinθ, max when v⊥B. Circular motion in B: r=mv/qB, T=2πm/qB (speed-independent). Force on conductor: F=BILsinθ. Fleming's LHR: index=field, middle=current, thumb=force. Torque on loop: τ=NIABsinθ — basis of electric motor. Magnetic moment m=NIA.

questions.question: Force on charge q moving at velocity v in field B (perpendicular): F = ?
questions.explanation: F = qvB sinθ. When v⊥B (θ=90°, sinθ=1): F = qvB (maximum force).

questions.question: A charge moving parallel to magnetic field experiences:
questions.explanation: F = qvB sin0° = 0. When velocity is parallel to B (θ=0°), no magnetic force acts.

questions.question: Radius of circular path of charge in B: r = ?
questions.explanation: Magnetic force = centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r → r = mv/(qB).

questions.question: Force on current-carrying conductor in B: F = ?
questions.explanation: F = BIL sinθ where I=current, L=length, θ=angle between current direction and B.

questions.question: Fleming's Left Hand Rule: index finger points in direction of:
questions.explanation: Fleming's LHR: Index=magnetic Field (B), Middle=current (I), Thumb=Force/thrust direction.

questions.question: Torque on current loop τ = ?
questions.explanation: τ = NIAB sinθ where θ is angle between B and the plane of loop. Maximum when θ=90° (B in plane of loop).

questions.question: Principle of electric motor involves:
options: Torque on current loop in magnetic field
questions.explanation: Electric motor: current-carrying coil in magnetic field experiences torque (τ=NIABsinθ) → rotation.

questions.question: Period of circular motion of charge in magnetic field is:
questions.explanation: T = 2πm/(qB). Period is independent of the speed — it only depends on mass, charge, and magnetic field.

questions.question: SI unit of magnetic field B:
questions.explanation: SI unit of magnetic field B is Tesla (T). 1T = 1 N/(A·m). CGS unit is Gauss (1T = 10⁴ Gauss).

questions.question: Lorentz force is the combined force due to:
questions.explanation: Lorentz force: F = q(E + v×B). The total force on a charged particle from electric (qE) and magnetic (qv×B) fields.

questions.question: Magnetic moment of current loop: m = ?
questions.explanation: Magnetic moment m = NIA where N=turns, I=current, A=area. Unit: A·m².

questions.question: Cyclotron uses the principle that orbital period in B is:
options: Independent of speed (same period at all speeds)
questions.explanation: Cyclotron exploits T=2πm/qB being constant regardless of speed — allows repeated acceleration in same-period alternating voltage.

questions.question: Direction of force on current-carrying wire in B (using Fleming's LHR) when current flows east and B points north:
questions.explanation: Fleming's LHR: index=North (B), middle=East (I), thumb=Upward (Force). The force is directed upward.

questions.question: If current in a conductor doubles (same B, L, angle), force:
questions.explanation: F=BILsinθ. Force directly proportional to current I. If I doubles, F doubles.

questions.question: A neutral atom in a magnetic field experiences:
questions.explanation: Magnetic force F=qvBsinθ. A neutral atom has q=0, so F=0. No magnetic force on neutral particles.

mag-3.title: Magnetic Field due to Current
mag-3.notes:
Moving charges and currents produce magnetic fields.

BIOT-SAVART LAW:
Magnetic field due to a current element IdL:
dB = (μ₀/4π) × (IdL sinθ)/r²
μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A (permeability of free space)

CIRCULAR LOOP at centre:
B = μ₀I/(2R)
R = radius of loop.

LONG STRAIGHT WIRE:
B = μ₀I/(2πr)
r = perpendicular distance from wire.
Direction: right-hand thumb rule (curl fingers = field direction, thumb = current)

SOLENOID:
B = μ₀nI
n = number of turns per unit length = N/L.
Field inside is uniform and strong. Outside is almost zero.
Magnetic field inside ∝ n and I.

TOROID:
B = μ₀nI (inside toroid)
B = 0 (outside toroid)

AMPERE'S LAW:
∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed
Used to find B in symmetric situations (long wire, solenoid, toroid).

FORCE BETWEEN PARALLEL WIRES:
Two parallel wires carrying currents I₁ and I₂, separated by d:
Force per unit length: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
Same direction currents: Attractive.
Opposite direction currents: Repulsive.
Definition of Ampere: 1A is the current in each of two parallel wires 1m apart that exerts force of 2×10⁻⁷ N/m on each other.
points: Biot-Savart: dB=μ₀IdLsinθ/(4πr²). μ₀=4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A.
Long straight wire: B=μ₀I/(2πr). Circles the wire.
Circular loop at centre: B=μ₀I/(2R).
Solenoid: B=μ₀nI. Uniform field inside; zero outside.
Toroid: B=μ₀nI inside; zero outside.
Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl=μ₀I_enclosed.
Parallel wires: same current→attract; opposite→repel.
Force per length: F/L=μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd).
Right-hand thumb rule for direction of B around wire.
1 Ampere defined from force between parallel wires.
examples: Wire carrying 5A, r=0.1m: B=4π×10⁻⁷×5/(2π×0.1)=10⁻⁵T=10μT
Circular loop R=10cm=0.1m, I=5A: B=4π×10⁻⁷×5/(2×0.1)=31.4μT
Two wires I₁=I₂=1A, d=1m: F/L=4π×10⁻⁷×1×1/(2π×1)=2×10⁻⁷N/m
Right-hand rule: current up page → B circles counterclockwise (view from top)
mag-3.summary: Biot-Savart law gives B from current element. Key results: straight wire B=μ₀I/(2πr); circular loop B=μ₀I/(2R); solenoid B=μ₀nI (uniform inside); Ampere's Law ∮B·dl=μ₀I. Parallel wires: same direction→attract, opposite→repel. F/L=μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd). μ₀=4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A.

questions.question: Magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying I:
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/(2πr). Field decreases inversely with distance from a long straight wire.

questions.question: μ₀ (permeability of free space) = ?
questions.explanation: μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A ≈ 1.257×10⁻⁶ T·m/A. This is the magnetic permeability of vacuum.

questions.question: Magnetic field inside a solenoid: B = ?
questions.explanation: B = μ₀nI where n = N/L (turns per unit length). Field is uniform inside a solenoid.

questions.question: Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction:
questions.explanation: Parallel wires with currents in same direction attract each other. (Opposite currents repel.)

questions.question: Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl = ?
questions.explanation: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed. The line integral of B around a closed loop equals μ₀ times enclosed current.

questions.question: Magnetic field at centre of circular loop of radius R:
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/(2R) at the centre of a circular current loop of radius R.

questions.question: Right-hand thumb rule for magnetic field: thumb points in direction of ___, fingers show direction of ___:
questions.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule: thumb points along current direction (I), curled fingers show direction of magnetic field B circles around wire.

questions.question: Field outside a toroid is:
questions.explanation: Ideal toroid: magnetic field is completely confined inside the toroid. Outside = zero.

questions.question: Solenoid with 1000 turns, L=0.5m, I=2A. B = ?
1 Ampere is defined as current that produces force of ___ per metre between two parallel wires 1m apart:
questions.explanation: Definition: 1A = current in each of two infinite parallel wires 1m apart that produces force of 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre on each other.

questions.question: Biot-Savart Law is used to calculate:
questions.explanation: Biot-Savart Law: dB = (μ₀/4π)(IdL sinθ/r²). Used to calculate magnetic field produced by current elements.

questions.question: If current doubles in a solenoid:
questions.explanation: B=μ₀nI. Field directly proportional to current. If I doubles: B doubles.

questions.question: Magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are:
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines around a long straight wire are concentric circles centered on the wire.

questions.question: Force per unit length between parallel wires: F/L = ?
questions.explanation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd). Force per unit length between two parallel wires separated by d.

questions.question: Field inside solenoid depends on:
options: Turns per unit length n and current I
questions.explanation: B=μ₀nI. Depends on n (turns per unit length = N/L) and current I. Not on total turns or length separately.

mag-5.title: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic and Ferromagnetic Materials
mag-5.notes:
All materials interact with magnetic fields, classified into three types.

MAGNETIC TERMS:
Magnetisation M: magnetic moment per unit volume.
Magnetic susceptibility χ: M = χH. Relates magnetisation to applied field H.
Relative permeability μ_r: B = μ₀μ_r H. Ratio of permeability to free space.
Relation: μ_r = 1 + χ

1. DIAMAGNETIC MATERIALS:
χ is small and negative (−10⁻⁹ to −10⁻⁵).
μ_r slightly less than 1.
Feebly repelled by magnets.
No permanent magnetic moment; induced moment opposes applied field.
Examples: Bismuth (Bi), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), Lead (Pb), Water, Gold, Nitrogen.
Not affected by temperature (independent of T).

2. PARAMAGNETIC MATERIALS:
χ is small and positive (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³).
μ_r slightly greater than 1.
Feebly attracted by magnets.
Have permanent atomic magnetic moments (randomly oriented).
Applied field → partial alignment → magnetisation in direction of field.
Curie's Law: M = C·H/T (magnetisation decreases with temperature).
Examples: Aluminium (Al), Platinum (Pt), Chromium (Cr), Oxygen (O₂), CuCl₂.

3. FERROMAGNETIC MATERIALS:
χ is large and positive (10³ to 10⁵).
μ_r >> 1.
Strongly attracted by magnets.
Form MAGNETIC DOMAINS (regions of aligned spins).
Can be permanently magnetised.
HYSTERESIS loop: non-linear B-H relationship.
Curie temperature (T_C): above this, ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.
Examples: Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), Cobalt (Co), Gadolinium.

HYSTERESIS:
Retentivity: B when H→0 (residual magnetism).
Coercivity: H needed to demagnetise completely.
Hard magnetic material (high coercivity): permanent magnets.
Soft magnetic material (low coercivity): electromagnets, transformer cores.
points: Diamagnetic: χ negative, repelled by magnet. Examples: Cu, Ag, Bi, water.
Paramagnetic: χ small positive, weakly attracted. Examples: Al, O₂, Pt.
Ferromagnetic: χ large positive, strongly attracted. Examples: Fe, Ni, Co.
Ferromagnetism due to magnetic domains (aligned atomic moments).
Curie temperature: above T_C, ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.
Curie's Law (paramagnet): M=CH/T. M decreases with temperature.
Hysteresis loop: retentivity (residual B) and coercivity (field to demagnetise).
Hard magnetic material (high coercivity): permanent magnets.
Soft magnetic material (low coercivity): transformer cores, electromagnets.
μ_r=1+χ. Diamagnetic: μ_r<1. Paramagnetic/ferromagnetic: μ_r>1.
examples: Bismuth is most diamagnetic common metal: χ≈−1.66×10⁻⁴
Iron: χ≈5000 (ferromagnetic). Compare: χ_Al≈2.3×10⁻⁵ (paramagnetic)
Curie temperature of iron: T_C=1043K=770°C (above this: paramagnetic)
Hard magnetic: Alnico (Al+Ni+Co) alloys — high retentivity, high coercivity → permanent magnets
Soft magnetic: soft iron — low coercivity → easy to magnetise/demagnetise → transformer cores
mag-5.summary: Diamagnetic: χ<0, weakly repelled (Cu, Ag, Bi). Paramagnetic: χ>0 small, weakly attracted (Al, O₂). Ferromagnetic: χ>>0, strongly attracted (Fe, Ni, Co), domains. Above Curie temperature: ferromagnetic→paramagnetic. Curie's Law: M∝H/T. Hysteresis: retentivity (residual B) and coercivity (H to demagnetise). Hard magnets: high coercivity (permanent). Soft: low coercivity (transformers).

questions.question: Diamagnetic materials are:
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic materials (Cu, Ag, Bi) have small negative susceptibility → feebly repelled by external magnetic fields.

questions.question: Which is a paramagnetic material?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is paramagnetic (χ≈2.3×10⁻⁵, positive). Iron and Nickel are ferromagnetic; Bismuth is diamagnetic.

questions.question: Magnetic domains exist in:
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials have magnetic domains — regions where atomic magnetic moments are aligned parallel.

questions.question: Above Curie temperature, a ferromagnet becomes:
questions.explanation: Above Curie temperature T_C, thermal energy destroys domain alignment → ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.

questions.question: Curie's Law states magnetisation M ∝:
questions.explanation: Curie's Law: M = C×H/T. Magnetisation proportional to applied field H and inversely proportional to temperature T.

questions.question: Susceptibility χ of diamagnetic material is:
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic: χ is small and negative (e.g., −10⁻⁵). Induced magnetisation opposes the applied field.

questions.question: Permanent magnets are made from:
questions.explanation: Permanent magnets need high coercivity (resist demagnetisation) and high retentivity (retain magnetism) — hard magnetic materials.

questions.question: Transformer cores use soft iron because:
questions.explanation: Transformer cores need to reverse magnetisation at 50Hz. Soft iron has low coercivity → easy and efficient reversal with low energy loss.

questions.question: Which metal is most commonly used to demonstrate ferromagnetism?
questions.explanation: Iron (Fe) is the most well-known ferromagnetic material with very high susceptibility and Curie temperature 770°C.

questions.question: Retentivity of a magnet is:
questions.explanation: Retentivity (residual magnetism): the value of B when the applied magnetic field H is reduced to zero.

questions.question: Relative permeability μ_r = 1 + χ. For diamagnetic material:
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic: χ is negative → μ_r = 1+χ < 1. Slightly less than 1.

questions.question: Which material is an example of diamagnetic substance?
questions.explanation: Copper is diamagnetic (χ≈−9.8×10⁻⁶). Iron, Nickel, Cobalt are ferromagnetic.

questions.question: Coercivity is the:
options: Magnetic field needed to completely demagnetise
questions.explanation: Coercivity (coercive field): the reverse magnetic field H needed to reduce magnetisation to zero.

questions.question: Oxygen gas is an example of:
questions.explanation: O₂ is paramagnetic — it has two unpaired electrons giving it a permanent magnetic moment. Used in liquid oxygen demonstrations.

questions.question: Bismuth is the most ___ common element:
questions.explanation: Bismuth (Bi) has one of the largest diamagnetic susceptibilities of all common elements: χ≈−1.66×10⁻⁴.

mag-6.title: Magnetic Properties and Earth's Magnetism
mag-6.notes:
Earth behaves like a giant magnet. Understanding Earth's magnetic field is important for navigation and geomagnetism.

EARTH'S MAGNETIC FIELD:
Earth has a magnetic field similar to a bar magnet tilted ~11° from the geographic axis.
Geographic North Pole ≈ Magnetic South Pole (north pole of compass points toward it).
Geographic South Pole ≈ Magnetic North Pole.
Strength of Earth's field ≈ 25–65 μT (microtesla).
Field has decreased by 10-15% in last 150 years.

MAGNETIC ELEMENTS:
1. Magnetic Declination (D): angle between geographic north and magnetic north.
2. Magnetic Dip/Inclination (I): angle between Earth's field B and horizontal plane.
   At equator: I ≈ 0°. At poles: I = 90°.
3. Horizontal Component (H): H = B cosI.
   Vertical Component (V): V = B sinI.
   tanI = V/H.

MAGNETIC POLES:
Magnetic poles are currently at ~85°N, 133°W (north) and ~64°S, 136°E (south).
They move and reverse periodically (geomagnetic reversal — last ~780,000 years ago).

BAR MAGNET FIELD:
At axial point (along axis): B = (μ₀/4π)(2M/r³) = (μ₀/4π)(2M/d³)
At equatorial point (perpendicular bisector): B = (μ₀/4π)(M/r³)
M = magnetic moment = m×2l (pole strength m, length 2l)

MAGNETIC FIELD LINES:
Emerge from N pole, enter S pole (outside magnet).
Inside magnet: S to N.
Never intersect.
Denser field lines = stronger field.
Tangent at any point = direction of B.

COMPASS:
Freely suspended magnet aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
Points toward magnetic north (geographic north approximately).
points: Earth's geographic north ≈ magnetic south (compass N points there).
Magnetic elements: declination D (angle from geographic N), inclination I (dip from horizontal).
At equator: dip ≈0°. At poles: dip=90°.
H=BcosI, V=BsinI, tanI=V/H.
Bar magnet axial field: 2M/r³ (μ₀/4π factor).
Bar magnet equatorial field: M/r³ (μ₀/4π factor). Axial=2×equatorial.
Magnetic moment M=m×2l (pole strength × effective length).
Field lines: from N to S outside; continuous loops (no monopoles).
Earth's field ≈25-65μT. Varies by location.
Geomagnetic reversal: poles flip every few hundred thousand years.
examples: Dip angle I=60°, B=50μT: H=50cos60°=25μT, V=50sin60°=43.3μT
Bar magnet M=1A·m², at axial point r=0.1m: B=μ₀/4π×2×1/0.001=2×10⁻³T=2mT
Equatorial point: B=μ₀/4π×M/r³=10⁻³T=1mT (half of axial at same distance)
Compass shows magnetic north; declination correction gives true geographic north
Dip at poles=90° means field is vertical; at equator≈0° means field is horizontal
mag-6.summary: Earth's geographic north=magnetic south (compass N points to geographic N approximately). Magnetic elements: declination (D), dip/inclination (I), horizontal component H=BcosI. Bar magnet: axial B=μ₀/4π×2M/r³, equatorial B=μ₀/4π×M/r³. Axial=2×equatorial field. Magnetic moment M=m×2l. Field lines from N to S (outside). Earth's field=25-65μT.

questions.question: A compass needle in Earth's field points toward:
questions.explanation: Compass points to magnetic north, which is close to (but not exactly) geographic north. Difference is the magnetic declination.

questions.question: Magnetic dip (inclination) at the equator is approximately:
questions.explanation: At the magnetic equator, Earth's field is horizontal → dip angle ≈ 0°. At poles: dip = 90° (field vertical).

questions.question: Horizontal component H = ?
questions.explanation: H = B cosI where B = total field, I = angle of dip (inclination). Vertical V = B sinI.

questions.question: Magnetic declination is:
options: Angle between geographic north and magnetic north
questions.explanation: Magnetic declination: angle between true geographic north and magnetic north at a location. Used for navigational corrections.

questions.question: At Earth's magnetic poles, dip angle is:
questions.explanation: At magnetic poles, Earth's field is vertical (pointing directly down/up) → dip = 90°.

questions.question: Axial field of bar magnet vs equatorial field at same distance:
questions.explanation: B_axial = μ₀/4π × 2M/r³. B_equatorial = μ₀/4π × M/r³. Axial = 2 × equatorial at same distance.

questions.question: Magnetic moment of a bar magnet M = ?
questions.explanation: Magnetic moment M = m × 2l where m = pole strength, 2l = magnetic length (distance between poles).

questions.question: Earth's geographic north pole is near the magnetic:
questions.explanation: Earth's geographic north is near the magnetic south pole — that is why compass needles (magnetic north poles) point toward geographic north.

questions.question: Magnetic field lines emerge from ___ and enter ___:
questions.explanation: Outside magnet: field lines emerge from N pole and enter S pole. Inside magnet: field lines run from S to N (continuous loops).

questions.question: tanI = V/H means:
options: tanI relates vertical to horizontal component
questions.explanation: tanI = V/H (V = vertical component, H = horizontal component). Also V=BsinI, H=BcosI, so V/H=sinI/cosI=tanI.

questions.question: Earth's magnetic field strength at surface is approximately:
questions.explanation: Earth's surface magnetic field ≈ 25-65 microtesla (μT) — very weak compared to a bar magnet (0.01-1T).

questions.question: Geomagnetic reversal means:
questions.explanation: Geomagnetic reversal: Earth's magnetic north and south poles completely swap. Evidence in rock magnetism. Last reversal ~780,000 years ago.

questions.question: Equatorial field of bar magnet: B = μ₀/4π × ?
questions.explanation: B_equatorial = (μ₀/4π) × M/r³. The equatorial field is directed antiparallel to the magnetic moment.

questions.question: If dip I=30°, B=50μT. Horizontal component H = ?
Magnetic dip is measured using:
questions.explanation: A dip circle (dip needle) measures the angle of dip (inclination) of Earth's magnetic field from the horizontal.

com-1.title: Communication Systems — Elements and Types
com-1.notes:
Communication is the transfer of information from one place to another. Modern communication uses electronics and electromagnetic waves.

BASIC ELEMENTS OF COMMUNICATION:
1. TRANSMITTER: Converts message into a suitable signal for transmission. Includes transducer (message→electrical signal), modulator, and amplifier.
2. CHANNEL (Medium): Path through which signal travels. Can be wired (cable, fibre optic) or wireless (atmosphere, space).
3. RECEIVER: Converts received signal back to original message. Includes demodulator, amplifier, and transducer.

NOISE: Unwanted signal added during transmission that degrades the information. Sources: thermal noise, electromagnetic interference.

SIGNAL TO NOISE RATIO (SNR): Ratio of signal power to noise power. Higher SNR = better quality.

TYPES OF COMMUNICATION:
Point-to-point: Between two specific points (telephone).
Broadcast: One transmitter, many receivers (radio, TV).

COMMUNICATION MODES:
Simplex: One direction only (radio broadcast, pager).
Half-duplex: Both directions, not simultaneously (walkie-talkie, CB radio).
Full-duplex: Both directions simultaneously (telephone, mobile phone).

BANDWIDTH:
Range of frequencies used by a signal. Larger bandwidth = more information capacity.
Audio signal bandwidth: ~20Hz to 20kHz.
Video bandwidth: ~4.2MHz.
TV channel: ~7MHz.

PROPAGATION OF EM WAVES:
Ground wave propagation: along Earth's surface (<2MHz, long waves).
Sky wave propagation: via ionosphere reflection (2MHz-30MHz, short waves).
Space wave propagation: line of sight (>30MHz, VHF/UHF/microwave).

IONOSPHERE: Layer of ionised atmosphere (80-400km altitude). Reflects radio waves below 30MHz.
points: Communication: transmitter → channel → receiver.
Noise: unwanted signal; SNR measures quality.
Simplex: one-way. Half-duplex: alternate two-way. Full-duplex: simultaneous two-way.
Bandwidth = frequency range used. More bandwidth = more data capacity.
Ground wave: low frequency (<2MHz), follows Earth's surface.
Sky wave: 2-30MHz, reflected by ionosphere, long-range.
Space wave: >30MHz, line-of-sight, for TV/mobile/satellite.
Ionosphere: 80-400km, reflects radio waves below 30MHz.
Transducer: converts one form of energy to another (mic, speaker).
Mobile phone: full-duplex, uses space wave propagation.
examples: Walkie-talkie = half-duplex (press to talk, release to listen)
FM radio = simplex broadcast (150kHz bandwidth, 88-108MHz)
AM radio sky wave: shortwave signals reflect off ionosphere → received thousands km away
Mobile phone: 700MHz-2.1GHz, space wave, full-duplex
Satellite communication: space wave at microwave frequencies
com-1.summary: Communication system: transmitter+channel+receiver. Noise degrades signal; SNR measures quality. Modes: simplex (one-way), half-duplex (alternate), full-duplex (simultaneous). Bandwidth = frequency range. Propagation: ground wave (<2MHz), sky wave (2-30MHz via ionosphere), space wave (>30MHz, line-of-sight). Ionosphere at 80-400km reflects HF waves.

questions.question: Basic elements of communication system are:
questions.explanation: Every communication system has three essential elements: Transmitter (sends), Channel (medium), and Receiver (receives).

questions.question: Simplex communication means:
questions.explanation: Simplex: information flows in one direction only. Example: radio broadcast (station transmits, you receive only).

questions.question: Walkie-talkie uses ___ communication:
questions.explanation: Walkie-talkie: half-duplex — press to talk, release to listen. Cannot transmit and receive simultaneously.

questions.question: Sky wave propagation uses:
questions.explanation: Sky wave propagation: radio waves reflect off the ionosphere (80-400km altitude) — enables long-distance HF communication.

questions.question: Mobile phones use ___ mode of communication:
questions.explanation: Mobile phones are full-duplex — you can speak and listen simultaneously (both directions at once).

questions.question: Bandwidth is:
questions.explanation: Bandwidth = highest frequency − lowest frequency of the signal band. Larger bandwidth → more information capacity.

questions.question: Ground wave propagation is suitable for frequencies:
questions.explanation: Ground waves travel along Earth's surface. Suitable for low frequencies (<2 MHz) — used by AM radio stations.

questions.question: Ionosphere is located at altitude:
questions.explanation: Ionosphere extends from about 80 km to 400 km altitude. Ionised by solar radiation — reflects radio waves 2-30 MHz.

questions.question: Space wave propagation is used for:
questions.explanation: Space wave (line-of-sight) propagation: used above 30MHz for TV (VHF/UHF), FM radio, mobile phones, microwave, satellite links.

questions.question: Noise in communication refers to:
questions.explanation: Noise: any unwanted electrical signal added to the desired signal during transmission — reduces signal quality.

questions.question: A transducer converts:
options: One form of energy to another
questions.explanation: Transducer: device that converts one form of energy to another. Microphone converts sound to electrical; speaker converts electrical to sound.

questions.question: SNR (Signal to Noise Ratio):
questions.explanation: SNR = Signal power / Noise power. Higher SNR = better signal quality = clearer communication.

questions.question: Sky wave propagation allows communication:
options: Over thousands of km by reflecting off ionosphere
questions.explanation: Sky wave (ionospheric) propagation reflects HF waves (2-30 MHz) off ionosphere, enabling communication over thousands of km.

questions.question: AM broadcast radio (550-1600 kHz) uses ___ propagation:
questions.explanation: AM radio at medium frequencies (550-1600 kHz) uses ground wave propagation during day and sky wave at night.

questions.question: Full-duplex communication example:
questions.explanation: Telephone: full-duplex — both parties speak and listen simultaneously without switching. Contrast with walkie-talkie (half-duplex).

com-2.title: Modulation — AM, FM and Digital
com-2.notes:
Modulation is the process of combining a low-frequency information (message) signal with a high-frequency carrier wave for efficient transmission.

WHY MODULATE?
1. Audio signals (20Hz-20kHz) have too short an antenna requirement at low frequency.
2. Multiple signals can be transmitted simultaneously (frequency division multiplexing).
3. Effective radiation from antenna requires antenna length ≈ λ/4. At 10kHz: λ/4=7500m (impractical). At 1MHz: λ/4=75m (practical).

AMPLITUDE MODULATION (AM):
The amplitude of the carrier wave is varied in proportion to the message signal.
Carrier: c(t) = A_c cos(2πf_c t)
Message: m(t) = A_m cos(2πf_m t)
AM wave: s(t) = A_c[1 + μcos(2πf_m t)]cos(2πf_c t)
where μ = A_m/A_c = modulation index (0 to 1 for no over-modulation)

AM SIDEBANDS:
AM wave contains: carrier (f_c), upper sideband (f_c + f_m), lower sideband (f_c - f_m)
Bandwidth of AM = 2f_m

FREQUENCY MODULATION (FM):
The frequency of the carrier is varied in proportion to the message signal.
FM wave: s(t) = A_c cos[2πf_c t + 2πk_f ∫m(t)dt]
FM bandwidth = 2(Δf + f_m) (Δf = frequency deviation)
Advantages over AM: less noise, better quality.
Disadvantage: requires more bandwidth.

DIGITAL MODULATION:
Message converted to binary (0s and 1s) first.
Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK), Frequency Shift Keying (FSK), Phase Shift Keying (PSK).

DEMODULATION: Recovering original message from modulated signal at receiver.
points: Modulation: combines message with carrier for long-distance transmission.
Need: audio (20Hz-20kHz) can't radiate efficiently; carrier at MHz can.
AM: carrier amplitude varies with message. μ=A_m/A_c (modulation index).
AM bandwidth=2f_m. Sidebands at f_c±f_m.
FM: carrier frequency varies with message.
FM bandwidth=2(Δf+f_m). Larger bandwidth than AM.
FM: less noise susceptibility, better audio quality than AM.
AM radio: 540-1600 kHz. FM radio: 88-108 MHz.
Digital: binary encoding + ASK/FSK/PSK modulation.
Demodulation: receiver recovers message from carrier.
examples: AM station at 1MHz, audio up to 5kHz: sidebands at 995kHz and 1005kHz, BW=10kHz
FM station at 98.3MHz, Δf=75kHz, f_m=15kHz: BW=2(75+15)=180kHz
Modulation index μ=0.5 means amplitude varies ±50% from carrier amplitude
Over-modulation μ>1: distortion occurs in AM
Antenna at 1MHz carrier: λ=300m, λ/4=75m — practical for AM tower
com-2.summary: Modulation mixes message signal with high-frequency carrier for practical transmission. AM: carrier amplitude varies, bandwidth=2f_m, sidebands at f_c±f_m. FM: carrier frequency varies, better noise immunity, larger bandwidth=2(Δf+f_m). AM radio 540-1600 kHz; FM 88-108 MHz. Digital modulation: ASK, FSK, PSK. Demodulation recovers original signal.

questions.question: Why is modulation necessary for transmission?
options: To make antenna size practical and allow multiple transmissions
questions.explanation: Modulation: (1) shifts frequency to band where antenna size is practical (λ/4 manageable); (2) allows FDM — multiple stations on different carriers.

questions.question: In AM, which property of carrier varies?
questions.explanation: Amplitude Modulation (AM): the amplitude of the carrier wave varies in proportion to the message signal.

questions.question: Modulation index μ in AM:
questions.explanation: Modulation index μ = A_m/A_c (ratio of message amplitude to carrier amplitude). Should be ≤1 to avoid distortion.

questions.question: AM bandwidth = ?
questions.explanation: AM bandwidth = 2f_m. Each AM signal occupies a band of 2×message frequency on either side of the carrier.

questions.question: FM has better noise performance than AM because:
options: Noise mainly affects amplitude, not frequency
questions.explanation: Most noise (atmospheric, electrical) affects signal amplitude. FM carries information in frequency variations → amplitude noise has little effect.

questions.question: FM radio band in India:
questions.explanation: FM radio in India operates in the 88-108 MHz frequency band (VHF band). AM radio is 540-1600 kHz.

questions.question: AM sidebands are at frequencies:
questions.explanation: AM wave contains three components: carrier (f_c), upper sideband (f_c+f_m), and lower sideband (f_c-f_m).

questions.question: In FM, carrier frequency deviation Δf is proportional to:
questions.explanation: In FM, the frequency deviation (how much carrier frequency changes) is proportional to the message signal amplitude.

questions.question: Over-modulation in AM (μ>1) causes:
questions.explanation: Over-modulation (μ>1): carrier amplitude goes negative → envelope folds → distortion in demodulated message.

questions.question: Demodulation is:
options: Recovering original message from modulated signal
questions.explanation: Demodulation: the reverse of modulation — extracting the original message signal from the received modulated carrier at the receiver.

questions.question: Antenna length ≈ λ/4 for efficient radiation. At f=1MHz, λ/4 = ?
questions.explanation: λ=c/f=3×10⁸/10⁶=300m. λ/4=75m. At audio frequency 10kHz: λ/4=7500m (impractical — hence need modulation)

questions.question: ASK, FSK, PSK are types of:
questions.explanation: ASK (Amplitude Shift Keying), FSK (Frequency Shift Keying), PSK (Phase Shift Keying) are digital modulation techniques.

questions.question: FM bandwidth = ?
questions.explanation: Carson's Rule: FM bandwidth ≈ 2(Δf+f_m) where Δf=frequency deviation, f_m=message bandwidth.

questions.question: AM radio frequency band:
questions.explanation: AM broadcasting uses the Medium Wave (MW) band: 540-1600 kHz in India.

questions.question: Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) allows:
options: Multiple users on same time slot
Multiple users on different frequency bands simultaneously
questions.explanation: FDM: different signals are transmitted on different carrier frequencies simultaneously — each station gets its own frequency band.

com-3.title: Internet, Mobile and Satellite Communication
com-3.notes:
Modern communication systems include the internet, mobile networks, and satellite systems.

INTERNET:
Global network of interconnected computers. Uses TCP/IP protocol.
Transmission via: optical fibre (undersea cables), radio waves, satellite.
Worldwide web (WWW): system of hyperlinked documents on internet.
Email, VoIP, streaming — all use internet infrastructure.

MOBILE COMMUNICATION:
Cellular concept: geographical area divided into cells, each with base station (BTS).
Frequency reuse: same frequencies used in non-adjacent cells.
Handoff/handover: call transfers to new cell as user moves.

GENERATIONS:
1G: Analog voice (1980s). AMPS.
2G: Digital voice, SMS. GSM. (1990s).
3G: Mobile internet, video calling. CDMA/WCDMA. (~2000s). Speed: 2Mbps.
4G/LTE: High speed internet, HD video. (~2010s). Speed: 100Mbps.
5G: Ultra-fast, low latency, IoT support. (2020s). Speed: 10Gbps.

FREQUENCY BANDS used:
2G/3G: 850/900/1800/1900 MHz.
4G: 700 MHz - 2.1 GHz.
5G: sub-6GHz and millimetre wave (24-100 GHz).

SATELLITE COMMUNICATION:
SATELLITE ORBITS:
LEO (Low Earth Orbit): 160-2000 km. Low latency. Starlink.
MEO (Medium): 2000-35,786 km. GPS satellites (~20,200km).
GEO (Geostationary): 35,786 km. Fixed in sky. INSAT, GSAT series.

APPLICATIONS:
DTH (Direct-to-Home) TV, Internet (VSAT), GPS navigation, Weather forecasting, Military reconnaissance.

OPTICAL FIBRE:
Uses Total Internal Reflection.
Bandwidth: terabits/second.
Low loss, immune to electromagnetic interference.
Used in: broadband internet, telephone trunk lines, medical endoscopes.
points: Internet: global TCP/IP network. Optical fibre, radio, satellite infrastructure.
Mobile: cellular concept with frequency reuse. Handoff as user moves between cells.
1G→2G(GSM)→3G(CDMA)→4G(LTE,100Mbps)→5G(10Gbps).
GEO (geostationary 36,000km): TV, VSAT. MEO: GPS. LEO: Starlink.
INSAT/GSAT: India's geostationary satellites for communication.
Optical fibre: TIR principle, terabit bandwidth, low loss.
5G: sub-6GHz and mmWave bands; supports IoT, autonomous vehicles.
DTH: direct satellite to home dish; bypasses cable.
GPS: 24-31 MEO satellites; triangulation gives position.
Cellular networks: BTS serves each cell; PSTN connects calls.
examples: 4G LTE: browsing at 50Mbps on phone — space wave propagation at 1.8GHz
INSAT-3D: geostationary at 82°E, provides DTH and weather data for India
GPS: 4+ satellites triangulate position to <10m accuracy
Optical fibre: submarine cable from India to Europe carries terabits/second
Starlink LEO: 550km orbit, latency ~20ms vs GEO ~600ms
com-3.summary: Internet uses TCP/IP over optical fibre/radio/satellite. Mobile networks: cellular (cells+frequency reuse). Generations 1G→5G (speeds up to 10Gbps). Satellite orbits: LEO (Starlink), MEO (GPS), GEO (INSAT, 36000km, DTH/weather). Optical fibre: TIR, terabit capacity, low loss. 5G supports IoT and autonomous vehicles.

questions.question: Geostationary satellites orbit at height:
questions.explanation: Geostationary orbit (GEO) is at ~35,786 km above equator — at this height, orbital period = 24h = Earth's rotation period.

questions.question: GPS satellites are in ___ orbit:
questions.explanation: GPS satellites orbit in Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) at ~20,200 km. They provide global navigation coverage.

questions.question: Cellular mobile networks use concept of:
questions.explanation: Cellular: area divided into cells, each with a base station. Same frequencies reused in non-adjacent cells → efficient spectrum use.

questions.question: 4G/LTE networks offer speeds up to approximately:
questions.explanation: 4G LTE: theoretical peak ~150-300 Mbps, typically ~100 Mbps. 5G offers up to 10 Gbps.

questions.question: Optical fibre communication uses:
questions.explanation: Optical fibre guides light using Total Internal Reflection (TIR) — light bounces off fibre walls with nearly zero loss.

questions.question: INSAT series satellites are operated by:
questions.explanation: INSAT (Indian National Satellite System) and GSAT series are operated by ISRO for India's communication and weather needs.

questions.question: 5G technology primarily features:
options: Ultra-high speed + low latency + massive IoT connectivity
questions.explanation: 5G offers: ultra-high speed (up to 10 Gbps), very low latency (<1ms), and massive device connectivity for IoT applications.

questions.question: Handoff (handover) in mobile networks refers to:
options: Transferring call to new cell as user moves
questions.explanation: Handoff/handover: seamless transfer of an ongoing call/data session from one base station (cell) to another as user moves.

questions.question: Starlink satellites are in:
questions.explanation: Starlink satellites are in Low Earth Orbit (~550 km altitude) — providing low-latency (~20ms) internet globally.

questions.question: DTH (Direct-to-Home) TV uses:
questions.explanation: DTH: geostationary satellites beam digital TV signals directly to small dish antennas at homes — no cable network needed.

questions.question: Latency of geostationary satellite link is approximately:
questions.explanation: GEO latency: signal travels 36,000km up + 36,000km back = 72,000km at speed of light → ~240ms one way, ~480-600ms round trip.

questions.question: The protocol used for internet communication is:
questions.explanation: Internet uses TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) — the fundamental communication protocol suite.

questions.question: 2G mobile technology introduced:
questions.explanation: 2G (GSM): first digital mobile generation — enabled digital voice calls and SMS text messaging.

questions.question: Optical fibre advantage over copper wire:
options: Higher bandwidth and immunity to electromagnetic interference
questions.explanation: Optical fibre: terabit bandwidth (vs Gbps for copper), immune to EMI, low signal loss, secure (no radiation).

questions.question: Frequency reuse in cellular networks allows:
options: All cells to use different frequencies (wasteful)
Same frequencies in distant cells (efficient spectrum use)
questions.explanation: Frequency reuse: same frequency bands assigned to cells far enough apart → minimal interference + efficient use of limited radio spectrum.

com-4.title: Digital Communication and Data Transmission
com-4.notes:
Digital communication converts information to binary (0s and 1s) before transmission.

ANALOG vs DIGITAL:
Analog: continuous signal varying smoothly (voice, music in original form).
Digital: discrete binary values (0 and 1). Advantages: less noise susceptibility, easier to process, store, and reproduce.

A-TO-D CONVERSION (Analog to Digital):
1. Sampling: measuring analog signal at regular intervals. Nyquist theorem: sampling rate ≥ 2f_max (twice highest frequency).
2. Quantisation: assigning discrete value to each sample.
3. Encoding: converting to binary numbers.

DATA RATE:
Bit rate (bps) = sampling rate × bits per sample.
Audio CD: 44,100 samples/s × 16 bits × 2 channels = 1.41 Mbps.

MULTIPLEXING:
Combining multiple signals on one channel.
FDM: Frequency Division Multiplexing — different frequency bands.
TDM: Time Division Multiplexing — different time slots.
CDM: Code Division Multiplexing — different codes (used in 3G).

ERROR DETECTION AND CORRECTION:
Parity bits, CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check), Hamming codes.

NETWORKING CONCEPTS:
LAN (Local Area Network): small area (building/campus). High speed.
WAN (Wide Area Network): large geographic area. Internet is WAN.
Protocol: set of rules for communication (TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP).
MAC address: hardware address of network device.
IP address: logical address (IPv4: 32-bit, IPv6: 128-bit).

WIRELESS STANDARDS:
WiFi (IEEE 802.11): LAN wireless. Frequencies 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHz.
Bluetooth: short range (~10m), 2.4GHz. Personal Area Network.
ZigBee: very low power, IoT devices.
NFC: Near Field Communication (<10cm). Contactless payments.
points: Digital: binary (0,1). Advantages: noise resistance, easy storage, processing.
A-to-D conversion: sampling → quantisation → encoding.
Nyquist theorem: sampling rate ≥ 2×highest frequency.
FDM: different frequencies. TDM: different time slots. CDM: different codes.
Bit rate = sampling rate × bits per sample.
LAN: local area. WAN: wide area. Internet = largest WAN.
WiFi: 2.4/5GHz wireless LAN. Bluetooth: short range 2.4GHz.
Protocol: rules for communication (TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP).
IP address: logical address. IPv4=32-bit; IPv6=128-bit.
NFC: <10cm contactless; Zigbee: IoT low power devices.
examples: Voice call: 8000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 kbps (standard telephone quality)
Audio CD: 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1.411 Mbps per stereo audio stream
WiFi 2.4GHz: up to 600Mbps (802.11n). 5GHz: up to several Gbps (802.11ac/ax)
Bluetooth: connects phone to headset over ~10m, 2.4GHz, ~3Mbps
IPv4: 192.168.1.1 (32 bits, ~4 billion addresses). IPv6: 128 bits (~3.4×10³⁸ addresses)
com-4.summary: Digital communication: analog→digital via sampling (Nyquist: f_s≥2f_max), quantisation, encoding. Bit rate=sampling×bits. Multiplexing: FDM/TDM/CDM combine channels. Networks: LAN (local), WAN (wide/internet), WiFi (2.4/5GHz), Bluetooth (10m). Protocols TCP/IP govern internet. IPv4=32-bit; IPv6=128-bit addresses. NFC for contactless payments.

questions.question: Nyquist sampling theorem requires sampling rate ≥ ?
questions.explanation: Nyquist theorem: to reconstruct analog signal without distortion, sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency (f_s ≥ 2f_max).

questions.question: FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing) assigns:
questions.explanation: FDM: each user/channel is assigned a different frequency band. All transmit simultaneously on different frequencies.

questions.question: Advantages of digital over analog communication:
options: More noise resistant, easier to store and reproduce
questions.explanation: Digital: binary signals are more noise-resistant, easier to store, process, copy without degradation, and error-correct.

questions.question: A-to-D conversion steps in order:
questions.explanation: Analog-to-Digital: 1. Sampling (measure at intervals), 2. Quantisation (assign discrete level), 3. Encoding (convert to binary).

questions.question: WiFi operates at which frequencies?
questions.explanation: WiFi (IEEE 802.11) uses 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and newer WiFi 6E uses 6 GHz unlicensed bands.

questions.question: Bluetooth is used for:
questions.explanation: Bluetooth: short-range (~10m) wireless communication at 2.4 GHz for Personal Area Networks (headsets, keyboards, speakers).

questions.question: TDM (Time Division Multiplexing) assigns:
questions.explanation: TDM: each user/channel gets a specific time slot in a repeating frame. All share same frequency but at different times.

questions.question: LAN stands for:
questions.explanation: LAN = Local Area Network — high-speed network within a limited area (building, campus). Connects computers locally.

questions.question: IPv4 address has ___ bits:
questions.explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses → ~4.3 billion unique addresses (e.g., 192.168.1.1). IPv6 uses 128-bit → virtually unlimited.

questions.question: NFC (Near Field Communication) operates at range:
questions.explanation: NFC works at very short range (<10 cm) at 13.56 MHz. Used for contactless payments (PhonePe, Google Pay), smart cards.

questions.question: Bit rate formula:
questions.explanation: Bit rate (bps) = Sampling rate (samples/s) × Bits per sample (bits/sample).

questions.question: Internet is an example of:
questions.explanation: Internet = largest Wide Area Network (WAN) — spanning the entire globe, connecting millions of smaller networks.

questions.question: Zigbee is used for:
questions.explanation: Zigbee: low-power, low-data-rate wireless protocol (2.4 GHz) designed for IoT applications like smart home sensors, meters.

questions.question: Error detection in digital communication uses:
questions.explanation: Error detection: parity bits (simple), CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check), and Hamming codes detect (and sometimes correct) transmission errors.

questions.question: Sampling an audio signal at 8000 samples/sec with 8 bits each gives bit rate:
questions.explanation: Bit rate = 8000 × 8 = 64,000 bps = 64 kbps. This is the standard bit rate for telephone voice quality.
